What is Testing? Why Testing? Principles Activities & Roles Skills & Practices

Chapter 1

Fundamentals of Testing

Software testing is a set of activities to discover defects and evaluate the quality of software work products — not only running code and checking results, but planning, analysis, design and reporting too. This chapter lays the groundwork: what testing is, why it exists alongside debugging and quality assurance, the seven principles every tester relies on, and the roles and skills that make testing effective.

  • coverageThe degree to which specified coverage items are exercised by a test suite, expressed as a percentage.Synonyms: test coverage
  • debuggingThe process of finding, analyzing and removing the causes of failures in a component or system.
  • defectAn imperfection or deficiency in a work product where it does not meet its requirements or specifications or impairs its intended use.Synonyms: bug, fault, flaw
  • errorA human action that results in a defect.Synonyms: mistake
  • failureAn event in which a component or system does not meet its requirements within specified limits during its execution.Synonyms: malfunction
  • qualityThe degree to which a work product satisfies stated and implied requirements.
  • quality assuranceActivities focused on providing confidence that quality requirements will be fulfilled.Abbreviation: QA
  • root causeA source of a defect such that if it is removed, the occurrence of the defect type is decreased or removed.
  • test analysisThe activity that identifies test conditions by analyzing the test basis.
  • test basisThe body of knowledge used as the basis for test analysis and test design.
  • test caseA set of preconditions, inputs, actions (where applicable), expected results and postconditions, developed based on test conditions.
  • test completionThe activity that makes testware available for later use, leaves test environments in a satisfactory condition and communicates the results of testing to relevant stakeholders.Synonyms: test closure
  • test conditionA testable aspect of a component or system that is intended to be tested.Synonyms: test situation, test requirement, test idea
  • test controlThe activity that develops and applies corrective actions to get a test project on track when it deviates from what was planned.
  • test dataData needed for test execution.Synonyms: test dataset
  • test designThe activity that derives and specifies test cases from test conditions.
  • test executionThe activity that runs a test on a component or system producing actual results.
  • test implementationThe activity that prepares the testware needed for test execution.
  • test monitoringThe activity that checks the status of testing activities, identifies any variances from planned or expected, and reports status to stakeholders.
  • test objectThe work product to be tested.
  • test objectiveThe purpose for testing.Synonyms: test goal
  • test planningThe activity of establishing or updating a test plan.
  • test procedureA sequence of test cases in execution order and any associated actions that may be required to set up the initial preconditions and any wrap-up activities after execution.
  • test processThe set of interrelated activities comprising test planning, test monitoring, test control, test analysis, test design, test implementation, test execution, and test completion.
  • test resultThe consequence/outcome of the execution of a test.Synonyms: outcome, test outcome, result
  • testingThe process within the software development lifecycle that evaluates the quality of a component or system and related work products.
  • testwareWork products produced during the test process for use in planning, designing, executing, evaluating and reporting on testing.
  • traceabilityThe ability to establish explicit relationships between related work products or items within work products.
  • verificationThe process of confirming that a work product fulfills its specification.
  • validationConfirmation by examination that a work product matches a stakeholder's needs.

1.1

What is Testing?

Software testing assesses software quality and helps reduce the risk of failure in operation. Two common misconceptions get in the way: that testing is only about executing tests, and that it only verifies a system against its specification. In fact testing also involves validation — checking that the system meets the real needs of users and other stakeholders in its operational environment. Testing can be dynamic (the software is executed) or static (it is not — reviews and static analysis, see chapter 3).

1.1.1 Test Objectives K1K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.

Evaluate work products

Requirements, user stories, designs, and code.

Cause failures, find defects

The most direct way to surface problems before users do.

Ensure required coverage

Of a test object, against a defined coverage criterion.

Reduce risk

Lower the risk level of inadequate software quality.

Verify requirements

Confirm specified requirements have been fulfilled.

Verify compliance

With contractual, legal and regulatory requirements.

Inform decisions

Give stakeholders information to decide with confidence.

Build confidence

In the quality of the test object.

Validate fitness for use

Confirm the test object works as stakeholders expect.

Objectives shift with context: the work product tested, the test level, risk, the SDLC in use, and business factors like time to market.

1.1.2 Testing and Debugging K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Testing and debugging are separate activities. Dynamic testing triggers a failure; debugging then finds and removes the defect behind it. When static testing is used, it finds the defect directly — no failure ever occurs, so there is nothing to reproduce.

01Reproduce the failureConfirm it happens reliably
→
02DiagnoseFind the defect causing it
→
03Fix the defectA non-testing activity
Note

Static testing skips straight to fixing: since it never executes the software, there is no failure to reproduce or diagnose — the defect is already in view.

Afterwards, not part of it

Debugging ends once the defect is fixed. Confirmation testing — ideally by the same person who ran the original test — is a separate, subsequent testing activity that checks whether the fix actually resolved the problem. Regression testing may follow it, to check the fix didn’t break anything else (see section 2.2.3).

1.2

Why is Testing Necessary?

Testing is a form of quality control: it helps achieve agreed test objectives within scope, time, quality and budget constraints — and every stakeholder, not only the test team, can contribute to that.

1.2.1 Testing’s Contributions to Success K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Cost-effective defect detection

Found defects can then be debugged, indirectly raising quality.

Quality evaluation across the SDLC

Feeds decisions such as whether to release.

Indirect user representation

Testers carry users’ needs into the development process.

Testing may also be required to meet contractual, legal or regulatory obligations.

1.2.2 Testing and Quality Assurance (QA) K1K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.

AspectTestingQuality Assurance
OrientationProduct-oriented, correctiveProcess-oriented, preventive
LogicFinds defects directly; removing them is debugging, a separate activityGood process → good product
ScopeA major form of quality controlApplies to development & testing; everyone’s responsibility
Use of resultsFix defectsFeedback on how well processes perform

1.2.3 Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

HumanErrorA mistake — time pressure, complexity, fatigue…
→
In code / docsDefectFault or bug left behind by the error
→
If executedFailureThe system does the wrong thing
Not every defect fails

Some defects always cause a failure when executed, some only in specific circumstances, and some never do. Failures can also come from environmental conditions alone (e.g. radiation flipping a bit in firmware) — with no defect involved at all.

Root cause

The fundamental reason a problem occurred. Root cause analysis, done after a failure or defect appears, aims to remove that cause so similar problems don’t recur.

1.3

Testing Principles K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Seven general guidelines apply across all testing, regardless of context.

  1. 1

    Testing shows the presence, not the absence, of defects

    It can prove defects exist, never that the object is defect-free.

  2. 2

    Exhaustive testing is impossible

    Except in trivial cases — use techniques, prioritization and risk to focus effort instead.

  3. 3

    Early testing saves time and money

    Defects removed early don’t cascade into later work products. Start static and dynamic testing as soon as possible.

  4. 4

    Defects cluster together

    A Pareto effect — a small number of components usually contain most defects or cause most failures.

  5. 5

    Tests wear out

    Repeating the same tests stops finding new defects — unless the point is automated regression testing.

  6. 6

    Testing is context dependent

    There is no single universal approach; testing is done differently in different contexts.

  7. 7

    Absence-of-defects is a fallacy

    A system can pass every specified test and still fail to meet real user needs and business goals — validation matters as much as verification.

1.4

Test Activities, Testware and Test Roles

Testing is context dependent, but a common set of activities — the test process — recurs across projects, tailored to the situation as part of test planning.

1.4.1 Test Activities and Tasks K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

PlanningDefine objectives & approach
→
Monitoring & controlTrack progress, steer the process
→
AnalysisWhat to test — test conditions
→
DesignHow to test — test cases
→
ImplementationBuild procedures & scripts
→
ExecutionRun tests, log results
→
CompletionReport, capture lessons learned

1.4.2 Test Process in Context K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

How this process is tailored depends on context: the SDLC in use, product and project risks, organizational factors (structure, policies, practices), and tool availability. Together these shape the test strategy, techniques, automation level, required coverage and reporting detail.

1.4.3 Testware K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

ActivityTypical work products
PlanningTest plan, schedule, risk register, entry & exit criteria
Monitoring & controlTest progress reports, control directives, risk information
AnalysisPrioritized test conditions, defect reports on the test basis
DesignTest cases, test charters, coverage items, data & environment requirements
ImplementationTest procedures, scripts, suites, data, execution schedule, stubs/drivers
ExecutionTest logs, defect reports
CompletionTest completion report, lessons learned, change requests

1.4.4 Traceability between the Test Basis and Testware K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Linking test basis elements to testware, results and defects keeps monitoring and control effective. Good traceability:

Verifies requirement coverage by tracing test cases back to requirements.

Evaluates residual risk by tracing test results back to risks.

Speeds up impact analysis when something changes.

Supports audits, IT governance, and clearer progress & completion reports.

1.4.5 Roles in Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Test management

Owns the test process

Overall responsibility for the test process, team and leadership: planning, monitoring, control and completion. Often shared with the Agile team.

Testing

Owns the engineering

The technical side: test analysis, design, implementation and execution.

One person can hold both roles at once; who does depends on project, product and organizational context.

1.5

Essential Skills and Good Practices in Testing

1.5.1 Generic Skills Required for Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Testing knowledge

E.g. applying test techniques, to raise the effectiveness of testing.

Thoroughness & care

Carefulness, curiosity, attention to detail, being methodical — to catch the defects that are hard to find.

Communication & teamwork

Active listening, reporting and discussing defects constructively.

Analytical & critical thinking

Plus creativity, to raise the effectiveness of testing.

Technical knowledge

Using the right tools raises testing efficiency.

Domain knowledge

Understanding and communicating with end users and the business.

People factor

Testers are often the bearers of bad news, and confirmation bias makes disagreeable information hard to accept. Communicating defects and failures constructively is a core skill, not a soft extra.

1.5.2 Whole Team Approach K1K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.

Borrowed from Extreme Programming: any team member with the right knowledge can perform any task, and everyone owns quality. Co-location improves communication and lets the team’s varied skills reinforce each other — testers help write acceptance tests, developers help shape test strategy and automation.

Not always the right fit

In safety-critical contexts, a high level of test independence may be needed instead.

1.5.3 Independence of Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Independence reduces the effect of the author’s cognitive biases — but it’s not a substitute for familiarity; developers still catch many defects in their own code efficiently.

NoneAuthorTests their own work
SomePeers, same teame.g. another developer
HighOutside the teamWithin the organization
Very highOutside the organizationFully independent testers

Most projects mix levels: developers handle component and component-integration testing, a test team handles system and system-integration testing, and business representatives handle acceptance testing. The trade-off: more independence can mean less collaboration and a risk of being seen as a bottleneck.

SDLC & Testing Test Levels & Types Maintenance

Chapter 2

Testing Throughout the Software Development Lifecycle

Testing does not stand apart from development — it has to fit whichever SDLC model a project follows, from sequential waterfall to fast-moving Agile iterations. This chapter covers how the lifecycle shapes testing, the five test levels and four test types used to organize test activities, and how confirmation, regression and maintenance testing keep a system trustworthy after it ships.

  • acceptance testingA test level that focuses on determining whether to accept the system.
  • black-box testingTesting based on an analysis of the specification of the component or system.Synonyms: specification-based testing
  • component integration testingThe integration testing of components.Synonyms: module integration testing
  • component testingA test level that focuses on individual hardware or software components.Synonyms: module testing
  • confirmation testingA type of change-related testing performed after fixing a defect to confirm that a failure caused by that defect does not reoccur.Synonyms: retesting
  • functional testingTesting performed to evaluate if a component or system satisfies functional requirements.
  • integration testingA test level that focuses on interactions between components or systems.
  • maintenance testingA test type that evaluates the effect of changes made to an operational system or its environment.
  • non-functional testingA test type to evaluate that a component or system complies with non-functional requirements.
  • regression testingA type of change-related testing to detect whether defects have been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas of the software.
  • shift leftA test approach to perform testing and quality assurance activities as early as possible in the software development lifecycle.
  • system integration testingA test level that focuses on the integration of systems.
  • system testingA test level that focuses on verifying that a system as a whole meets specified requirements.
  • test levelA specific instantiation of a test process.Synonyms: test stage
  • test objectThe work product to be tested.
  • test typeA group of test activities based on specific test objectives aimed at specific characteristics of a component or system.
  • white-box testingTesting based on an analysis of the internal structure of the component or system.Synonyms: clear-box testing, code-based testing, glass-box testing, logic-coverage testing, logic-driven testing, structural testing, structure-based testing

2.1

Testing in the Context of a Software Development Lifecycle

An SDLC model defines how development phases relate to each other, logically and chronologically.

Sequential

Waterfall, V-model. Dynamic testing usually waits for later phases.

Iterative

Spiral, prototyping. Each iteration can carry both static and dynamic testing.

Incremental

e.g. Unified Process. Builds the system in growing slices.

2.1.1 Impact of the SDLC on Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

The chosen SDLC affects the scope and timing of test activities, the level of test documentation detail, the choice of techniques, the extent of automation, and the tester’s role. Agile projects favor lightweight documentation, heavy test automation for fast regression, and experience-based techniques for manual testing.

2.1.2 SDLC and Good Testing Practices K1K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.

Every development activity has a corresponding test activity — quality control touches everything.

Each test level has its own objectives, so testing stays comprehensive without being redundant.

Test analysis and design for a level start alongside the matching development phase (early testing).

Testers review work products as soon as drafts exist — supporting shift left.

2.1.3 Testing as a Driver for Software Development K1K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.

TDD, ATDD and BDD all define tests before the code, applying early testing and shift left.

ApproachTests come fromDistinguishing trait
TDDThe next small piece of behaviorWrite test → write code to pass it → refactor
ATDDAcceptance criteria, as part of system designWhole team defines tests before the feature is built
BDDDesired behavior in natural languageGiven/When/Then, auto-translated into executable tests

2.1.4 DevOps and Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

DevOps bridges development (including testing) and operations to ship high-quality code faster through CI/CD.

CodeSubmit with component tests
→
CIBuild, static analysis, auto tests
→
CDAutomated regression, staged release
→
OperateMonitor real usage
↺
FeedbackFast, back into Code
Benefits

Fast feedback, shift left via CI, stable automated environments, better non-functional visibility, less repetitive manual testing, lower regression risk.

Risks

The pipeline itself must be built and kept running; CI/CD tooling needs upkeep; automation needs real investment. Manual, user-perspective testing is still needed.

2.1.5 Shift Left K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Shift left means testing earlier in the SDLC — without neglecting testing later on.

Review specifications from a tester’s viewpoint to catch ambiguity early.

Write tests before the code; run code in a test harness as it’s built.

Use CI/CD for fast feedback and automated component tests.

Run static analysis before dynamic testing, or as part of automation.

2.1.6 Retrospectives and Process Improvement K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Held at project or iteration milestones, retrospectives ask: what worked, what didn’t, and how to improve? Results feed the test completion report and drive continuous improvement — better test effectiveness, higher-quality testware, stronger team bonds, and better dev–test cooperation.

2.2

Test Levels and Test Types

Test levels are groups of activities organized and managed together, each an instance of the test process at a given development phase. Test types are activities tied to specific quality characteristics, applicable across most levels.

2.2.1 Test Levels K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

ComponentUnit testing, in isolation
→
Component integrationInterfaces between components
→
SystemWhole system, end-to-end
→
System integrationInterfaces to other systems
→
AcceptanceReady for deployment?

Levels are told apart by test object, objectives, test basis, typical defects, and who’s responsible — not by a fixed order in time; in iterative models they can overlap.

2.2.2 Test Types K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Functional

“What” the object should do — completeness, correctness, appropriateness.

Non-functional

“How well” it behaves — the ISO/IEC 25010 quality characteristics.

Black-box

Specification-based; derived without looking at internal structure.

White-box

Structure-based; derived from code, architecture or data flow.

  • performance efficiency
  • compatibility
  • usability (interaction capability)
  • reliability
  • security
  • maintainability
  • portability (flexibility)
  • safety

2.2.3 Confirmation Testing and Regression Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

AspectConfirmation testingRegression testing
ChecksThe original defect is actually fixedNo new failures were introduced elsewhere
HowRe-run previously failing tests, or add new onesRun a broader suite, ideally automated
Automation fitOften manual, tied to the specific fixStrong candidate — suite grows every release
Before regression testing

Run an impact analysis first to scope how far a change could reach — the same component, other components, or connected systems.

2.3

Maintenance Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Testing continues after release. Maintenance can be corrective, adaptive, or aimed at improving performance or maintainability, and covers both planned releases and unplanned hot fixes. An impact analysis beforehand helps decide whether — and how safely — to make the change.

Modifications

Planned enhancements, corrective changes, hot fixes.

Upgrades & migrations

Platform changes, or data migration into the maintained system.

Retirement

End of life — may need archiving, restore and retrieval testing.

Scope depends on the degree of risk in the change, the size of the existing system, and the size of the change itself.

Static Testing Basics Feedback & Reviews

Chapter 3

Static Testing

Static testing examines a work product without executing it — through manual review or a tool. Because it can be applied to requirements, designs and other non-executable artifacts as soon as a draft exists, it is one of the most direct ways to put the “early testing” principle into practice. This chapter covers what static testing can examine, how it complements dynamic testing, and the structured review process — roles, types and success factors — that makes feedback effective.

  • anomalyA condition that deviates from expectation.
  • dynamic testingA test approach that involves test execution of a test item.
  • formal reviewA review that follows a defined process with a formally documented output.
  • informal reviewA type of review that does not follow a defined process and has no formally documented output.
  • inspectionA type of formal review that uses defined team roles and measurement to identify defects in a work product, and improve the review process and the software development process.
  • reviewA type of static testing in which the quality of a work product or process is evaluated by individuals.
  • static analysisThe automated process of evaluating a component or system without executing it, based on its form, structure, content, or documentation.
  • static testingA test approach that does not involve the execution of a test item.
  • technical reviewA formal review by technical experts that examine the quality of a work product and identify discrepancies from specifications and standards.
  • walkthroughA type of formal review in which an author leads members of the review through a work product and the members ask questions and make comments.Synonyms: structured walkthrough

3.1

Static Testing Basics

In static testing, the software under test does not run. Code, requirements, architecture specs or other work products are evaluated by manual examination (reviews) or with a tool (static analysis) — assessing readability, completeness, correctness, testability and consistency. It supports both verification and validation.

3.1.1 Work Products Examinable by Static Testing K1K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.

Almost anything readable can be reviewed: requirement specifications, source code, test plans and cases, backlog items, contracts, models. Static analysis needs a formal structure to check against (code, models, formally-specified text). Third-party executable code, for legal or practical reasons, generally isn’t appropriate for either.

3.1.2 Value of Static Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Finds defects at the earliest possible SDLC phase — the early-testing principle in action.

Catches defects dynamic testing structurally can’t: unreachable code, mismatched design patterns, issues in non-executable work products.

Builds confidence in a work product and verifies it reflects stakeholders’ actual needs.

Creates shared understanding and improves communication between stakeholders, early.

Lowers overall project cost: reviews take effort, but far less than fixing the same defects later.

Static analysis catches certain code defects more efficiently than dynamic testing — fewer defects, less overall development effort.

3.1.3 Differences between Static Testing and Dynamic Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

AspectStatic testingDynamic testing
ExecutionNot requiredRequired
Finds defects byDirect examinationTriggering a failure, then analysis
ReachesRarely-executed or hard-to-reach code pathsOnly what actually runs
Applies toExecutable & non-executable work productsExecutable work products only
MeasuresQuality independent of execution (e.g. maintainability)Quality dependent on execution (e.g. performance)

Typical static-testing catches: requirement inconsistencies and ambiguities, poor database or module design, undeclared variables and dead code, naming-standard deviations, mismatched interface parameters, certain security flaws (e.g. buffer overflows), and coverage gaps in the test basis.

3.2

Feedback and Review Process

3.2.1 Benefits of Early and Frequent Stakeholder Feedback K1K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.

Little stakeholder involvement risks building the wrong thing — costly rework, missed deadlines, even project failure. Frequent feedback prevents requirement misunderstandings, keeps changes understood early, and helps the team focus on what delivers the most value and reduces the most risk.

3.2.2 Review Process Activities K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

→

→

A large work product may need several passes through this process to be fully covered.

3.2.3 Roles and Responsibilities in Reviews K1K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.

Manager

Decides what’s reviewed and provides resources.

The right level of formality depends on the SDLC, process maturity, criticality, regulatory needs, and whether an audit trail is required — the same work product can go through more than one type.

3.2.5 Success Factors for Reviews K1K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.

Clear objectives and measurable exit criteria — never evaluating participants.

The right review type for the objective, work product and context.

Small chunks, so concentration doesn’t lapse.

Feedback that actually reaches stakeholders and authors.

Enough preparation time for participants.

Reviews made part of the organization’s culture.

Adequate training so everyone knows their role.

Meetings that are properly facilitated.

Techniques Overview Black-Box White-Box Experience-Based Collaboration-Based

Chapter 4

Test Analysis and Design

This is the largest chapter in the syllabus for a reason: test techniques are how testers turn a test basis into a small, targeted, well-justified set of test cases rather than a guess. It covers three families — black-box, white-box, and experience-based — plus the collaboration-based approaches (user stories, acceptance criteria, ATDD) that turn requirements discovery itself into a testing activity.

  • acceptance criteriaThe criteria that a work product must satisfy to be accepted by the stakeholders.
  • acceptance test-driven developmentA collaboration-based test-first approach that defines acceptance tests in the stakeholders' domain language.Abbreviation: ATDD
  • black-box test techniqueA test technique based on the specification of a component or system.Synonyms: black-box test design technique, specification-based test technique
  • boundary value analysisA black-box test technique in which test cases are designed based on boundary values.Abbreviation: BVA
  • branch coverageThe coverage of branches in a control flow graph.
  • checklist-based testingAn experience-based test technique in which test cases are designed to exercise the items of a checklist.
  • collaboration-based test approachAn approach to testing that focuses on defect avoidance by collaborating among stakeholders.
  • coverageThe degree to which specified coverage items are exercised by a test suite, expressed as a percentage.Synonyms: test coverage
  • coverage itemAn attribute or combination of attributes derived from one or more test conditions by using a test technique.
  • decision table testingA black-box test technique in which the test conditions are the combinations of conditions and the resulting actions shown in a decision table.Abbreviation: DTT
  • equivalence partitioningA black-box test technique in which test conditions are equivalence partitions exercised by one representative member of each partition.Abbreviation: EPSynonyms: partition testing
  • error guessingA test technique in which the test conditions are based on the tester's knowledge of past failures or failure modes.
  • experience-based test techniqueA test technique based on the tester's experience, knowledge and intuition.Synonyms: experience-based test design technique, experience-based technique
  • exploratory testingA test approach in which tests are dynamically designed and executed based on the tester's knowledge, exploration of a test item, and previous test results.
  • state transition testingA black-box test technique in which test conditions are state transitions or sequences of them.Synonyms: finite state testing
  • statement coverageThe coverage of executable statements.
  • test techniqueA procedure used to define test conditions, design test cases, and specify test data.Synonyms: test design technique
  • white-box test techniqueA test technique based on the internal structure of a component or system.Synonyms: white-box test design technique, structure-based test technique

4.1

Test Techniques Overview K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Test techniques support test analysis (what to test) and test design (how to test), helping define test conditions, coverage items and test data systematically.

Black-box

Specification-based

From the object’s specified behavior, not its internals. Survives implementation changes.

White-box

Structure-based

From the internal structure — code, architecture, data flow. Needs a design or build to exist first.

Experience-based

Tester-knowledge-based

Effectiveness scales with the tester’s skill. Catches what the other two families miss — they’re complementary, not competing.

4.2

Black-Box Test Techniques

4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning (EP) K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

EP divides data into partitions where the theory holds that testing one value from a partition is representative of all of them — so one test per partition is enough. Partitions apply to inputs, outputs, configuration, internal values, timing, and interface parameters alike. Partitions must not overlap and must each be non-empty; a partition of valid values is a valid partition, one of invalid values an invalid partition — the trick in practice is defining both carefully.

The coverage items are the partitions themselves. Coverage = partitions exercised ÷ total partitions identified, so 100% coverage means every partition, including invalid ones, is hit at least once. When a test item has several sets of partitions (e.g. more than one input parameter), the simplest criterion is Each Choice coverage: exercise every partition of every set at least once, without worrying about combinations between sets.

4.2.2 Boundary Value Analysis (BVA) K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

BVA exercises the edges of ordered partitions, since implementation errors cluster at boundaries — misplaced by one, or missing entirely. 2-value BVA tests a boundary and its closest neighbor in the adjacent partition; 3-value BVA adds the value exactly on the boundary’s other side too, so it can catch defects (e.g. ≤ coded as =) that 2-value BVA overlooks.

2-value coverage = boundary values exercised ÷ total boundary values · 3-value coverage = (boundaries + neighbors) exercised ÷ total identified. Both reach 100% only once every coverage item for every boundary has been exercised.

4.2.3 Decision Table Testing K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Decision tables record how combinations of conditions map to actions — ideal for business rules. Columns are rules; coverage is the percentage of feasible columns exercised.

Example decision table: discount eligibility
Condition / actionRule 1Rule 2Rule 3Rule 4
Loyalty member?TTFF
Cart ≥ $50?TFTF
Apply 10% discountXX––
Free shippingX–X–

A limited-entry table uses only true/false; an extended-entry table allows ranges or discrete values. Tables can be minimized by merging columns where a condition doesn’t affect the outcome.

4.2.4 State Transition Testing K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

A state diagram models a system’s states and the valid transitions between them, each triggered by an event (and optionally a guard condition), written as event [guard] / action.

State table

The same model as a table: rows are states, columns are events (with any guard condition), and each cell holds the target state and resulting action. Unlike the diagram, a state table shows invalid transitions explicitly — as empty cells.

All states

Every state is visited at least once. The weakest criterion — achievable without exercising every transition.

Coverage = states exercised ÷ total states

Valid transitions (0-switch)

Every valid transition is exercised. The most widely used; full coverage here guarantees full all-states coverage.

Coverage = valid transitions exercised ÷ total valid transitions

All transitions

Every valid transition, plus an attempt at each invalid one — one per test case, to avoid defect masking. Guarantees both other criteria, and should be the minimum for mission- and safety-critical software.

4.3

White-Box Test Techniques

White-box techniques are read from a control flow graph — the possible sequences in which code statements execute.

4.3.1 Statement Testing and Statement Coverage K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Coverage items are executable statements. Coverage = statements exercised ÷ total executable statements. 100% guarantees every statement ran at least once — but not that every decision outcome was tested.

4.3.2 Branch Testing and Branch Coverage K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Coverage items are branches — both conditional and unconditional transfers of control. Coverage = branches exercised ÷ total branches. Branch coverage subsumes statement coverage: 100% branch coverage guarantees 100% statement coverage, never the reverse.

4.3.3 The Value of White-box Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Strength

Considers the whole implementation, so it finds defects even when the specification is vague, outdated or missing.

Weakness

Can’t detect a missing requirement — an omission that was never implemented leaves no code to cover.

Also static

White-box techniques apply in static testing too — dry runs of code, or reviewing pseudocode and other high-level logic not yet ready to execute.

Objective measure

Black-box testing alone gives no measure of actual code coverage. White-box coverage is an objective measurement that shows where to add tests, raising confidence in the code.

4.4

Experience-based Test Techniques K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Error guessing

Anticipate errors, defects and failures from experience — how the app failed before, how similar apps fail. “Fault attacks” make this systematic with a prepared list.

Exploratory testing

Design, execution and evaluation happen together as the tester learns the object. Session-based testing adds structure: a timeboxed charter, then a debrief.

Checklist-based testing

Tests cover conditions from a checklist built on experience or known failure modes — kept current as new high-severity defects appear.

Experience-based techniques work best paired with a skilled, domain-aware tester, and complement black-box and white-box techniques rather than replacing them.

4.5

Collaboration-based Test Approaches

Where the techniques above focus on defect detection, collaboration-based approaches focus on defect avoidance through shared understanding.

4.5.1 Collaborative User Story Writing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

A user story captures value for a user or purchaser, commonly as “As a [role], I want [goal], so that I can [business value]”, built from three parts — the 3 C’s:

Card

The medium that describes the story.

Conversation

How the software will be used — documented or verbal.

Confirmation

The acceptance criteria.

  • Independent
  • Negotiable
  • Valuable
  • Estimable
  • Small
  • Testable

4.5.2 Acceptance Criteria K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Acceptance criteria are the conditions an implementation must meet to be accepted — effectively the test conditions the tests will exercise. They:

Define the scope of the user story.

Reach consensus among the stakeholders.

Describe both positive and negative scenarios.

Serve as the basis for acceptance testing.

Allow accurate planning and estimation.

FormatLooks like
Scenario-orientedGiven/When/Then (the BDD format)
Rule-orientedA bullet-point checklist, or an input→output table

4.5.3 Acceptance Test-driven Development (ATDD) K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Specification workshopAnalyze & write acceptance criteria together
→
Create test casesBefore the story is implemented
→
Positive testsConfirm expected behavior
→
Negative testsExceptions & error conditions
→
Non-functionale.g. performance, usability

Chapter 5

Managing the Test Activities

Techniques only pay off inside a well-run process. This chapter covers planning a test effort and estimating it honestly, managing risk as the thing that actually drives test priority, monitoring and reporting progress so decisions stay informed, and the two supporting disciplines — configuration management and defect management — that keep everything traceable and under control.

  • defect managementThe process of recognizing, recording, classifying, investigating, fixing and disposing of defects.
  • defect reportDocumentation of the occurrence, nature, and status of a defect.Synonyms: bug report
  • entry criteriaThe set of conditions for officially starting a defined task.
  • exit criteriaThe set of conditions for officially completing a defined task.Synonyms: test completion criteria, completion criteria
  • product riskA risk that impacts the quality of a product.
  • project riskA risk that impacts project success.
  • riskA factor that could result in future negative consequences.
  • risk analysisThe overall process of risk identification and risk assessment.
  • risk assessmentThe process to examine identified risks and determine the risk level.
  • risk controlThe overall process of risk mitigation and risk monitoring.
  • risk identificationThe process of finding, recognizing and describing risks.
  • risk levelThe measure of a risk defined by risk impact and risk likelihood.Synonyms: risk exposure
  • risk managementThe process for handling risks.
  • risk mitigationThe process through which decisions are reached and protective measures are implemented for reducing or maintaining risks to specified levels.
  • risk monitoringThe activity that checks and reports the status of known risks to stakeholders.
  • risk-based testingA test approach in which the management, selection, prioritization, and use of test activities and resources are based on corresponding risk types and risk levels.
  • test approachThe manner of implementing test tasks.
  • test completion reportA type of test report produced at completion milestones that provides an evaluation of the corresponding test items against exit criteria.Synonyms: test summary report
  • test controlThe activity that develops and applies corrective actions to get a test project on track when it deviates from what was planned.
  • test monitoringThe activity that checks the status of testing activities, identifies any variances from planned or expected, and reports status to stakeholders.
  • test planDocumentation describing the test objectives to be achieved and the means and the schedule for achieving them, organized to coordinate testing.
  • test planningThe activity of establishing or updating a test plan.
  • test progress reportA type of periodic test report that includes the progress of test activities against a baseline, risks, and alternatives requiring a decision.Synonyms: test status report
  • test pyramidA graphical model representing the relationship of the amount of testing per level, with more at the bottom than at the top.
  • test strategyA description of how to perform testing to reach test objectives under given circumstances.
  • testing quadrantsA classification model of test types/test levels in four quadrants, relating them to two dimensions of test objectives: supporting the product team versus critiquing the product, and technology-facing versus business-facing.

5.1

Test Planning

5.1.1 Purpose and Content of a Test Plan K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

A test plan documents the means and schedule for reaching test objectives, confirms testing will meet its criteria, communicates the approach to stakeholders, and shows how testing follows — or knowingly deviates from — the test policy and strategy.

Context — scope, objectives, test basis

Assumptions & constraints of the project

Stakeholders — roles, responsibilities, training needs

Communication — forms, frequency, templates

Risk register — product and project risks

Test approach — levels, types, techniques, criteria, independence, metrics

Budget and schedule for the test project

5.1.2 Tester’s Contribution to Iteration and Release Planning K1K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.

AspectRelease planningIteration planning
Looks ahead toThe whole releaseThe end of one iteration
Works fromThe product backlogThe iteration backlog
Tester contributesTestable stories & acceptance criteria, project/quality risk analysis, effort estimates, overall test approachDetailed risk analysis, testability of stories, task breakdown, effort per task

5.1.3 Entry Criteria and Exit Criteria K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Entry criteriaResources, testware, initial quality
→
The activitye.g. a test level
→
Exit criteriaCoverage, defect counts, yes/no checks

Skipping entry criteria makes the activity slower, costlier and riskier. Running out of time or budget can itself be a valid exit criterion, if stakeholders accept the risk. In Agile: exit criteria → Definition of Done; entry criteria for a story → Definition of Ready.

5.1.4 Estimation Techniques K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Ratio-based

Derive standard ratios from the organization’s own historical projects.

Extrapolation

Use metrics from this project’s own early iterations to project the remaining effort.

Wideband Delphi

Experts estimate in isolation, discuss outliers, then re-estimate until they converge. Planning Poker is the Agile variant.

Three-point estimation

Optimistic (a), likely (m), pessimistic (b): E = (a + 4m + b) / 6, error SD = (b − a) / 6.

5.1.5 Test Case Prioritization K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Risk-based

Highest-risk coverage runs first.

Coverage-based

Highest (additional) coverage runs first.

Requirements-based

Highest-priority requirements run first.

5.1.6 Test Pyramid K1K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.

Layers trade granularity for speed: lower layers are small, isolated and fast, so you need many of them; higher layers are broad, slow, end-to-end checks, so a few go a long way.

UI / end-to-end testsfew · slow · broad
Integration / service testssome · moderate
Unit testsmany · fast · isolated

5.1.7 Testing Quadrants K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Brian Marick’s model maps test levels, types and techniques onto two axes so no test type gets forgotten.

Support the teamCritique the product
Business-facingTechnology-facing
Q1

Component & component integration tests — automated, in CI.

Q3

Exploratory, usability, user acceptance testing — often manual.

Q2

Functional tests, story tests, API tests, simulations.

Q4

Smoke tests, non-functional tests (except usability) — usually automated.

5.2

Risk Management

5.2.1 Risk Definition and Risk Attributes K1K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.

A risk is a potential event whose occurrence causes harm. Its level is a function of two attributes: risk likelihood — the probability of occurrence, greater than zero and less than one — and risk impact (harm), the consequences if it occurs. The higher the risk level, the more important its treatment.

Low impact
Medium impact
High impact
High likelihood
Medium
High
High
Medium likelihood
Low
Medium
High
Low likelihood
Low
Low
Medium

This risk matrix is how the level is determined qualitatively, during risk assessment (see 5.2.3). A quantitative approach instead multiplies likelihood by impact directly.

5.2.2 Project Risks and Product Risks K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

AspectProject risksProduct risks
AboutManaging & controlling the projectThe quality of the product itself
ExamplesDelays, poor estimates, staff shortage, tool problems, supplier failureMissing functionality, wrong calculations, poor architecture, security gaps
ImpactSchedule, budget, scopeUser trust, revenue, safety, in the worst case injury

5.2.3 Product Risk Analysis K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Risk analysis = risk identification (brainstorming, workshops, interviews, cause–effect diagrams) + risk assessment (categorizing, rating likelihood/impact/level). Results shape scope, test levels and types, techniques and coverage, effort estimates, and prioritization — ideally starting early in the SDLC.

5.2.4 Product Risk Control K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Risk control = mitigation (acting to lower the risk) + monitoring (checking mitigation is working, catching new risks). Once a risk is analyzed, the response options are: mitigation by testing, acceptance, transfer (e.g. to a third party), or a contingency plan.

Testing mitigates product risk by:

Choosing testers with the right skills for the risk type.

Applying the right level of test independence.

Reviewing and running static analysis.

Applying the right techniques, coverage and test types — and dynamic testing, including regression.

5.3

Test Monitoring, Test Control and Test Completion

5.3.1 Metrics used in Testing K1K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.

  • project progress
  • test progress
  • product quality
  • defects
  • risk
  • coverage
  • cost

AspectTest progress reportTest completion report
WhenRegularly (daily, weekly…) during testingOnce, when a level/type/project completes
PurposeSupport ongoing control — adjust schedule or planSummarize & hand off to future testing
Typical contentProgress vs schedule, impediments, metrics, new risks, next period’s planSummary vs plan, deviations, unmitigated risks, lessons learned

5.3.3 Communicating the Status of Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Verbal communication with team members and stakeholders.

Dashboards — CI/CD boards, task boards, burn-down charts.

Electronic communication channels — email, chat.

Online documentation.

Formal test reports (see 5.3.2).

More formal, written communication suits distributed teams; tailor content, since different stakeholders want different things.

5.4

Configuration Management K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Configuration management (CM) identifies, controls and tracks work products — test plans, cases, scripts, results, reports — as configuration items. Once approved for testing, an item becomes a baseline, changeable only through formal change control, and CM keeps enough history to revert to an earlier baseline and reproduce past results.

Every item is uniquely identified, versioned, and linked to related items — preserving traceability.

Documentation and software are referenced unambiguously in testware.

5.5

Defect Management K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

A defect management process handles anomalies from discovery to closure — whether they turn out to be real defects, false positives, or change requests.

LogRecord the anomaly
→
Analyze & classifySeverity, priority
→
Decide responseFix, defer, reject…
→
CloseAfter confirmation testing

A defect report typically includes: unique identifier, title, date/author/status, test object & environment, context, reproduction steps with logs or screenshots, expected vs actual result, severity, priority, status, and references.

Tool Support Automation Benefits & Risks

Chapter 6

Test Tools

The shortest chapter carries a simple warning: tools multiply whatever process you already have, good or bad. This closing chapter surveys the categories of test tools and weighs the real benefits of test automation against the risks that catch teams off guard.

  • test automationThe conversion of test activities to automated operation.

6.1

Tool Support for Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Tools support and facilitate test activities — they don’t replace the thinking behind them.

Test management

SDLC, requirements, tests, defects, configuration — managed together.

Static testing

Supports reviews and static analysis.

Design & implementation

Generates test cases, data and procedures.

Execution & coverage

Automated runs and coverage measurement.

Non-functional testing

Handles what’s impractical to test manually — load, performance.

DevOps

Pipeline workflow, automated builds, CI/CD.

Collaboration

Facilitates communication across the team.

Scalability & deployment

Virtual machines, containerization.

Anything that helps

Even a spreadsheet counts, in the right context.

6.2

Benefits and Risks of Test Automation K1K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.

Acquiring a tool doesn’t guarantee success — introduction, maintenance and training all take real, ongoing effort.

Benefits

Less repetitive manual work; fewer human errors through consistency; more objective, otherwise-impossible measurements; easier access to test data and reporting; faster execution for earlier feedback; more tester time for designing deeper tests.

Risks

Unrealistic expectations; underestimated cost and effort; automating where manual testing fits better; over-reliance at the expense of critical thinking; vendor dependency — the vendor may fold, retire the tool, sell it on, or give poor support; open-source abandonment, or components needing frequent updates; platform incompatibility; non-compliant tooling for regulated environments.

Automation risk
Over-reliance, vendor lock-in, and unrealistic expectations.
