GenAI Foundations Core Principles

Chapter 1 · CT-GenAI

Introduction to Generative AI for Software Testing

Before prompting an LLM to help with testing, it helps to know what it actually is. This chapter places generative AI on the wider AI spectrum, explains how LLMs turn language into something a model can compute over, and surveys where GenAI can realistically help across the test process.

  • generative AIA type of artificial intelligence system that uses machine learning models to generate (new) intellectual content that resembles human-created content.
  • large language modelA computer program that uses very large collections of language data to understand and produce text in a way that is similar to the way humans do.Abbreviation: LLM
  • symbolic AIAn AI approach that uses symbols, rules, and structured knowledge to model reasoning.
  • machine learningThe process using computational techniques to enable systems to learn from data or experience.Source: ISO/IEC TR 29119-11
  • deep learningMachine learning using neural networks with multiple layers.
  • tokenizationThe process of breaking down text into smaller units for processing by language models.
  • embeddingA technique used to represent tokens as dense vectors in a continuous space, learned during training to capture semantic, syntactic, and contextual relationships.
  • transformerA deep learning model architecture that utilizes self-attention mechanisms to capture long-range dependencies in input sequences.
  • context windowThe span of text, measured in tokens, that a language model considers when generating responses, influencing the relevance and coherence of its outputs.
  • generative pre-trained transformerA type of transformer-based deep learning model pre-trained on vast amounts of text data to understand and generate human-like text.Abbreviation: GPT
  • foundation LLMGeneral-purpose models pre-trained on a wide range of text data, capable of predicting the next word based on learned linguistic patterns.Synonym: base LLM
  • instruction-tuned LLMA foundation LLM trained to follow instructions, often reinforced by feedback to encourage correct answers.
  • reasoning LLMAn LLM building upon instruction-tuned models by refining their ability to emulate human-like reasoning processes.
  • multimodal modelGenAI models that are capable of processing and generating content across multiple data types, such as text, images, and audio.
  • AI chatbotA conversational agent that uses LLMs to process queries and generate human-like text responses, enabling interactive communication with users.
  • featureAn individual measurable attribute of the input data used for training by an ML algorithm and for prediction by an ML model.

1.1

Generative AI Foundations and Key Concepts K2K2: UnderstandExplain the basics of generative AI and LLMs; distinguish LLM categories.

Generative AI (GenAI) is a branch of AI that uses large, pre-trained models to generate human-like text, images or code. Large language models (LLMs) are pre-trained on huge textual datasets, letting them determine context and produce relevant responses to prompts. In software testing, LLMs can support reviewing acceptance criteria, generating test cases or scripts, identifying potential defects, analyzing defect patterns, generating synthetic test data, and supporting documentation — across the whole test process.

1.1.1 AI Spectrum: Symbolic AI, Classical Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Generative AI

Symbolic AI

Rule-based; represents knowledge with symbols and logical rules to mimic human decision-making.

Classical machine learning

Data-driven: data preparation, feature selection, model training — e.g. defect categorization, predicting software problems.

Deep learning

Neural networks that automatically learn features from large, complex data — images, video, audio, text — though tuning and validation still need human involvement.

Generative AI

Uses deep learning to create new content by learning and mimicking training-data patterns; LLMs can generate text, write code, and simulate reasoning within their training scope.

GenAI’s key advantage for testing: pre-trained models apply directly to test tasks with no extra training phase — though that comes with risks (see chapter 3).

1.1.2 Basics of Generative AI and LLMs

LLMs are built on the generative pre-trained transformer model and trained on very large datasets — books, articles, websites. Small language models (SLMs) are compact, lighter-weight alternatives with fewer parameters. Two concepts convert language into a form an LLM can process: tokenization (breaking text into tokens, from characters to sub-words to whole words) and embeddings (numerical vectors encoding a token’s meaning, positioning similar tokens close together in a high-dimensional space). The transformer architecture processes long text sequences and predicts the next token during inference — producing text that is statistically plausible, not necessarily correct.

Non-determinism

LLMs behave non-deterministically because of the probabilistic nature of inference and hyperparameter settings — the same input can produce different outputs across runs (see 3.1.4 for mitigation).

Context window

The amount of preceding text (in tokens) an LLM can consider. A larger window keeps coherence over longer passages (e.g. large test logs), but costs more compute and processing time.

1.1.3 Foundation, Instruction-Tuned and Reasoning LLMs

FoundationGeneral-purpose, vast diverse pretraining
→
Instruction-tunedFine-tuned on prompt/response pairs
→
ReasoningLogical inference, multi-step, chain-of-thought

Both instruction-tuned (sometimes called non-reasoning) and reasoning LLMs are used in GenAI testing applications — the choice depends on the task’s complexity and reasoning demands.

1.1.4 Multimodal LLMs and Vision-Language Models

Multimodal LLMs extend the transformer to process text, images, sound and video together, adapting tokenization per data type — images, for instance, are converted to embeddings via vision-language models before entering the transformer. In testing, this lets an LLM analyze screenshots or GUI wireframes alongside textual defect reports or user stories, spotting discrepancies between expected and actual visuals, and generating richer test cases that combine text and visual cues.

1.2

Leveraging Generative AI in Software Testing: Core Principles K2K2: UnderstandGive examples of key LLM capabilities; compare interaction models.

LLMs excel at processing natural language and code: generating coherent text and code, answering questions, summarizing, translating, and analyzing images multimodally. Testers can access this in two complementary ways — conversational AI chatbots, and LLM-powered applications integrated into test tools.

1.2.1 Key LLM Capabilities for Test Tasks

Requirements analysis

Spot ambiguities, inconsistencies or gaps; generate clarifying questions for stakeholders.

Test case creation

Generate test cases and suggest objectives from requirements, user stories, or other test basis elements.

Test oracle generation

Help generate expected results.

Test data generation

Generate datasets, boundary values, and combinations of test data.

Test automation support

Generate test scripts from test case descriptions; suggest improvements and applicable techniques.

Test result analysis

Summarize results; classify anomalies by severity and priority.

Testware creation

Draft and keep updated test plans, reports and defect reports as the project evolves.

1.2.2 AI Chatbots and LLM-Powered Testing Applications for Software Testing

AI chatbotsLLM-powered testing applications
InteractionConversational, direct natural-language inputIntegrated via APIs into test frameworks
Best forRoutine tasks, exploratory testing, onboarding new testersWell-defined, automated, repetitive or complex tasks at scale
StrengthAccessible even to non-technical stakeholdersCustomizable, scalable; can power dedicated AI agents (chapter 4)
Either way, prompting quality decides the outcome

Whether through a chatbot or an integrated application, getting useful results from an LLM depends on strong prompt engineering — carefully designed, specific prompts (see chapter 2).

LLM

Prompt Development Applying Techniques Evaluate & Refine

Chapter 2 · CT-GenAI

Prompt Engineering for Effective Software Testing

The largest chapter in the syllabus, and the practical core: how to structure a prompt, which of three core techniques to reach for, how system and user prompts differ, where GenAI fits across the test process, and how to tell whether a prompt is actually working.

  • acceptance criteriaThe criteria that a work product must satisfy to be accepted by the stakeholders.
  • test caseA set of preconditions, inputs, actions (where applicable), expected results and postconditions, developed based on test conditions.
  • test conditionA testable aspect of a component or system that is intended to be tested.Synonyms: test situation, test requirement, test idea
  • test dataData needed for test execution.Synonyms: test dataset
  • test designThe activity that derives and specifies test cases from test conditions.
  • test scriptA sequence of instructions for the execution of a test.
  • test reportDocumentation summarizing testing and test results.
  • promptA natural language input provided to elicit a specific response in generative AI and large language models.
  • prompt engineeringThe process of designing and refining input prompts to guide LLMs toward producing desired outputs.
  • system promptA predefined instruction set, typically hidden from the chatbot’s users, that consistently establishes the context, tone, and boundaries for an LLM’s responses and guides its behavior throughout interactions.
  • user promptAn instruction or query entered by a user into an LLM that directs the model’s response to fulfil specific tasks or provide desired information.
  • prompt chainingA prompting technique that involves using the output of one prompt as the input for another, creating a sequence of prompts.
  • few-shot promptingA technique where a model is given a few examples within the prompt to guide it in generating appropriate responses.
  • one-shot promptingA prompt writing technique where the prompt contains one example to guide the LLM’s response.
  • zero-shot promptingA prompt writing technique where the prompt contains no examples, relying on the model’s pre-existing knowledge to generate a response.
  • meta promptingThe crafting of higher-level instructions that generate specific prompts for exploring or automating capabilities.
  • natural language processingThe processing of data encoded in natural language by computers to retrieve information and for knowledge representation.

2.1

Effective Prompt Development K2K2: UnderstandGive examples of prompt structure; differentiate core prompting techniques; distinguish system and user prompts.

2.1.1 Structure of Prompts for Generative AI in Software Testing

A structured prompt for software testing typically has six components:

Role

The persona the model adopts — e.g. tester, test manager, automation engineer — shaping tone and responsibilities.

Context

Background the model needs: the test object, functionality under test, relevant surrounding detail.

Instruction

A clear, imperative, concise description of the task and its requirements.

Input data

User stories, acceptance criteria, screenshots, code, existing test cases, output examples.

Constraints

Restrictions or special considerations governing how instructions apply to the input data.

Output format

The expected format, structure or characteristics of the response.

2.1.2 Core Prompting Techniques for Software Testing

Three techniques are commonly combined with the 6-component structure above:

Prompt chaining

Breaks a task into intermediate steps, each checked/refined before the next — greater accuracy for complex, decomposable tasks.

Few-shot prompting

Gives the model examples. Zero-shot gives none; one-shot gives one; few-shot gives several, to consolidate the desired pattern.

Meta prompting

The LLM generates or refines its own prompts, iteratively evaluated by the tester — a form of pairing that reduces manual prompt-crafting effort.

These techniques combine well — e.g. meta prompting to draft an initial prompt, few-shot to lock in a pattern, then prompt chaining to validate each step (see 2.2.5).

2.1.3 System Prompt and User Prompt

System promptUser prompt
Set byDeveloper or testerThe chatbot’s user, per interaction
VisibilityUsually hidden/not editable by the userDirectly visible
DurationConstant for the whole sessionChanges with each interaction
Typical contentRole, context, constraints, tone, domain rulesSpecific instructions, questions, tasks
Example

System prompt: “You are a professional software testing assistant. Always respond clearly, use formal language, and focus on ISTQB-aligned practices.” User prompt: “List the key differences between black-box and white-box testing with examples.”

2.2

Applying Prompt Engineering Techniques to Software Test Tasks K3K3: ApplyApply generative AI to test analysis, test design/implementation, regression testing, and test monitoring/control.

2.2.1 Test Analysis with Generative AI

Identify potential defects in the test basis

Flag inconsistencies, ambiguities or missing information by comparing requirement patterns and prior defect data.

Generate test conditions

Break requirements/user stories into measurable, testable statements via NLP.

Prioritize by risk

Recommend priority using likelihood, impact, regulatory compliance, and historical defect data.

Coverage analysis

Map requirements/stories to test conditions to surface gaps.

Suggest test techniques

Recommend e.g. boundary value analysis or equivalence partitioning for a given requirement type.

Output accuracy tracks input quality directly — vague or incomplete input data yields vague or incomplete results.

2.2.2 Test Design and Test Implementation with Generative AI

Test case generation

Draft preconditions, inputs, expected results and coverage from requirements — from basic checks to complex end-to-end flows.

Test data synthesis

Privacy-preserving synthetic data resembling production, including edge cases, without exposing sensitive information.

Automated test script generation

Translate structured test steps into code for various automation frameworks; update as requirements change.

Execution scheduling & prioritization

Optimize schedules using priority, risk, dependencies and resource availability.

2.2.3 Automated Regression Testing with Generative AI

Regression suites grow every iteration, making them prime automation targets, especially in CI/CD. GenAI can perform impact analysis to focus regression effort where recent changes actually matter.

Keyword-driven script implementation

Map predefined keywords to specific test cases, generating scripts from a keyword library.

Self-healing, adaptive tests

Auto-adjust scripts for minor UI/API changes, avoiding unnecessary failures.

Automated reporting

Timely reports with success metrics, failures, and predictive insight into likely failure points.

Defect reporting & root cause analysis

Auto-compile defect reports with logs, screenshots and environment data.

Trust, but verify

GenAI can make mistakes. Generated regression output must be checked, proportionate to the risk involved (see chapter 3).

2.2.4 Test Monitoring and Test Control with Generative AI

Monitoring & metrics analysis

Analyze trends, predict risks, alert on plan deviations.

Test control

Insights for reprioritizing tests, adjusting schedules, reallocating resources.

Completion insights

Generate completion reports highlighting successes and lessons learned.

Metrics visualization

Dynamic dashboards and natural-language summaries for stakeholders.

2.2.5 Choosing Prompting Techniques for Software Testing

TechniqueRecommended use case
Prompt chainingComplex tasks needing precision with human verification at each step — test analysis, design, automation.
Few-shot promptingRepetitive or tightly-formatted output — Gherkin-style cases, keyword-driven testing, formatted reports.
Meta promptingFlexible or novel tasks — crafting prompts for new problems, e.g. report analysis or anomaly detection.

It’s common to combine all three: meta prompting to draft, few-shot to lock a pattern, chaining to validate step by step.

2.3

Evaluate Generative AI Results and Refine Prompts for Software Test Tasks K2K2: UnderstandUnderstand metrics for evaluating results; give examples of refinement techniques.

2.3.1 Metrics for Evaluating the Results of Generative AI on Test tasks

MetricWhat it measures
AccuracyOverall correctness against expert-written cases/requirements/standards.
PrecisionCorrectness with respect to a specific objective, e.g. correctly flagged anomalies.
RecallAbility to find all relevant instances, e.g. valid and invalid equivalence partitions.
Relevance & contextual fitWhether output is applicable to the given test basis and domain.
DiversityBreadth of scenarios covered, including edge cases, without repetition.
Execution success rateShare of generated artefacts that run as-is without errors.
Time efficiencyTime saved versus equivalent manual effort.

Given GenAI’s non-deterministic behavior, these metrics need statistically meaningful sample sizes, not a single run.

2.3.2 Techniques for Evaluating and Iteratively Refining Prompts

Iterative modification

Start with a base prompt, add context or adjust wording as results come in.

A/B testing of prompts

Compare versions against predefined metrics to find the better phrasing/structure.

Output analysis

Examine inaccuracies against the test basis to understand recurring error types.

Integrate user feedback

Gather tester input on usefulness and detail level; fold it back into the prompt.

Adjust length & specificity

More context sometimes helps; shorter prompts sometimes generalize better.

Sharing prompt libraries and refinement practices across a test team standardizes quality and speeds up everyone’s learning curve.

Chapter 2 in one screen

Prompt chaining

Few-/one-/zero-shot prompting
How many examples the prompt supplies, from none to several.
Meta prompting
Let the LLM help draft or refine its own prompt.
System prompt vs. user prompt
Constant governing rules vs. the changing per-turn request.
GenAI across the test process
Test analysis, design/implementation, regression, monitoring/control — all supportable, none unattended.
Evaluation metrics

Prompt refinement

Hallucinations & Bias Privacy & Security Environmental Impact Regulations & Standards

Chapter 3 · CT-GenAI

Managing Risks of Generative AI in Software Testing

GenAI helps, but it also fails in specific, recognizable ways. This chapter covers hallucinations, reasoning errors and bias; the data privacy and security exposure that comes with feeding testware to an LLM; the environmental cost of running these models; and the regulatory frameworks now shaping how they can be used.

  • securityProtection of systems and data against unauthorized access, breaches, or malicious manipulation — a specific concern for LLM-powered test infrastructure.
  • vulnerabilityA weakness in a system or process that can be exploited, e.g. by manipulative prompts sent to an LLM.
  • data privacyProtection of personally identifiable or sensitive information from unintended exposure, especially when processed by GenAI.
  • hallucinationWrong information created by an LLM.In testing, this can mean a fictitious test case or a script that verifies non-existent acceptance criteria.
  • reasoning errorA misinterpretation of logical structure — cause-effect, conditional logic, step-by-step reasoning — leading to incorrect conclusions.
  • biasA systematic skew in LLM output originating from its training data, favoring certain information, approaches or assumptions.
  • temperatureA parameter that controls the randomness or creativity of an LLM’s outputs.
  • context manipulationAn attack that sends requests designed to extract confidential training data, e.g. by overloading the context window.

3.1

Hallucinations, Reasoning Errors and Biases K3K3: ApplyIdentify hallucinations, reasoning errors and biases in LLM output; summarize mitigation techniques.

LLMs are prone to specific defects that degrade the quality of test-task output. Non-determinism (1.1.2) makes them slippery to fix — a defect that appears gone in one conversation can reappear in another with the same model.

3.1.1 Hallucinations, Reasoning Errors and Biases in Generative AI

Hallucinations

Factually incorrect or irrelevant output — fictitious test cases, broken scripts, tests for acceptance criteria that don’t exist.

Reasoning errors

LLMs pattern-match rather than truly reason logically, so cause-effect, conditional logic and multi-step problems (e.g. test planning, prioritization) can go wrong.

Biases

Rooted in training data; can skew generated test data or acceptance-criteria refinement toward overrepresented patterns (e.g. English-language assumptions).

3.1.2 Identify Hallucinations, Reasoning Errors and Biases in LLM Output

Defect typeDetection approaches
HallucinationCross-verification against documentation/requirements; domain expert consultation; consistency checks across outputs.
Reasoning errorLogical validation of the generated content’s coherence; output testing — run the generated test cases/scripts and check results.
BiasReview whether generated testware fairly represents the test strategy and coverage; check for underrepresented test types.

How rigorously to detect these is a risk-based call, matched to the estimated risk level of the test task.

3.1.3 Mitigation techniques of GenAI hallucinations, reasoning errors and biases in software test tasks

Provide complete context in the prompt — missing information is a common root cause.

Split complex prompts via prompt chaining, verifying each step before the next.

Use clear, structured, unambiguous data formats.

Select an LLM actually suited to the task (see 5.1.3).

Compare results across multiple LLMs to catch outliers.

Chapter 4 introduces two more complementary techniques: Retrieval-Augmented Generation and fine-tuning.

3.1.4 Mitigation of Non-Deterministic Behavior of LLMs

Non-determinism comes from probabilistic sampling during inference, and gets worse for longer outputs.

Lower the temperature

Narrows the probability distribution for more consistent output — at the cost of creativity and diversity.

Set a random seed

Where supported, fixes the pseudo-random sequence used, improving reproducibility.

3.2

Data Privacy and Security Risks of Generative AI in Software Testing K2K2: UnderstandExplain key data privacy and security risks; summarize mitigation strategies.

3.2.1 Data Privacy and Security Risks Associated with Using Generative AI

Unintentional data exposure

Outputs may accidentally reveal sensitive information from training or context.

Lack of control over data usage

Tools may store/process sensitive data without explicit consent or oversight.

Compliance risk

Using GenAI outside data protection regulations (e.g. GDPR) risks legal exposure.

3.2.2 Data Privacy and Vulnerabilities in Generative AI for Test processes and Tools

Attack vectorDescriptionExample
Context manipulationRequests designed to extract confidential training data.Overloading the context window with long prompts to leak training-data snippets.
Request manipulationIntroducing data that disrupts the AI’s output.Images that push the model into a different context, provoking hallucinated acceptance criteria.
Data poisoningManipulating training data.Submitting fake evaluations when rating an AI-generated test report.
Malicious code generationManipulating an LLM into generating backdoors.Generating code that opens a channel to a malicious IP.

3.2.3 Mitigation Strategies to Protect Data Privacy and Enhance Security in Testing with Generative AI

Data minimization

Process only the non-sensitive data actually needed, unless sensitive processing is legally permitted.

Anonymization / pseudonymization

Mask or replace identifiable information.

Secure storage & transmission

Strong encryption and access controls.

Resource training

Clear policies for responsible, ethical GenAI use.

Systematic output review

Human evaluation for quality and accuracy.

Cross-model evaluation

Compare outputs from several LLMs on the same task.

Secure operational environment

Commercial secure offering, secure cloud, or in-house infrastructure, per confidentiality needs.

Regular security audits

Ongoing vulnerability assessment as tools and threats evolve.

These strategies are complementary, not alternatives — involve Security Engineers, Legal, the CTO or CISO where they exist.

3.3

Energy Consumption and Environmental Impact of Generative AI in Software Testing K2K2: UnderstandExplain the impact of task characteristics and model usage on GenAI energy consumption.

3.3.1 The Impact of Using GenAI on Energy Consumption and CO₂ Emissions

Training and running LLMs demands intensive specialized compute, and as web-based GenAI services scale up, so does load on devices, networks and data centers. Task complexity and computational resources drive energy use — generating a single AI image can use roughly as much energy as fully charging a smartphone, while generating text uses only a small fraction of that. Accurate environmental-impact data is hard to obtain, but the cumulative CO₂ effect across millions of users worldwide is significant even if any one interaction seems negligible.

Practical takeaway

Limiting unnecessary model interactions is a concrete, low-effort way to reduce GenAI’s environmental footprint in a test organization.

3.4

AI Regulations, Standards, and Best Practice Frameworks K1K1: RememberRecall examples of AI regulations, standards and best practice frameworks relevant to GenAI in software testing.

3.4.1 AI Regulations, Standards and Frameworks Relevant to GenAI in Software Testing

NameTypeRelevance to testing
ISO/IEC 42001:2023StandardRequirements for managing AI systems within an organization — consistency and reliability of GenAI in testing.
ISO/IEC 23053:2022StandardAI lifecycle framework emphasizing safety and transparency — data quality and transparency in GenAI testing.
EU AI ActRegulationLegal framework classifying AI by risk; mandates transparency, accountability and bias mitigation.
NIST AI Risk Management FrameworkFrameworkGuidelines for fairness, transparency and security; helps prevent biased test results.

The regulatory landscape keeps moving — test organizations need to track new regulations, standards, national laws and best-practice frameworks as they emerge.

Test Infrastructure Fine-Tuning & LLMOps

Chapter 4 · CT-GenAI

LLM-Powered Test Infrastructure for Software Testing

Beyond a single chatbot conversation, GenAI in testing can be architected as real infrastructure: systems that retrieve an organization’s own data before answering, agents that act semi-autonomously on test tasks, and models tuned and operated for the long run.

  • test infrastructureThe test environments, test tools, office environment and procedures needed to perform testing.
  • retrieval-augmented generationA technique combining LLM capabilities with a retriever to fetch relevant data for generating accurate, contextually relevant responses.Abbreviation: RAG
  • vector databaseA database optimized for storing and querying high-dimensional vector representations of data.
  • LLM-powered agentAn application that integrates LLM reasoning, decision-making, and memory, using tools to perform tasks.
  • fine-tuningA supervised learning process using a dataset of labeled examples to update LLM weights and adapt them for specific tasks or domains.
  • Large Language Model OperationsPractices and tools focused on deploying, monitoring, and maintaining LLMs in production environments.Abbreviation: LLMOps

4.1

Architectural Approaches for LLM-Powered Test Infrastructure K2K2: UnderstandExplain key architectural components; summarize RAG; explain LLM-powered agents.

4.1.1 Key Architectural Components and Concepts of LLM-Powered Test Infrastructure

Unlike a conversational chatbot, an LLM-powered test tool processes test-related queries, analyzes requirements, generates test cases, and evaluates outputs. Its architecture typically has three layers:

Front-end

Where testers input queries or commands.

Back-end

Handles authentication, data retrieval, prompt preparation, and interaction with the LLM — and post-processes its output to align with test conditions.

LLM

Hosted third-party (via API) or a custom in-house model; the smart processing component that reasons over testware, not just a server.

The back-end typically integrates both relational databases (structured data like test cases) and vector databases (semantic retrieval via embeddings).

4.1.2 Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds LLM responses in additional data sources rather than relying solely on pre-existing training. Documents are chunked (e.g. 256–512 tokens), cleaned, and encoded into embeddings stored in a vector database.

RetrievalFind chunks matching the query by semantic similarity
→
GenerationLLM combines retrieved chunks with its own knowledge

For testing, RAG lets LLM-powered infrastructure reach into an organization’s own databases, documentation and repositories in real time — keeping test analysis or design aligned with the latest specifications and requirements, not just what the model was originally trained on.

4.1.3 The Role of LLM-Powered Agents in Automating Test processes

LLM-powered agents go beyond question-response: they can “act” by invoking predefined functions (“tools”) to interact with external systems.

Autonomous agents

Operate independently with minimal human intervention, using predefined rules and adaptive feedback loops.

Semi-autonomous agents

Perform tasks with periodic human oversight to keep output aligned with defined goals.

Multi-agent architectures coordinate several specialized agents — called orchestration — automating tasks across the whole test lifecycle: test analysis, design, implementation, execution and reporting, shifting automation from script-based execution toward goal-driven, agent-based automation.

Same risks apply

Agents can still hallucinate, reason incorrectly, or carry bias (3.1) — mitigated with automated verification of their results, or by keeping critical tasks semi-autonomous.

4.2

Fine-Tuning and LLMOps: Operationalizing Generative AI for Software Testing K2K2: UnderstandExplain fine-tuning; explain LLMOps and its role in deploying and managing LLMs.

4.2.1 Fine-Tuning LLMs for Test tasks

Fine-tuning further trains a pre-trained LLM or SLM on a targeted dataset, teaching it domain-specific knowledge, vocabulary and reasoning. For example, training on an organization’s own user stories and test cases aligns the model with that organization’s process and terminology. SLMs (smaller, less resource-intensive) can be fine-tuned for high performance on a specific task without an LLM’s computational overhead.

Data quality

Biased or low-quality training data produces biased or inaccurate fine-tuned output.

Overfitting

Over-specialization to training data hurts generalization to new, unseen situations.

Opacity

Lack of transparency into the model’s reasoning complicates debugging and validation.

Compute cost

Fine-tuning an LLM (less so an SLM) demands significant computational resources.

4.2.2 LLMOps when Deploying and Managing LLMs for Software Testing

LLMOps covers the practices, tools and processes for developing, deploying and maintaining LLMs in production. How an organization brings GenAI into its test process shapes its LLMOps decisions:

AI chatbot

Main concerns: data privacy/security and cost — LLM-as-a-Service, or in-house open-source deployment for more control.

Test tool with GenAI capability

Similar concerns, plus evaluating the tool vendor’s own data security and performance assurances.

In-house GenAI test tool

Full control over privacy/security, but requires real expertise, resource planning, and validation processes of its own.

These approaches aren’t mutually exclusive — an organization might mix a chatbot for some tasks with custom in-house tools for others, layering in RAG and fine-tuning as needed.

Chapter 4 in one screen

LLM-powered test infrastructure

RAG

LLM-powered agent
Acts via tools, not just answers — autonomous, semi-autonomous, or orchestrated multi-agent.
Fine-tuning
Further trains a model on domain data; risks overfitting, opacity, and compute cost.
LLMOps

Adoption Roadmap Managing Change

Chapter 5 · CT-GenAI

Deploying and Integrating Generative AI in Test Organizations

The closing chapter zooms out from technique to organization: how to roll GenAI out deliberately instead of letting it arrive as shadow IT, how to pick the right model, and how testing roles and responsibilities actually shift once GenAI becomes part of daily work.

  • shadow AIThe use of GenAI tools or systems within an organization without formal approval or oversight.

5.1

Roadmap for the Adoption of Generative AI in Software Testing K2K2: UnderstandExplain key strategy aspects; summarize LLM/SLM selection criteria; recall shadow AI risks and adoption phases.

5.1.1 Risks of Shadow AI

Security & privacy weaknesses

Personal AI tools may lack robust security, risking data breaches.

Compliance & regulatory issues

Unapproved tools risk non-compliance with industry standards (see 3.4.1).

Vague intellectual property

Unclear licensing can expose the organization to IP disputes over copyrighted training data.

5.1.2 Key Aspects of a Generative AI Strategy in Software Testing

A workable strategy starts with measurable objectives — productivity, shorter cycles, better quality — and selects LLMs aligned with those objectives and existing infrastructure. Data quality is critical, since LLM-powered testing is only as good as the input it receives, protected by proper security. Training programs build the technical and ethical skills test teams need, backed by metrics that actually measure GenAI effectiveness (2.3.1). Process guidelines cover sensitive-data rules, transparency about what was AI-generated, and quality gates for reviewing generated testware.

5.1.3 Selecting LLMs/SLMs for Software Test Tasks

Model performance

Evaluate against organizational benchmarks for the targeted test tasks.

Fine-tuning potential

Whether domain-specific fine-tuning is possible and worthwhile for the use case.

Recurring cost

Licensing and operational expenses against the organization’s budget.

Community & support

Active community and documentation ease implementation and troubleshooting.

5.1.4 Phases when Adopting Generative AI in Software Testing

DiscoveryAwareness, training, experimenting with initial use cases
→
Initiation & usage definitionPrioritize use cases; evaluate infrastructure and expertise
→
Utilization & iterationFull integration; continuous monitoring and measurement

Phases can run in parallel across different use cases — and early concerns like fear of job displacement need addressing directly, since they shape adoption and morale.

5.2

Manage Change when Adopting Generative AI for Software Testing K2K2: UnderstandExplain essential skills; recall capability-building strategies and how roles shift.

5.2.1 Essential Skills and Knowledge for Testing with Generative AI

Testers need prompt engineering skill, an understanding of context windows, and methods for reviewing AI-generated testware — combining domain and test expertise with AI literacy. Essential knowledge includes GenAI’s inherent risks and mitigations, the data-security implications of sharing testware with an LLM (including sanitizing sensitive data), and awareness of environmental trade-offs when choosing models and usage patterns.

5.2.2 Building Generative AI Capabilities in Test Teams

A hands-on approach works best: practicing with real LLMs/SLMs, following structured learning paths, and building know-how gradually through internal sharing. Testers progress from basic prompt-writing to reusable prompt patterns — templates for reliably guiding GenAI toward consistent output. Communities of practice keep the whole team learning together: sharing prompt libraries, discussing what worked, and documenting lessons learned.

5.2.3 Evolving Test Processes in AI-Enabled Test organizations

Testers

Evolve into AI-assisted test specialists: reviewing AI-based output, refining prompts, and maintaining test-specific prompt libraries alongside traditional test technique expertise.

Test managers

Take on AI-based test strategy and risk management, AI governance for use cases, and balancing human and AI capabilities — coordinating hybrid teams of people and GenAI agents.

Testers, evolved

Fundamentals Evaluating Usability & UX Human-Centered Design

Chapter 1 · CT-UT

Basic Concepts

Usability, user experience and accessibility are related but distinct qualities of a software product. This chapter defines all three, compares the three evaluation approaches (review, testing, survey), and places usability evaluation inside the human-centered design process.

  • accessibilityThe degree to which a product or system can be used by people with the widest range of characteristics and capabilities to achieve a specified goal in a specified context of use.
  • context of useUsers, tasks, equipment (hardware, software and materials), and the physical and social environments in which a software product is used.
  • effectivenessThe extent to which correct and complete goals are achieved.
  • efficiencyResources expended in relation to the extent with which users achieve specified goals.
  • formative evaluationA type of evaluation designed and used to improve the quality of a component or system, especially when it is still being designed.
  • human-centered designAn approach to design that aims to make software products more usable by focusing on the use of the software products and applying human factors, ergonomics, and usability knowledge and techniques.
  • summative evaluationA type of evaluation designed and used to gather conclusions about the quality of a component or system, especially when a substantial part of it has completed design.
  • usabilityExtent to which a software product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified context of use.
  • usability evaluationA process through which information about the usability of a system is gathered in order to improve the system (formative evaluation) or to assess the merit or worth of a system (summative evaluation).
  • usability requirementA requirement on the usability of a component or system.
  • user experienceA person’s perceptions and responses resulting from the use or anticipated use of a software product.
  • user interfaceAll components of a system that provide information and controls for the user to accomplish specific tasks with the system.Abbreviation: UI

1.1

Fundamentals K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

This section covers three fundamental concepts that recur throughout the syllabus: usability, user experience, and accessibility.

1.1.1

Usability

Usability is the extent to which a software product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified context of use [ISO 9241-210]. The user interface is all the components of a product that provide information and controls for the user to accomplish tasks.

Usability evaluation covers three principal activities: usability reviews, usability testing, and user surveys.

Example

A car rental app conforms fully to its specification and works effectively and efficiently — but users think it looks unprofessional. That is a usability problem affecting satisfaction, even though nothing is technically broken.

Usability always relates to a specific context of use: the users, tasks, equipment, and environment involved. The same software can be highly usable in one context and unusable in another — an office worker using Word daily and an elderly first-time user writing an invitation face very different usability demands from the identical product.

Users

A person who interacts with the product by providing input or using its output.

Tasks

Particular activities performed by users or user groups (e.g. inexperienced users, administrators).

Equipment

The hardware, software and materials required to use the product.

Environment

Physical, social and technical conditions of use, including organizational conditions.

1.1.2

User Experience Concepts

User experience (UX) is a person’s perceptions and responses resulting from the use, or anticipated use, of a product [ISO 9241-210]. It spans emotions, beliefs, preferences, perceptions, physical/psychological responses, and behaviors — occurring before, during, and after use.

UX is shaped by brand image, presentation (appearance, packaging, documentation), functionality, performance, interactive behavior, help/support/training, learnability, the user’s own prior experience and state, and the context of use.

Usability criteria map onto UX aspects: satisfaction assesses brand image and presentation; effectiveness assesses functionality; efficiency assesses product performance.

1.1.3

Accessibility

Accessibility is the degree to which a product can be used by people with the widest range of characteristics and capabilities to achieve a specified goal in a specified context of use.

1.2

Evaluating Usability, User Experience and Accessibility K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Evaluation typeTarget groupKey objective
Usability evaluationAll usersEvaluate the direct interaction between users and the software product.
User experience evaluationAll usersEvaluate services received before use, the direct interaction, and services received after use.
Accessibility evaluationUsers with disabilitiesEvaluate the direct interaction, focused on accessibility barriers rather than general efficiency or satisfaction.
TechniqueUsers involved?Key characteristic
Usability reviewOptionallyExperts and/or users evaluate the interface for usability problems based on their experience (Chapter 4).
Usability testingYesUsers are observed while performing typical tasks with the product (Chapter 5).
User surveysYesUsers fill out questionnaires about their satisfaction with the product (Chapter 6).

1.2.1

Usability Evaluation

Usability evaluation gathers information about a system’s usability in order to improve it (formative evaluation) or to assess its merit or worth (summative evaluation).

Formative evaluation

Conducted early — during design and prototyping — to understand and guide (“form”) the design by identifying problems. Qualitative.

Summative evaluation

Conducted late, shortly before or after implementation, to measure usability quantitatively against usability requirements.

Both types can be conducted iteratively. Objectives of usability evaluation: assess whether usability requirements are met; uncover usability problems so they can be corrected; measure the usability of the product against effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction.

1.2.2

User Experience Evaluation

Usability is part of user experience, so usability evaluation is part of UX evaluation — using the same principal techniques. UX evaluation additionally covers advertisements, training, touchpoints beyond the screen (support, letters, delivered goods), and problems the user interface itself doesn’t handle, such as delay notifications or complaint handling.

1.2.3

Accessibility Evaluation

Accessibility evaluation is a usability evaluation focused on the interaction between a user with disabilities and the product. Recommended approach:

1. Set an ambition level. WCAG defines three levels: A, AA, AAA. AA is the recommended baseline.

2. Create or adapt accessible-design guidelines that comply with legal requirements and the chosen ambition level; review for accuracy and staff an accessibility hotline.

3. Train development teams on legal requirements, guidelines, tools/techniques, and the usability–accessibility relationship.

4. Focus accessibility testing on understanding accessibility-barrier mistakes (via think-aloud) rather than general efficiency/satisfaction, using tasks targeted at specific areas of concern.

1.3

Usability Evaluation in Human-Centered Design K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Human-centered design makes products more usable by focusing on their use and applying human factors, ergonomics and usability knowledge [ISO 9241-210]. The process cycles through four activities:

Analyze

Talk with people and discover what the problem is; specify the context of use.

Design

Prototype what you assume is a solution; convert insights into testable user requirements.

Evaluate

Watch people use the prototype and learn from their experience — via usability review, think-aloud testing, and surveys.

Iterate

Repeat design ↔ evaluate until usability requirements are achieved.

Three key elements underpin the process: users (observed and interviewed throughout; in agile, typically represented by the product owner), evaluation (can occur at any point, from early analysis to delivery and beyond — early evaluation is more cost-effective), and iterations between design and evaluation, most often via successively refined prototypes.

1.3.1

Usability Requirements

A usability requirement is a requirement on the usability of a component or system, providing the basis for evaluating whether the product meets identified user needs. Sources: explicit statements (requirements docs, user stories), implicit undocumented expectations, or adopted standards (Chapter 3).

Example

“As a frequent user of the airline’s booking portal, an overview of my currently booked flights shall be shown automatically after I log on.” — an effectiveness requirement. “As a help-desk assistant, I must be able to log a customer request in no more than two steps.” — an efficiency requirement.

1.3.2

Agile Usability Evaluation

Usability evaluation adapts well to agile’s short, collaborative iterations. Approaches that work particularly well:

RITE — Rapid Iterative Testing and Evaluation

Qualitative method where the interface is changed as soon as a problem is identified and a fix is clear — sometimes after just one test participant — then confirmed with the remaining participants.

Informal, quick sessions

Under fifteen minutes, run wherever potential users are found (a cafe, a conference), using think-aloud and heuristic evaluation.

Weekly testing

Participants recruited in advance for a fixed weekday so each build gets tested; tasks are often exploratory, guided by heuristic checklists.

Chapter 1 in one screen

Usability
Effectiveness × efficiency × satisfaction, in a specified context of use.
User experience
Broader than usability: perceptions and responses before, during and after use.
Accessibility
Usable by the widest range of people and capabilities.
Formative vs. summative
Improve the design (qualitative, early) vs. measure the design (quantitative, late).
Three evaluation techniques
Usability review (Ch. 4), usability testing (Ch. 5), user surveys (Ch. 6).
Human-centered design cycle
Analyze → Design → Evaluate → Iterate, built on users, evaluation, and iteration.
RITE
Change the interface as soon as a problem and fix are clear — a strong fit for agile.

Introduction Typical Risks

Chapter 2 · CT-UT

Risks in Usability, User Experience and Accessibility

A risk is a factor that could lead to negative consequences, expressed as impact and likelihood. This chapter separates product risks — usability, UX and accessibility problems in the software itself — from project risks that threaten an organization’s ability to meet its usability objectives.

  • product riskA risk directly related to the test object.
  • project riskA risk related to management and control of the (test) project, e.g., lack of staffing, strict deadlines, changing requirements, etc.

2.1

Introduction

Product risks impact the overall quality of the software; project risks impact a project’s ability to deliver its usability objectives. A risk assessment identifies both: product risks are tested using usability testing techniques, while project risks are tracked so the project stays on course.

Risks can be identified through interviews, risk workshops, brainstorming, and drawing on past experience — supported by checklists such as the ones in section 2.2. The assessment looks at factors like number and type of users, usage frequency, the damage caused when a task can’t be completed, task criticality to the business, and external visibility. Involving the broadest possible group of stakeholders — domain experts, end users, usability experts, acceptance testers, design team members, customer representatives — makes the identified risks more complete.

2.2

Typical Risks K2–K4K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences.

2.2.1

Usability Risks

Users won’t buy or use the product because it lacks effectiveness, efficiency or satisfaction.

Users buy it, then return it demanding a refund because they can’t make it work — even though it works as specified.

Users buy it but repeatedly call support because they don’t understand how to use it.

Users report dissatisfaction on social media, damaging consumer trust and brand equity.

Users resist a product essential to their daily work; forced use generates stress, falling productivity and an oppressive atmosphere.

Increased liability from risk to health or financial loss caused by a poorly designed or deceptive interface.

2.2.2

User Experience Risks

UX risks can cause failures in the product or its surrounding support systems — for example, shopping-cart abandonment when an app is slow, awkward, or unpleasant. Usability can also be fine while everything around it fails:

Support

Answers customer inquiries slowly, rudely, superficially, or not at all.

Documentation

User documentation is deficient or missing.

Delivery

Delays are not communicated to the user.

Fulfillment

The delivered product doesn’t match expectations, or arrives in unattractive/impractical packaging.

2.2.3

Accessibility Risks

An accessibility risk is a potential product failure relating to accessibility — most seriously, the product cannot be used by people with disabilities (violating regulations), or it is incompatible with the assistive software or hardware those users rely on.

2.2.4

Project Risks

CategoryTypical risks
OrganizationalLack of qualified usability specialists; insufficient basic usability knowledge among designers/developers; low usability maturity; management dismissing results as subjective; releasing despite clear evaluation findings; poor or missing usability requirements.
TechnicalNo usability evaluation performed; evaluation happens too late to act on; unrealistic test environments or sample data; unusable (too long, opinion-based) test reports; unclear definition of a “typical” user system; limited availability of qualified test participants.
SupplierSuppliers lack usability testing qualifications; don’t follow agreed evaluation guidelines; deliver results late or not at all.

Chapter 2 in one screen

Product risk
Threatens usability, UX, or accessibility quality — tested with usability testing techniques.
Project risk
Threatens the project’s ability to meet its usability objectives — organizational, technical, or supplier-side.
Risk identification
Interviews, workshops, brainstorming, past experience, checklists — broadened by involving diverse stakeholders.

Usability Standards Accessibility Standards

Chapter 3 · CT-UT

Usability and Accessibility Standards

Standards and manufacturer guidelines give reviewers and designers a shared, low-interpretation baseline for what counts as acceptable usability and accessibility. This chapter covers the ISO 9241 family, manufacturer platform guidelines, ISO 9241-171, WCAG’s three conformance levels, and the main UK/US accessibility laws.

  • user interface guidelineA low-level, specific rule or recommendation for user interface design that leaves little room for interpretation so designers implement it similarly.
  • Web Content Accessibility GuidelinesA part of a series of web accessibility guidelines published by the Web Accessibility Initiative (WAI) of the W3C.Abbreviation: WCAG

3.1

Usability Standards and Manufacturer Guidelines K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

A usability standard is a collection of user interface guidelines for designing efficient and satisfactory dialogues. A user interface guideline is a low-level, specific rule that leaves little room for interpretation, so designers implement it consistently — covering control size/placement, instruction clarity, error messages, layout, color, sound and more.

Example

“The company logo must appear in the upper-left corner of every page, in the same position as on the home page. Clicking it must return to the home page.” — precise enough that two designers implement it identically.

3.1.1

ISO Usability Standards

StandardCovers
ISO 9241-110Seven dialogue principles for effective, efficient interactive systems: suitability for the task, self-descriptiveness, conformity with user expectations, suitability for learning, controllability, error tolerance, suitability for individualization. General and heuristic-like, so open to interpretation.
ISO 9241-210Human-centered design for interactive systems — principles and activities (see section 1.3).
ISO 25066 (2016)Common Industry Format (CIF) for usability evaluation reports — classifies evaluation approaches and specifies report content.

There is currently no ISO standard specifically for usability evaluation or usability testing methodology itself.

3.1.2

Manufacturer Guidelines

GuidelineExample section titles
Apple OS X Human Interface GuidelinesStarting/stopping, modality, interoperability, feedback and assistance, interaction and input, animation, branding, color and typography, icons and graphics.
Android User Interface Guidelines (Google)Animation, style, layout, components, patterns, usability.
Microsoft Windows UX Interaction GuidelinesDesign principles, controls, commands, text, messages, interaction, windows, visuals.
SAP design guidelines and resourcesAction, container, data visualization, display, filter, list, loading, popover, table, toolbar, user input.

3.2

Accessibility Standards K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

An accessibility standard is a collection of user interface guidelines for designing accessible dialogues.

3.2.1

ISO Standards

ISO 9241-171 — Guidance on software accessibility — provides definitions (e.g. a screen reader is “assistive technology that allows users to operate software without needing to view the visual display”) plus over 140 guidelines with notes and examples, such as: “Each name of a user interface element and its association shall be made available by the software system to assistive technology in a documented and stable fashion.”

3.2.2

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)

WCAG is published by the W3C’s Web Accessibility Initiative (WAI) and defines three conformance levels.

LevelDescriptionExample
AHigh impact across a broad array of users; not focused on one disability type; lowest implementation cost.All non-text content has an equivalent text alternative; all functionality is keyboard-operable.
AAAlso high impact, sometimes for specific populations; may require presentation/business-logic changes.Text can be resized up to 200% without loss of content or function.
AAAImprovements for specific populations; can be costly or platform-limited; often lower priority.All functionality is keyboard-operable without requiring specific keystroke timing.

AA is the recommended baseline conformance level (see section 1.2.3).

3.2.3

Accessibility Legislation

Equality Act 2010 (UK)

Protects against discrimination; a Statutory Code of Practice brings websites under “provision of services.” Organizations must take “reasonable” steps toward accessibility — WCAG Level A is generally seen as the legal minimum, Level AA as the minimum for proper accessibility.

Americans with Disabilities Act (US)

Prohibits disability discrimination; requires private websites be accessible to blind/visually impaired users. The Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (Section 508) requires federal agencies’ electronic/IT to be accessible.

Chapter 3 in one screen

User interface guideline
A precise, low-interpretation rule ensuring consistent implementation.
ISO 9241-110
Seven dialogue principles for effective interactive systems.
ISO 9241-171
140+ software accessibility guidelines.
WCAG levels
A (broad, low cost) → AA (recommended baseline) → AAA (specialized, costly).
UK / US law
Equality Act 2010 and the ADA / Section 508 both push toward WCAG-aligned accessibility.

Introduction & Approach Types of Review

Chapter 4 · CT-UT

Usability Reviews

A usability review relies on the judgment of one or more reviewers examining a product to spot potential usability problems, without necessarily involving real users. This chapter covers the six-step review approach, its risks, and the three main review types — informal, expert, and heuristic evaluation — including Nielsen’s ten usability heuristics.

  • expert usability reviewAn informal usability review in which the reviewers are experts. Experts can be usability experts or subject matter experts, or both.
  • heuristicA generally recognized rule of thumb that helps to achieve a goal.

4.1

Introduction and Approach K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

A usability review evaluates a product against usability requirements, user interface guidelines, usability standards, or prior experience of usability problems. Reviewers are typically usability experts, subject matter experts, design team members, testers, customer representatives, or potential users. Reviews work best when the interface itself can be seen — screenshots are easier to interpret than narrative descriptions.

4.1.1

Step-By-Step Approach to Usability Reviews

1. Prepare

Agree goals with stakeholders; select a method (informal, expert, heuristic); select reviewers.

2. Optional walkthrough

The author may present the application for information only — care is taken not to bias reviewers before they evaluate it.

3. Individual evaluation

Each reviewer works alone, asking: who is using this, why, what are their goals, and what perspective do they bring? Then evaluates and writes down findings.

4. Consensus

Multiple reviewers meet to agree on findings; only consensus findings make the report — removing anything peculiar to one reviewer.

5. Present findings

Findings with majority agreement are presented to the author and stakeholders (may be combined with step 4).

6. Report

One reviewer writes the usability review report, structured like the usability test report (section 5.6.4).

4.1.2

Risks and Challenges

Reviews are opinion-based, which risks arguments over views rather than facts — often a sign of low usability maturity or inexperienced reviewers. The value of a review is diminished if:

Reviewers don’t discuss candidly, so an incorrect finding from one reviewer gets accepted unchallenged.

Reviewers aren’t familiar enough with the product to produce useful findings.

Reviewers lack the respect of peers, so their good findings get dismissed.

Reviewers fixate on minor guideline violations and miss serious effectiveness/efficiency problems.

4.2

Types of Usability Review K2–K4K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences.

4.2.1

Informal Usability Review

Based on the judgment of one or more reviewers examining the product to identify potential problems — often relying on opinion, personal experience, and common sense. No formal usability qualification is required, though a reviewer with a year or two of experience adds value.

4.2.2

Expert Usability Review

An expert usability review is an informal review in which the reviewers are experts — recognized as such by independent peers — drawing on extensive experience from usability tests and introspection (observing themselves performing tasks). Expert review is often combined with heuristic evaluation: start with the expert review, then re-check against heuristics to catch anything missed.

4.2.3

Heuristic Evaluation

Reviewers — preferably experts — compare the interface against a list of heuristics: generally recognized, comprehensible rules of thumb, typically grouped in sets of about ten. Jakob Nielsen’s widely used set:

#HeuristicIn short
1Visibility of system statusKeep users informed via timely, appropriate feedback.
2Match between system and the real worldSpeak the user’s language; follow real-world conventions.
3User control and freedomProvide a clearly marked emergency exit; support undo/redo.
4Consistency and standardsSame words/actions should mean the same thing; follow platform conventions.
5Error preventionPrevent problems before they occur, or confirm before committing.
6Recognition rather than recallMake objects, actions and options visible; minimize memory load.
7Flexibility and efficiency of useAccelerators for experts that novices never need to notice.
8Aesthetic and minimalist designEvery extra unit of information competes with the relevant ones.
9Help users recognize, diagnose, recover from errorsPlain-language messages that precisely state the problem and suggest a fix.
10Help and documentationEasy to search, task-focused, concrete steps, not too large.

Risks of heuristic evaluation: usability issues are often too complex for a limited heuristic set to capture; heuristics can’t account for context of use; it’s easy to evaluate on intuition first and retrofit a heuristic label afterward (the correct order is heuristic-first); and heuristics require experience to interpret — reviewers should resist inventing their own.

Chapter 4 in one screen

Usability review
Judgment-based evaluation by reviewers, not necessarily involving end users.
Six-step approach
Prepare → (optional walkthrough) → individual evaluation → consensus → present → report.
Informal review
Any reviewer, opinion and common sense.
Expert review
Reviewers recognized as experts by their peers; often paired with heuristic evaluation.
Heuristic evaluation
Compares the interface against ~10 recognized rules of thumb, e.g. Nielsen’s set.

Chapter 5 · CT-UT

Usability Testing

The largest chapter in the syllabus, and its practical core: how to plan a usability test, script and task it, run test sessions with real participants, analyze and rate the findings, write a report stakeholders will actually read, and quality-control the whole process.

  • findingA result of an evaluation that identifies some important issue, problem, or opportunity.
  • moderator(1) The leader of an inspection or review process. (2) A neutral person who conducts a usability test session.Synonyms: facilitator
  • think aloud usability testingA technique where test participants share their thoughts with the moderator and observers while solving usability test tasks.
  • usability test participantA representative user who solves typical tasks in a usability test.
  • usability test scriptA document specifying a sequence of actions for the execution of a usability test.
  • usability test sessionA test session in which a usability test participant executes tests, moderated by a moderator and observed by a number of observers.
  • usability test taskA usability test execution activity specified by the moderator, to be accomplished by a participant within a given time.
  • usability testingTesting to evaluate the degree to which the system can be used by specified users with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

5.1

Introduction

Usability testing evaluates the degree to which a system can be used by specified users with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified context of use. A usability test consists of a series of usability test sessions: in each, a usability test participant performs representative tasks on the product or a prototype, moderated by a moderator and watched by observers. Testing should happen under conditions as close as possible to real use — sometimes a mock office or living room — ideally observable from a neighboring room.

5.2

Step-By-Step Approach to Usability Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

1. Prepare usability test

Create the test plan; recruit participants; write the test script(s); define test tasks; run a pilot session.

2. Conduct test sessions

Prepare the session; brief with pre-session instructions; pre-session interview; moderate; post-session interview.

3. Communicate results

Analyze findings; write the usability test report; sell the findings to stakeholders.

5.3

Prepare Usability Test K2–K3K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

5.3.1

Usability Test Plan

A short (one-to-two page) document describing the purpose and extent of the test, reviewed by stakeholders and management. Its contents:

Goals — assess whether usability requirements are met, uncover problems, and (uniquely for testing) convincingly demonstrate problems exist to stakeholders.

User group(s) and the people involved: moderator, test participant, note-taker, and observers (see Chapter 8 for roles).

Reference to the usability requirements being evaluated, if applicable.

Techniques to be used, such as think-aloud — participants voice their thoughts so the moderator, note-taker and observers understand their reasoning.

Planned number of participants, schedule, session length, responsible moderator, and a resource/cost estimate (hours, incentives).

Location: face-to-face is typical, but remote testing (participant and moderator in different locations) and unmoderated testing (section 7.1.1) are also used.

How findings will be communicated.

5.3.2

Usability Test Script

A checklist the moderator uses to run the session: pre-session preparation, briefing instructions, pre-session interview questions, usability test tasks, and post-session interview questions.

5.3.3

Usability Test Tasks

A good task matches the test plan’s goals, is meaningful from the participant’s point of view (not a system-oriented chore like “log in”, but a real goal like “order a product”), and matters to stakeholders. Each task specifies: the exact scenario wording; preconditions and available resources; a justification for what it’s meant to evaluate; any data supplied; and completion/abandonment criteria (e.g. “abandon after 10 minutes without an answer”).

Ordering matters: start and end with something simple so participants aren’t stressed or left on a frustrating note; put essential tasks before minor ones; sequence tasks the way a real user naturally would (order before cancel); and avoid one task depending on a previous task’s success.

5.3.4

Test Location

Options range from a dedicated usability test lab, two rooms linked by video, an ordinary office room, the participant’s own home or workplace, to a public place like a cafe for quick sub-ten-minute sessions. Observers — the primary users of the test setup — must be able to come, go, and discuss freely without disturbing the session; any rule that restricts their behavior is a sign the setup itself has a usability problem. Remote screen-sharing for observers is possible but loses the value of in-person stakeholder discussion.

5.3.5

Usability Test Lab

Typically two rooms — a test room for the participant and an observation room for observers/note-takers — separated by a one-way mirror, with cameras (C) in the test room feeding monitors (M) in the observation room.

Advantages

Group observation; easy to observe and video-record; consistent test conditions; observers can enter/leave freely; visibly demonstrates organizational commitment to usability.

Disadvantages

The context is artificial; expensive to set up and maintain.

5.3.6

Pilot Usability Test Session

A dry run against the test script to verify the script and setup work. If serious problems surface, the script is revised and re-piloted. Real users are preferred as pilot participants; colleagues are an acceptable substitute, but never the people who designed the product. Findings from a pilot session can sometimes be folded into the real test — e.g. if an over-qualified pilot participant still hits a genuine usability problem.

5.4

Conduct Usability Test Sessions K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

ActivityWhat happens
PreparationThe moderator sets up hardware, software and tasks before the participant arrives.
BriefingThe moderator explains the test’s purpose and the participant’s role.
Pre-session interviewQuestions about the participant’s background and prior experience with the product.
ModerationThe participant solves tasks while thinking aloud; the moderator quietly observes and only nudges them onward if they’re completely stuck.
Post-session interview“Which 2–3 things did you like most?” and “which 2–3 things most need improvement?”

5.5

Analysis of Findings K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

The process for extracting findings from session observations:

1. The note-taker records observations during each session.

2. Moderator and note-taker meet right after each session for a candid discussion while memory is fresh.

3. After all sessions, each separately extracts ~20–30 usability findings and ~5–10 positive findings.

4. They meet again and merge into one common list of the same rough size.

5. The moderator logs problems in the usability/defect tracking tool.

6. The moderator tracks problems to resolution and reviews the fix — re-testing if the fix itself carries risk.

Note

Discussions must be candid and observation-based, not opinion-based. Reporting all seventy problems found, unfiltered, is not acceptable — prioritizing and limiting the list is the moderator’s job.

5.6

Communicate Results and Findings K2–K3K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

5.6.1

Results

Test results show what representative users can actually accomplish on representative tasks — not their opinions. A task like “is the home page design appropriate?” is opinion-based and inappropriate for a test. A spontaneous remark shared by a majority of participants (“the home page is really pretty”) can be reported; a single participant’s prediction about “most others” is personal opinion worth following up (“why do you think so?”) rather than reporting directly.

5.6.2

Usability Findings

A finding identifies an important issue, problem or opportunity. Positive findings matter too: they balance the report, tell the team what not to break, and give a complete picture. Each finding should include a classification and severity rating, a short header, a description backed by at least two examples, optional participant quotes, optional recommendations, and optional screenshots.

ClassificationMeaning
Usability problemRequires a severity rating (below).
Positive findingWorks well; recommend keeping this approach.
Good ideaA participant suggestion that could meaningfully improve UX.
Functional problemA defect, not a usability issue.
SeverityMeaning
MinorMinor dissatisfaction, noticeable delays, or superficial difficulty.
MajorSubstantial delays or moderate dissatisfaction.
CriticalParticipants gave up — a showstopper causing substantial dissatisfaction or minor financial damage.
CatastrophicExistential threat — potential bodily harm or substantial financial damage.

Ratings weigh frequency (how often it occurs), impact (how badly it hurts the user), and persistence (how fast users learn to avoid it).

5.6.3

Selling Findings to Stakeholders

Non-usability stakeholders may need convincing — some developers see “their” interface as an extension of themselves. If findings aren’t accepted, little changes. Where organizational usability maturity is low, testing (and then persuasively presenting the results) may be the only way to make the cost of ignoring usability visible. Involving stakeholders throughout — in risk assessment, plan/script/task review, recruitment, and observing sessions — builds buy-in and makes findings easier to accept. Agile development implicitly supports this: the product owner participates directly, and the whole-team approach builds shared ownership of quality.

5.6.4

Usability Test Report

Mandatory for every usability test, usually written by the usability tester or moderator, and aimed squarely at the people who decide what changes get made.

SectionContents
1Executive summary — object of evaluation, techniques used, top findings, recommendations.
2Table of contents.
3Findings and recommendations (section 5.6.2).
4Objectives of the evaluation.
5Purpose, including relevant usability requirements.
6Evaluation method — approach, physical/technical environment, test script, anonymized participant list.
7Contacts — moderator(s) and note-taker(s).

5.6.5

Best Practices in Usability Test Reporting

Involve and respect stakeholders

Have the development team help write the report; incorporate their findings even when they differ; avoid usability jargon.

Keep it short

At most ~25 findings and ~20 pages, regardless of test size.

Usable executive summary

One page, only the most important findings, placed at the front.

Keep to the point

Crisp descriptions; avoid lengthy explanations of what usability is; short participant quotes are fine.

Rate severity, include positives

Every finding rated; positive findings included for balance.

Respect privacy

Exclude recruitment details like screener copies and participant confirmations.

In agile development these practices apply more loosely: documentation is lighter, sometimes a verbal briefing rather than a full report; findings often flow straight into backlog items or bug reports; and results are discussed and agreed within the whole team, often undocumented, in daily standups or retrospectives.

5.7

Quality Control of a Usability Test K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Check the test plan contains everything section 5.3.1 requires, and that it was properly reviewed and approved.

Check the script (especially tasks) matches the plan’s purpose, and that participant profiles match it too.

Observe the first two or three sessions to confirm they follow the script.

Compare the moderator’s and note-taker’s notes against your own observations; raise an issue if important findings went unnoted.

Compare actual time/resources consumed against the plan’s estimates; raise discrepancies.

Check findings were communicated as planned and the report meets the best practices of 5.6.5.

Discuss the report with representative stakeholders; attend result discussions and confirm they’re two-way and constructive.

5.8

Challenges and Frequent Mistakes K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

MistakeDescription
Unclear purposeNot described in the test plan and approved before testing starts.
Scheduling too lateNo time left to fix problems before release (less likely under agile).
Critical results ignoredManagement overrules serious findings.
Incorrect focusChasing minor guideline violations while real effectiveness/efficiency problems go unaddressed.
Moderator too activeShould passively observe — not interview, entertain, or demo the product.
No post-session interviewLoses the participant’s summary impression.
No stakeholder involvementStakeholders excluded from planning and review.
Unusable reportToo long, too many findings, no one-page summary.
No positive findingsUndermines acceptance of the results.
Findings not categorizedReaders can’t quickly tell critical from minor.

Chapter 5 in one screen

Three-step approach
Prepare → conduct sessions → communicate results.
Test plan vs. script vs. tasks
Plan = why/who/how (1–2 pages); script = the moderator’s checklist; tasks = the concrete scenarios given to participants.
Usability test lab
Two rooms, one-way mirror; realistic but artificial and expensive.
Analysis
Note-taker + moderator merge ~20–30 findings and ~5–10 positives from candid, evidence-based discussion.
Severity scale
Minor → Major → Critical → Catastrophic, weighted by frequency, impact, persistence.
Report best practice
≤25 findings, ≤20 pages, one-page executive summary, stakeholder-involved, positives included.
