Introduction User Surveys Standardized Questionnaires

Chapter 6 · CT-UT

User Surveys

A user survey gathers subjective, questionnaire-based feedback from a representative sample of users — the third evaluation technique alongside review and testing. This chapter covers the six-step survey process and three standardized, publicly available questionnaires: SUS, SUMI and WAMMI.

  • user surveyA usability evaluation whereby a representative sample of users report subjective evaluation into a questionnaire based on their experience.
  • System Usability ScaleA simple, ten-item attitude scale giving a global view of subjective usability assessments.Abbreviation: SUS
  • Software Usability Measurement InventoryA questionnaire-based usability test technique for measuring software quality from the end user’s point of view.Abbreviation: SUMI
  • Website Analysis and Measurement InventoryA questionnaire-based usability test technique for measuring website quality from the end user’s point of view.Abbreviation: WAMMI

6.1

Introduction

A user survey asks a representative sample of users to report subjective evaluation via a questionnaire, based on their experience with a component or system. Surveys evaluate levels of user satisfaction.

6.2

Step-By-Step Approach to User Surveys K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

1. Write a survey plan

Similar to a usability test plan — goals, resources, schedule — reviewed and approved by stakeholders.

2. Interview users and stakeholders

Gather input on what the survey should focus on, drawing on recent, vivid experience.

3. Select a questionnaire

Choose between a standard questionnaire or building a dedicated one (not covered in this syllabus).

4. Deploy the questionnaire

Recruit participants, publish the survey, and follow up with non-responders where possible.

5. Analyze responses

Process the collected data.

6. Communicate results

Write a report that answers stakeholders’ questions and present the results.

6.3

Standardized Questionnaires K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Standardized questionnaires are preferred over self-invented ones because they permit benchmarking against a database of prior measurements and yield concrete usability numbers usable as completion or acceptance criteria.

SUS — System Usability Scale

A simple ten-item attitude scale, referenced in 1,300+ publications. Participants score each item from Strongly Agree to Strongly Disagree. Sample items: “I think that I would like to use this system frequently”; “I found the system unnecessarily complex”; “I thought the system was easy to use.”

SUMI — Software Usability Measurement Inventory

Fifty statements, each answered Agree / Don’t Know / Disagree. Sample items: “This software responds too slowly to inputs”; “The instructions and prompts are helpful.”

WAMMI — Website Analysis and Measurement Inventory

Twenty statements focused specifically on website usability — attractiveness, controllability, efficiency, helpfulness, and learnability — scored Strongly Agree to Strongly Disagree.

Chapter 6 in one screen

User survey
Subjective, questionnaire-based evaluation of user satisfaction.
Six-step process
Plan → interview → select questionnaire → deploy → analyze → communicate.
SUS
10 items, general usability attitude scale.
SUMI
50 items, Agree/Don’t Know/Disagree, software quality.
WAMMI
20 items, website-specific usability.

✦ Study Hub
Selecting a Method

Chapter 7 · CT-UT

Selecting Appropriate Methods

With usability review, usability testing and user surveys all available, this short chapter gives the criteria for choosing between them — purpose, organizational usability maturity, time available, project stage, resources, end-user availability, and lifecycle model — for usability, UX, and accessibility evaluation alike.

7.1

Criteria for Selecting a Method K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences.

7.1.1

Selecting a Usability Evaluation Method

1. Purpose

Effectiveness → usability testing or review. Efficiency, or measuring improvement → quantitative usability test. Satisfaction → user survey. Raising usability awareness/maturity → usability testing, to convince skeptical stakeholders.

2. Usability maturity of the organization

High: a full human-centered design process with milestones. Medium: quality/time/resource needs are known and controlled. Low: individuals follow human-centered practice unsystematically. Very low: indifference or hostility to usability. Favor testing over review when maturity is low or very low — a review’s conclusions are too easily dismissed as opinion.

3. Completion time

Reviews are fastest, often completed within days; unmoderated tests can also be fast.

4. Project stage

Early design, prototypes only → a formative method: review, quantitative evaluation, or survey.

5. Resources

If time, money or specialists are scarce: run a short-form test (moderator doubles as note-taker, no lab, 3–5 participants, a short report of ~15 findings), an unmoderated test (fast recruiting, cheaper, same analysis effort), or RITE (fix as soon as one participant reveals a clear problem).

6. Availability of end users

If real end users are scarce or expensive to recruit, prefer usability review over testing.

7. Lifecycle model

All methods work with sequential models like the V-Model. Agile’s short iterations favor RITE and short-form testing, where fast turnaround matters most.

Mixing methods across a project is common practice — reviews early to catch the worst problems cheaply, then testing later; or a quick informal test at a cafe followed by formal in-depth sessions.

7.1.2

Selecting a User Experience Evaluation Method

The same criteria used for selecting a usability evaluation method apply to selecting a user experience evaluation method.

7.1.3

Selecting an Accessibility Evaluation Method

Key criteria: legal requirements, organizational requirements, and the number of users with disabilities in the product’s target groups.

Chapter 7 in one screen

Purpose drives method
Effectiveness/awareness → testing or review; efficiency → quantitative test; satisfaction → survey.
Low usability maturity
Favor testing — review findings are too easy to dismiss as opinion.
Tight resources
Short-form test, unmoderated test, or RITE.
Accessibility method choice
Driven by legal/organizational requirements and the size of the affected user group.
Mixing methods
Common and recommended — match the method to the lifecycle stage.

Usability Tester Moderator & Note-Taker

Chapter 8 · CT-UT

Summary of Roles and Responsibilities

A closing look at who does what across a usability evaluation: the usability tester who owns the process end to end, and the moderator and note-taker who run individual test sessions — roles the usability tester steps into directly when a project has no one else to fill them.

8.1

Usability Tester K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

TaskReference
Organize and participate in usability risk assessmentChapter 2
Write a usability test plan; prepare the test session (scripts, briefing instructions, interview questions, tasks)Section 5.3
Prepare a usability review: determine goals, select method(s), select reviewersSection 4.1.1
Conduct a usability survey: create the survey plan, select a questionnaire, analyze responses, report resultsSection 6.2
Perform the Moderator role if none is separately definedSection 8.2
Perform the Note-Taker role if none is separately definedSection 8.2

8.2

Moderator and Note-Taker K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Moderator

Participates in usability risk assessment; conducts test sessions (briefing, running the script, communicating with the participant, post-session interview); analyzes and discusses findings; logs and tracks usability problems to resolution and reviews implemented solutions; performs the Note-Taker role if none is separately defined.

Note-Taker

Records important usability findings during the session; analyzes and discusses findings alongside the moderator.

Note

The moderator is the only person permitted to talk to the test participant during a session (section 5.3.1) — a rule that keeps observers and stakeholders from unintentionally biasing the participant.

Chapter 8 in one screen

Usability Tester
Owns risk assessment, test/review/survey planning, and steps into Moderator or Note-Taker if no one else is assigned.
Moderator
The only person who talks to the participant during a session; drives analysis and tracks problems to resolution.
Note-Taker
Records findings during the session and helps analyze them afterward.

Fundamental Relationships Business Analysis & Testing

Chapter 1 · CT-AcT

Introduction and Foundations

Acceptance testing sits at the intersection of business analysis and testing: business goals cascade down into requirements, then into acceptance criteria, then into acceptance tests. This chapter traces that chain, shows where business analysts and testers collaborate along the way, and introduces the two approaches — ATDD and BDD — that let acceptance testing actively shape development instead of just checking it afterward.

  • acceptance criteriaThe criteria that a component or system must satisfy in order to be accepted by a user, customer, or other authorized entity.
  • acceptance testingFormal testing with respect to user needs, requirements, and business processes conducted to determine whether or not a system satisfies the acceptance criteria and to enable the user, customer or other authorized entity to determine whether or not to accept the system.
  • requirementA provision that contains criteria to be fulfilled.
  • user storyA high-level user or business requirement commonly used in Agile software development, typically consisting of one sentence in the everyday or business language capturing what functionality a user needs and the reason behind this, any non-functional criteria, and also includes acceptance criteria.

1.1

Fundamental Relationships K1–K2K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

The roles of tester and business analyst are different, but their work is complementary — what one does can strongly affect the other, positively or negatively. This matters most at acceptance level, where the system’s readiness for deployment and real customer use is being assessed, so close collaboration between the two roles is essential.

1.1.1

Business Goals, Business Needs and Requirements

Business analysts first understand an organization’s overall business goals and identify current business processes and stakeholders. From there they describe specific business needs and build a business case that addresses them. Only once that groundwork is done can requirements for the business solution be elicited.

Business goals → business needs → business requirements → product requirements — four levels of abstraction describing what shall be achieved. In Agile development the same principle applies, just under different names (e.g. features and user stories).

In this syllabus, “requirements” refers to both business requirements and product requirements.

1.1.2

Requirements / User Stories, Acceptance Criteria and Acceptance Tests

During requirements elicitation, business analysts and testers — ideally together with developers — should start drafting acceptance criteria and acceptance tests as a joint effort, right from the start of the project. This builds a shared understanding of what “acceptable” means from the business, development and testing perspectives before anyone has written code.

Acceptance criteria

Attached directly to a requirement or user story (extending it, if a user story). Measurable statements that are either true or false, used to check whether the requirement was implemented as expected. They define what to test, not the detailed test procedure.

Acceptance test cases

Derived from acceptance criteria. They specify how the verification of each criterion should actually be performed.

1.1.3

The Importance of the Quality of the Requirements

Acceptance criteria and tests built on vague or ambiguous requirements force testers to guess at stakeholder expectations — producing flawed acceptance tests, rework, or worse, tests that run but validate nothing, all while creating risk and uncertainty about product quality.

Note

Testers need to work closely with business analysts to keep requirements clear and resolve ambiguity before it reaches acceptance tests. In Agile development, the INVEST criteria [Cohn04] give business analysts, developers and testers a shared checklist for assessing user story quality; the ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2011 standard provides good practice for the requirements engineering process more broadly.

1.2

Business Analysis and Acceptance Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Business analysts and testers who work in separate silos risk letting misunderstandings about business and customer expectations stay hidden until release is near. Working together — and considering acceptance criteria and testing as early as possible — lets the two roles positively shape the development process instead.

1.2.1

Relationship between Business Analysis and Testing Activities

Business analysis (IQBBA®)

Strategy definition; management of the business analysis process; requirements engineering; solution evaluation and optimization.

Test process (ISTQB®)

Test planning; test monitoring and control; test analysis; test design; test implementation; test execution; test completion.

These activities interlock throughout the project:

Business analysis phaseMeets testing at…
Requirements engineeringRequirements become the test basis for test planning, analysis and design. Testers contribute to defining and verifying acceptance criteria; both roles jointly assess the impact of requirement changes.
Solution evaluationBusiness analysts support test implementation and execution — reviewing scripts, clarifying issues, helping create business-related test data, evaluating results, and assisting with test completion.

The relationship is symbiotic from the very start of a project through to acceptance or release.

1.2.2

Collaboration between Business Analysts and Testers in Acceptance Testing

Both roles share one goal: producing the highest possible value for the customer. Beyond joint discussions and artifact reviews, risk-based test planning is a particularly good collaboration opportunity — it helps ensure the right test cases get developed and prioritized.

Note

Working together also cross-trains the team: the more testers understand business needs, and the more business analysts understand structured testing, the better the two groups collaborate.

1.2.3

How Acceptance Testing Can Drive the Development Process: ATDD and BDD

In sequential lifecycles, acceptance test analysis, design and implementation happen after requirements are finalized. In Agile, acceptance criteria and tests are created during requirements analysis, refinement sessions and backlog refinement — putting the “Early Testing” principle into practice by using test-case design as part of defining the requirement itself.

ATDD — Acceptance Test-Driven Development

Acceptance tests are produced collaboratively during requirements analysis by business analysts, product owners, testers and developers together.

BDD — Behavior-Driven Development

Uses the Gherkin scripting language, based on natural-language statements in a “Given – When – Then” format. These requirements become the acceptance test cases and the basis for test automation (see section 2.2.2).

Both approaches engage the whole Agile team, keep development focused on business goals, and treat acceptance tests as living documentation that business analysts and other stakeholders can read and understand. In practice the terms are sometimes used interchangeably: BDD is associated specifically with Gherkin, while ATDD covers other textual or graphic test-design forms too — for example a visual ATDD approach built on workflow diagrams.

Chapter 1 in one screen

Business goals → needs → requirements
Increasing levels of detail describing what shall be achieved; requirements cover both business and product requirements.
Acceptance criteria vs. acceptance tests
Criteria define what to test (measurable, true/false); tests define how to verify it.
Requirement quality
Vague requirements produce flawed acceptance tests; INVEST criteria help assess user-story quality.
Business analysis ↔ testing
Requirements engineering feeds test planning/analysis/design; solution evaluation feeds test implementation/execution/completion.
ATDD
Acceptance tests written collaboratively during requirements analysis by the whole team.
BDD
Gherkin, Given–When–Then; requirements become the acceptance tests and the automation basis.

Writing Acceptance Criteria Designing Acceptance Tests Experience-Based Approaches

Chapter 2 · CT-AcT

Acceptance Criteria, Acceptance Tests and Experience-Based Practices

The largest chapter in the syllabus: how to write acceptance criteria that are actually testable, which techniques turn them into acceptance tests, how the Gherkin “Given – When – Then” pattern works, and where experience-based approaches — exploratory testing and beta testing — complement the more formal ones.

  • beta testingSimulated or actual operational testing conducted at an external site, by roles outside the development organization.
  • experience-based test techniqueA procedure to derive and/or select test cases based on the tester’s experience, knowledge and intuition.Synonyms: experience-based test design technique, experience-based technique
  • exploratory testingAn approach to testing whereby the testers dynamically design and execute tests based on their knowledge, exploration of the test item and the results of previous tests.
  • keyword-driven testingA scripting technique that uses data files to contain not only test data and expected results, but also keywords related to the application being tested.Synonyms: action word-driven testing
  • test caseA set of preconditions, inputs, actions (where applicable), expected results and postconditions, developed based on test conditions.

2.1

Writing Acceptance Criteria K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Specifying acceptance criteria refines a requirement or user story and gives acceptance tests something solid to build on. Business analysts and testers should collaborate closely here — it lifts the business value of the acceptance phase and improves the odds of a successful release.

Writing the criteria forces both roles to think through functionality, performance and other characteristics from a stakeholder or usage perspective — supporting early verification and validation, and surfacing inconsistencies, contradictions or missing information while they’re still cheap to fix.

Precise, measurable, concise. Each criterion must let the tester measure whether the test object complies with it.

No technical solution details. Focus on “What shall be achieved?”, not “How shall it be achieved?”

Cover non-functional as well as functional requirements.

Like requirements and user stories, acceptance criteria should be reviewed — via walkthroughs, technical reviews, or iteration planning meetings.

2.2

Designing Acceptance Tests K2–K3K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

2.2.1

Test Techniques for Acceptance Testing

In a requirements-based approach, the tester derives test cases from the acceptance criteria of each requirement or user story using black-box techniques such as equivalence partitioning or boundary value analysis. Acceptance testing can also be augmented with:

Business process-based testing

Validates business processes and rules, often combined with decision table testing (see Chapter 3).

Experience-based testing

Leverages the tester’s experience, knowledge and intuition (see section 2.3.1).

Risk-based testing

Prioritization and rigor scale with previously identified product risk.

Model-based testing

Uses graphical or textual models to obtain acceptance tests.

Every acceptance criterion should be verified by an acceptance test, with traceability maintained between requirement/user story and test case.

2.2.2

Using the Gherkin Language to Write Test Cases

In ATDD and BDD, acceptance tests are often written in Gherkin: a structured, declarative pattern that phrases a test case in three parts.

  1. 1

    Given [a situation]

    Puts the test object into a defined state before any test action runs.

  2. 2

    When [an action on the system]

    The user action being tested.

  3. 3

    Then [the expected result]

    The observable consequence of the action.

Gherkin test cases describe user actions on the system, not user-interface elements — structured natural language that every stakeholder can read, and that can also be parsed automatically to drive keyword-driven test script generation. Gherkin began as a tool-specific format for BDD but is now effectively synonymous with the “Given – When – Then” acceptance-test design pattern itself.

2.3

Experience-based Approaches for Acceptance Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

All experience-based test techniques are relevant to acceptance testing; this section focuses on exploratory testing as an acceptance technique and on beta testing as a source of real-world usage feedback.

2.3.1

Exploratory Testing

Exploratory testing is not based on detailed predefined procedures. It runs in an uninterrupted block of time called a session, carried out by domain experts who know the user needs, requirements and business processes — but not necessarily the product itself. During a session the tester learns how to work with the product, designs tests, performs them, and interprets the results, all at once.

Good practice

Prepare a test charter beforehand (often jointly, by a business analyst and a tester): its purpose, target and scope, the test setup, session duration, and any tactics to use (e.g. the type of user to simulate). Time-box the session, and consider pairing or team-based exploration.

In Agile development, exploratory sessions can run within an iteration, led by the product owner and/or testers, to acceptance-test the iteration’s user stories — complementing more formal techniques, e.g. giving rapid feedback on a new feature before methodical testing begins.

2.3.2

Beta Testing

Beta testing is common for commercial off-the-shelf software (COTS) and SaaS platforms, gathering market feedback once in-house development and testing are complete. Unlike other acceptance forms, it’s performed by potential or existing users at their own location, without predefined procedures or a test charter — and usually with little documentation beyond the findings observed.

Because real users test real configurations in their own business context, beta testing can surface defects that escaped every earlier stage — helping organizations avoid costly hotfixes or large-scale recalls.

Note

Beta testing alone isn’t enough: it’s neither systematic nor measurable, gives no guarantee of requirement coverage, and happens late — while acceptance-criteria-based testing supports the “Early Testing” principle instead.

Chapter 2 in one screen

Good acceptance criteria
Precise, measurable, concise; no solution detail; cover functional and non-functional needs.
Acceptance test techniques
Requirements-based (black-box) plus business-process-based, experience-based, risk-based, model-based.
Gherkin
Given – When – Then: declarative, stakeholder-readable, machine-parseable for automation.
Exploratory testing
Session-based, charter-guided, domain-expert-led; complements formal techniques.
Beta testing
Real users, real locations, late in the process; valuable but not systematic or a substitute for criteria-based testing.

Business Process Modeling Deriving Acceptance Tests Modeling Good Practices

Chapter 3 · CT-AcT

Business Process and Business Rules Modeling

A graphical, shared language for what a business process is supposed to do makes acceptance testing precise instead of implicit. This chapter covers BPMN and DMN as that shared language, how a coverage criterion turns a business process model into a concrete set of acceptance tests, and the good practices that keep the models themselves useful.

  • coverageThe degree to which specified coverage items have been determined or have been exercised by a test suite expressed as a percentage.Synonyms: test coverage
  • model-based testingTesting based on or involving models.Abbreviation: MBT

3.1

Modeling Business Processes and Rules K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Organizations need confidence that critical business processes — order-to-cash, HR onboarding, production planning — run without disruption: business process assurance, an essential objective of acceptance testing. Two standards give business analysts and testers a common graphical language for this:

BPMN — Business Process Model and Notation

Maintained by the OMG; a flowcharting technique for representing workflows — the flow of tasks, alternative paths, and start/end/intermediate events. This syllabus uses a small, defined subset of BPMN 2.0.1 (Appendix A1), enough to draw simple process models for acceptance testing.

DMN — Decision Model and Notation

Also an OMG standard, complementary to BPMN: where BPMN represents workflow, DMN represents decisions, business rules and outcomes within that workflow. This syllabus uses a defined subset of DMN 1.2 (Appendix A2).

A business process is a flow of tasks, alternative paths and events; business rules define the explicit criteria that guide behavior, judgments or decisions within that flow.

3.2

Deriving Acceptance Tests from Business Process/Rule Models K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

A business process model with its business rules, in BPMN and/or DMN, is a precise definition of the scenarios to test — a strong basis for generating acceptance tests using coverage-based test selection, as in a model-based testing approach.

The business analyst and tester first agree on which coverage items shall be fully tested. Typical coverage items for business process models:

User stories, requirements and risks annotated on the model

Decisions in the decision tables describing the business rules

User scenarios defined by different paths through the process

All paths (usually excluding loops) through the process

Once coverage items are defined, the tester identifies test cases covering them — full coverage means the test suite exercises every occurrence of each coverage item at least once. Different criteria can be combined: e.g. covering every path of the main scenario, but only one path per alternative scenario.

3.3

Business Process Modeling for Acceptance Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Business process/rule models describe the business flow and expected behavior of the test object, and are grounded in good modeling practice that also supports visual ATDD.

3.3.1

Good Practices for Business Process Modeling for Acceptance Testing

Don’t model everything. Focus BPMN diagrams on the requirements to be tested — a workflow that only partially covers system behavior is fine, as long as it covers what will actually be tested.

Use decision tables for rule-based processes. DMN helps manage dependencies by defining conditions and outcomes for the business rules under test.

Keep diagrams simple. Structure into sub-processes to limit elements per diagram — improves readability and makes reviews easier.

Model collaboratively. Business analysts and testers should share and review the artifacts together — early, close communication improves both requirement and test quality.

Annotate. Add links to user stories, requirements, risks and priorities directly on the diagram, so decisions and their reasoning stay in one place.

3.3.2

Using Business Process Models for ATDD

During requirement/user-story refinement sessions, business process and rule models help the team get into the details of expected behavior and acceptance criteria — the BPMN workflow and DMN rules let testers design test cases that directly verify the acceptance criteria.

Business analysts and testers collaborate to model workflows and rules using BPMN/DMN.

Models are reviewed with stakeholders and help validate requirements and acceptance criteria.

Testers derive tests from the models to demonstrate coverage across paths and rules.

Models help identify changes that require test-case maintenance, and support regression test selection.

Maintained models serve as living documentation of the test object’s actual behavior.

Automated test generation can produce and maintain scripts, optionally combined with keyword-driven and data-driven approaches.

The key difference from BDD/Gherkin (Chapter 2): business process/rule modeling for ATDD gives a visualization of the workflow being tested, rather than a textual Given–When–Then specification.

Chapter 3 in one screen

Business process assurance
Confidence that critical business processes run without disruption — a core acceptance testing objective.
BPMN
Workflow notation: tasks, paths, events.
DMN
Decision/rule notation, complementary to BPMN.
Coverage items
User stories/requirements/risks, rule-table decisions, scenario paths, all paths — agreed before deriving tests.
Good modeling practice
Model only what’s tested, keep diagrams simple, collaborate, annotate.
ATDD via models
Visual workflow, vs. Gherkin’s textual Given–When–Then.

Non-functional Characteristics Usability & UX Performance Efficiency Security

Chapter 4 · CT-AcT

Acceptance Testing for Non-Functional Requirements

Acceptance testing covers functional and non-functional requirements — and non-functional quality is only growing more important as software becomes more embedded in everyday life. This chapter maps ISO 25010’s non-functional characteristics and quality-in-use model onto acceptance testing, then goes deeper on the three that most often need a dedicated approach: usability/UX, performance efficiency, and security.

  • performance efficiencyThe degree to which a component or system uses time, resources, and capacity to perform its functions under specified conditions.
  • securityThe degree to which a component or system protects information and data so that persons or other components or systems have the degree of access appropriate to their types and levels of authorization.Synonyms: information security
  • usabilityThe degree to which a component or system can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals in a specified context of use.
  • user experienceA person’s perceptions and responses resulting from the use or anticipated use of a software product.

4.1

Non-functional Characteristics and Quality in Use K1–K2K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Non-functional requirements matter more than ever for acceptance testing, given how much everyday software now depends on data-driven processes and integrated systems of systems.

4.1.1

Non-functional Quality Characteristics and Sub-characteristics

Failing to meet non-functional expectations can mean customer dissatisfaction, lost sales, rejection of the solution, liability risk, or public exposure — regardless of how well the functional requirements were met. ISO 25010 defines a quality model of seven non-functional characteristics, each with its own sub-characteristics:

CharacteristicSub-characteristics
Performance efficiencyTime-behavior, resource utilization, capacity
CompatibilityCo-existence, interoperability
UsabilityAppropriateness recognizability, learnability, operability, user error protection, user interface aesthetics, accessibility
ReliabilityMaturity, availability, fault tolerance, recoverability
SecurityConfidentiality, integrity, non-repudiation, accountability, authenticity
MaintainabilityModularity, reusability, analyzability, modifiability, testability
PortabilityAdaptability, installability, replaceability

An acceptance testing strategy should explicitly define which of these to select and prioritize for a given context. Usability, performance and security get their own sections below because they often demand a dedicated approach to reach the desired coverage.

4.1.2

Quality in Use

Alongside the product-quality model, ISO 25010 defines a quality in use model with five characteristics describing outcomes of an interaction with a system — particularly useful in acceptance testing because they relate directly to the user’s experience:

Effectiveness

Can users accomplish their goals accurately and completely?

Efficiency

What resources does that accomplishment cost?

Satisfaction

Are user needs met, including comfort and trust?

Freedom from risk

Are economic, health, safety or environmental risks mitigated?

Context coverage

Does effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction hold across all intended contexts of use?

4.2

Usability and User Experience K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Per ISO 25010, usability is the degree to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified context of use — assessable via heuristics against objectives like learnability, efficiency, memorability, satisfaction, and error prevention. Poor usability risks frustration and refusal to use the software, and in critical systems, injury or death.

User experience (UX) broadens usability to include aesthetic and emotional factors: an appealing design, confidence-building, pleasure, comfort. Context strongly shapes UX — location (desk, car, hiking), weather, the user’s health (fatigue, age), environment (stressful, noisy) can all change the experience of the same product.

Further detail on usability testing methods is in the ISTQB Foundation Level Usability Testing syllabus.

4.2.1

UX Requirements Analysis

UX requirements analysis rests on four pillars:

User analysis

Categorize users by physical/intellectual characteristics, technical skill, business knowledge, socio-economic and cultural background — sometimes via personas.

Task analysis

Identify and formalize functionality (use cases, scenarios); analyze user behavior and expectations to design an optimized product.

Context analysis

Analyze external conditions (light, temperature, movement), physical conditions (sitting, standing, hands-free), and psychological conditions (stress, motivation, private vs. professional use), plus devices/platforms/form-factors.

Competition analysis

Learn from competitors’ successful implementations — or from other sectors entirely — unless the goal is a deliberately disruptive design.

Note

Human limitations and biases — cognitive or perceptive bias, visual impairment, inexperience — can create specific and sometimes severe difficulties for some users. Business analysts and testers should factor accessibility into acceptance criteria and test cases accordingly.

4.2.2

Usability Testing

ApproachWhat it does
Checklist-based evaluationUsers evaluate the system against a checklist to evaluate, compare and qualify their experience.
Expert reviewUsability experts assess the interface against pre-defined criteria/heuristics to find its strong and weak points.
Walkthrough / think-aloudUsers explore the product, narrating their actions and impressions out loud, sometimes given specific tasks.
Biometrics-based evaluationEye-tracking or mouse-movement recording to see what draws attention or goes unnoticed.
Log file analysisRetrospective review of real usage logs to find improvement areas and check actual use against the intended profile.

4.3

Performance Efficiency K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Performance efficiency — often just “performance” — matters at every test level and across fixed and mobile platforms alike. During acceptance testing it’s particularly addressed in Operational Acceptance Testing (OAT), usually run by operations teams, though business analysts and testers should still be involved when defining acceptance criteria and tests. Criteria should give objective measures, avoiding subjective judgment calls during execution.

4.3.1

High-level Performance Acceptance Tests

Performance testing determines a system’s responsiveness and stability under given conditions: tools simulate concurrent users or transactions to mimic real workload, response times of key components (web server, application server, database) are measured and compared against requirements — and the same can be done for memory, I/O, CPU and access to security devices, depending on where the bottleneck is expected. Results drive architecture changes (e.g. more server capacity), and testing/analysis/improvement cycles repeat until the target is reached.

Load, stress, and endurance/stability tests are the main types, using steady-state, increasing, scenario-based or artificial workload models.

4.3.2

Acceptance Criteria for Performance Acceptance Tests

Performance acceptance criteria need to address three different perspectives together:

User perspective

Perceived response time — e.g. users abandoning a site after a 10-second wait.

Business perspective

Concurrent users, scenario/transaction types, expected response times, and factors like location or time zone.

Technical perspective

Available resources (bandwidth, CPU, RAM) and architecture (load balancing, caching) — e.g. limited bandwidth degrading performance under high load.

4.4

Security K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Information security management should sit within an organization’s overall security policy (see the ISTQB Advanced Level Security Tester syllabus and ISO/IEC 27005:2011). Business analysts and testers use that policy as a basis for managing security risk on their projects, considering it at every stage:

Risk management. Information security is part of non-functional requirements elicitation: assess the value of information in the system/process, then evaluate and prioritize security risks.

Measurable acceptance criteria. Covering authentication, authorization and accounting, input sanitization, cryptography, and data privacy constraints.

High-level security test cases. Defined from the requirements and criteria — context, main steps, and expected results.

Split by complexity. Some security acceptance tests suit the acceptance tester; more technically complex ones go to specialized security testers.

Chapter 4 in one screen

ISO 25010 characteristics
Performance efficiency, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability, portability — each with its own sub-characteristics.
Quality in use
Effectiveness, efficiency, satisfaction, freedom from risk, context coverage.
UX’s four analysis pillars
User, task, context, competition.
Usability testing methods
Checklist, expert review, walkthrough/think-aloud, biometrics, log analysis.
Performance criteria
Must cover user, business, and technical perspectives together.
Security
Risk-driven, measurable criteria, high-level test cases — split between acceptance and specialized security testers by complexity.

Collaboration Activities Tool Support

Chapter 5 · CT-AcT

Collaborative Acceptance Testing

Acceptance testing brings together an unusually wide mix of people and perspectives. This closing chapter is about what makes that collaboration work: the social and communication skills it depends on, how defects get analyzed and reported to a non-technical audience, the QA activities that keep acceptance testing itself trustworthy, and the tooling that supports all of it.

  • defectAn imperfection or deficiency in a work product where it does not meet its requirements or specifications.Synonyms: bug, fault
  • quality assurancePart of quality management focused on providing confidence that quality requirements will be fulfilled.

5.1

Collaboration K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Acceptance testing routinely involves business analysts, technical analysts, testers, business representatives, business sponsors, automation specialists and more — each with different objectives, skills, and views inside one shared project. Social skills are what turn that diversity into gathered requirements, aligned expectations, and effective collaboration, rather than friction.

With the help of appropriate tools and techniques (serious games, role playing, dedicated workshops), testers and business analysts need the team to:

Know each other

Understand who’s who, shared goals, and common ground — keeping team cohesion high.

Communicate openly

Trust and respect that lets people voice doubts, concerns or fears — taboo-free, so problems get identified and solved.

Share a vision

A common view of the objective and the steps to reach it — what success looks like, what failure looks like, what it takes.

Defuse tension

Humor, positive communication, or negotiation technique (e.g. principled negotiation) to work through major disagreements.

5.2

Activities K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Defect analysis, reporting, and quality assurance for acceptance testing artifacts are the recurring activities that keep the process itself trustworthy.

5.2.1

Defect Analysis

Testers report discrepancies between actual and expected outcomes through defect reports, giving the business analyst what they need to understand what happened and assess the deviation. Analysis is a joint activity: the tester identifies which acceptance criteria weren’t satisfied, and the business analyst assesses the impact on the related business process — including setting a priority (low/medium/high/critical) based on business impact.

Explore the process paths

Where in the business process model the defect was found.

Explore the failed rules

Which business rules weren’t implemented correctly, and their priority from a usage standpoint.

The impact analysis and the resulting decision are documented directly in the defect report.

5.2.2

Reporting

Acceptance testing reports target business managers, product managers and domain experts — application experts who aren’t necessarily familiar with implementation detail. Progress, results and defects should be presented without technical jargon, in the audience’s own language, with metrics as an important part of tracking progress.

The test summary report is the overall result: it summarizes execution and results across test phases, adds impact analysis of any open defects, and indicates whether the targeted quality criteria have been reached. From it, decision makers determine the outcome:

Released as-is

Rolled out without restrictions.

Released with reservations

Known workaroundable errors communicated to users/support; high-risk features excluded from roll-out.

Rejected

Roll-out postponed (or replaced) until critical defects are fixed and re-tested.

5.2.3

QA Activities for Acceptance Testing

High-quality acceptance tests are how business risk from defects escaping to production gets managed. QA activities include:

Review of acceptance criteria. Clear, consistent, comprehensive; covering non-functional characteristics with measurable pass/fail criteria.

Review of acceptance test cases. Covering the defined acceptance criteria as well as business processes, rules and risks.

Traceability. Between requirements/user stories, acceptance criteria, test cases and defects — clarifying dependencies and making related information easy to find.

Coverage analysis. Systematic, once bi-directional traceability is established.

Review of test reports. Clear, consistent, comprehensive — containing everything needed to support the release decision.

5.3

Tool Support K1K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.

Acceptance testing tooling draws from both the business analysis and software testing domains.

Tool typeUsage for acceptance testing
Requirements management toolDescribes acceptance criteria; traceability between tests and requirements; coverage analysis.
Agile project management toolDescribes acceptance criteria; traceability between tests and user stories; coverage analysis.
Business process management toolModels business processes and rules; analyzes defect impact on business processes.
Test management and automation toolManages acceptance tests and test execution campaigns; manages test execution results.
Model-based testing toolGenerates test cases from business process models; manages traceability between models, rules, requirements and test cases.
Defect / incident management toolManages the defect/incident lifecycle.

Chapter 5 in one screen

Collaboration skills
Know each other, communicate openly, share a vision, defuse tension — essential given how many roles converge on acceptance testing.
Defect analysis
Joint tester/business-analyst activity: which criteria failed, and what’s the business impact and priority.
Reporting
Non-technical, audience-appropriate; test summary report drives release/reservation/rejection decisions.
QA activities
Review criteria, review test cases, traceability, coverage analysis, review reports.
Tooling
Requirements/Agile PM tools, business process management tools, test management, model-based testing tools, defect trackers.

Objectives & Motivations Activities & Work Products Lifecycle Integration

Chapter 1 · CT-MBT

Introduction to Model-Based Testing

Model-Based Testing extends classic test design techniques by generating test cases automatically from a model of the system, its environment, or the tests themselves. This chapter covers why teams adopt MBT and where it can mislead them, the activities and work products it adds to the test process, and how it integrates into both sequential and Agile lifecycles.

  • MBT modelAny model used in model-based testing.
  • model-based testingTesting based on or involving models.Abbreviation: MBT

1.1

Objectives and Motivations for MBT K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Model-Based Testing (MBT) is an advanced test approach that extends and supports classic test techniques — equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision table testing, state transition testing — rather than replacing them. The basic idea: design a comprehensive MBT model based on the project’s test objectives, then use that model as a test design specification formal enough to generate test cases from it automatically.

1.1.1

Main Motivations for MBT

Two aspects drive the case for MBT:

Effectiveness

Modeling fosters close communication with stakeholders, creating a shared understanding of requirements and surfacing misunderstandings early. Graphical models let business analysts get involved directly. The model’s abstraction level makes it easier to spot the parts of a system most likely to hide defects — and test cases can be generated and analyzed before any real system exists.

Efficiency

Early modeling and model verification help avoid defects before they’re expensive to fix — supporting the “early testing” principle. Work products are reusable across projects, MBT supports automation, and different test suites can be generated from the same model to adapt efficiently to changing requirements or objectives.

With tool support, MBT extends test coverage through automated generation, shortening the test cycle and reducing the testing bottleneck.

1.1.2

Misleading Expectations and Pitfalls of MBT

“MBT solves all problems”

MBT doesn’t replace traditional test techniques — it supports them. A team that ignores or misuses those techniques won’t fix that by introducing MBT.

“MBT is just a matter of tooling”

Tool support is essential, but acquiring a tool shouldn’t be the first step. Introducing MBT impacts the whole test process (section 1.2) and needs strong management support to lead process and tool change.

“Models are always correct”

Testers can introduce defects while building a model, just as in manual test design. Models need real verification and validation — reviews, static analysis, simulation — since any change propagates to all testware generated from that element.

“Test case explosion will occur”

Pure combinatorial generation can cause explosion, but it’s addressed by adapting generation strategies/algorithms and applying intelligent filters — not a reason to avoid MBT.

1.2

MBT Activities and Work Products in the Test Process K1–K2K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

1.2.1

MBT Specific Activities

Deploying MBT adds activities not found in classic test analysis and design: MBT modeling activities (administering the model, developing its structure and elements, defining modeling guidelines, tooling) and generation of testware from the model and selection criteria.

At minimum, MBT impacts test analysis and design; depending on test objectives, it can touch the whole test process:

Test planning

MBT tooling, guidelines, specific metrics, and MBT work products as part of the project baseline.

Test analysis and design

MBT modeling, choice and application of test selection criteria and coverage metrics — in a shift-left approach, analysis and design can merge into one activity.

Test implementation and execution

MBT test generation and test adaptation.

Test monitoring and control

Advanced coverage metrics and model-based impact analysis.

Test completion

Establishing model libraries for reuse in future projects.

MBT shifts test design activities earlier, can serve as an early requirements verification method, improves communication (especially with graphical models), and complements other techniques such as exploratory testing.

1.2.2

Essential MBT Work Products (Inputs and Outputs)

MBT models can be built dedicated to testing or reused from system design (section 2.3.5), and support different abstraction levels depending on the modeling concept applied.

Input work products

Test strategy; the test basis (requirements, other test targets, test conditions, oral information, existing design/models); incident/defect reports and test logs from previous execution; method/process guidelines and tool documents.

Output work products

MBT models; parts of the test plan and schedule/metrics; test scenarios, suites, execution schedules, design specifications; test cases, procedures, data, scripts, and the test adaptation layer; a bi-directional traceability matrix between generated tests and the test basis.

1.3

Integrating MBT into the Software Development Lifecycles K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

1.3.1

MBT in Sequential and Iterative Software Development Lifecycles

In both sequential (e.g. V-model) and iterative-incremental (e.g. Agile) lifecycles, the MBT approach should primarily adapt to the project’s test objectives — MBT might focus on acceptance testing in one project and automated system testing in another.

Test levels

MBT is mostly used at higher levels — system, system integration, acceptance — where it can abstract complex functional requirements and behavior. It’s less common in component/component-integration testing, though some approaches use code annotation.

Test types

Primarily functional testing, with models representing expected system/environment behavior; enriched or dedicated models can support non-functional testing (security, load/stress, reliability).

Testers typically own the MBT model, though in Agile this can be shared with the team — developers may want the model for test automation, especially for continuous integration feedback.

In sequential lifecycles

Start MBT modeling as early as possible — to stimulate stakeholder communication and catch unclear/incomplete/inconsistent requirements early — and adapt planning to include new testware elements and progress reporting on MBT activities.

In Agile lifecycles

Models are developed iteratively and incrementally, tests generated per iteration; user stories are part of the test basis and linked in the model for automatic traceability. MBT can drive ATDD, and MBT testers are part of the whole Agile team alongside developers and business representatives.

1.3.2

Supporting Requirements Engineering

Facilitates communication. Graphical MBT models (business process models, state transition diagrams) give business, development and testing a shared way to discuss and validate expected behavior.

Clarifies requirement quality. Sharing full or partial models with business representatives/developers builds a common understanding; tests generated from the model represent user scenarios that stakeholders can review.

Supports early validation. Even while requirements are still subject to change.

Requirements and their risks feed MBT modeling and generation; MBT in turn automates the creation and maintenance of bi-directional traceability between requirements and tests.

Chapter 1 in one screen

MBT

MBT Modeling Modeling Languages Good Practices

Chapter 2 · CT-MBT

MBT Modeling

The largest chapter in the syllabus: what an MBT model needs to contain to support test generation, the categories of modeling language available and how to match them to test objectives, and the good practices — quality characteristics, guidelines, tool support, iterative review — that keep a model trustworthy.

  • MBT modelAny model used in model-based testing.
  • test modelA model describing testware that is used for testing a component or a system under test.

2.1

MBT Modeling K2–K3K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

An MBT model exists to derive test cases: it needs enough information to select reasonable tests for the project’s objectives, generate a test oracle, and support bi-directional traceability to requirements. Designing it well matters — model quality strongly shapes the quality of everything the MBT-based process produces, and tools generally require the model to follow a strict syntax.

2.1.1

MBT Modeling Activities

Every model is expressed in a specific modeling language, which defines its elements and the rules for building it. Three questions shape any MBT modeling activity:

What quality characteristics get modeled?

Usually functionality, though performance and other non-functional aspects (e.g. security) can be included. Model only what’s relevant to the test objectives to keep things manageable.

Which modeling language fits?

Many languages exist to represent structure, behavior, or other aspects (data, workflows, protocols) of the test object or its environment.

What abstraction level is right?

Abstraction masters complexity and keeps focus on objectives — but more abstraction means more demanding test adaptation later, and determines which stakeholders can engage with the model.

Two simplified graphical modeling languages — workflow-based and state-transition-based — are defined in this syllabus’s Appendix A, and both are part of exam preparation.

2.1.2

Focus of MBT Models

Structural models

Describe static structure — e.g. class diagrams for data-object relationships, or classification trees for data modeling.

Behavioral models

Describe dynamic interactions — e.g. activity diagrams or business process models for workflows, state transition diagrams for inputs/outputs.

Three model subjects are considered in this syllabus, and a real MBT model usually combines several:

Model subjectDescribesExample
System modelThe system as intended — tests check conformance to it.Class diagrams; state transition diagrams for reactive systems.
Environment / usage modelThe system’s environment.Markov chain models of expected usage.
Test modelOne or more test cases, including expected behavior and evaluation.Abstract test case descriptions; graphical test procedures.

2.1.3

MBT Models Depend on Test Objectives

Test objectiveExample model
Verify the business workflow is implemented correctlyA business process model describing the workflow
Verify the system responds correctly to requests in a specific stateA UML state machine
Verify the availability of an interfaceA description of the interface’s structure
Gain confidence the system suits expected usage by usersA usage model describing user behavior

2.2

Languages for MBT Models K1–K2K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

2.2.1

Main Categories of Modeling Languages for MBT

A modeling language is defined by its concepts (abstract syntax), its syntax (grammar rules), and its semantics. Diagrams are graphical representations of models — class, sequence or state machine diagrams in UML, for example.

Structural

Interfaces, components, hierarchies — e.g. UML component diagrams.

Data

Data types and values — e.g. UML class diagrams, value specifications.

Behavioral

Events, actions, reactions, interactions — e.g. UML activity/interaction diagrams, state machines, BPMN.

Integrated

Not limited to one aspect — UML itself combines diagram types to describe different aspects together.

2.2.2

Language Categories Relevant for Different Systems and Project Objectives

Language choice is closely tied to the project’s original objectives and the properties of the system being built. Examples:

State transition diagrams for expected behavior of a control/command test object.

Activity diagrams or BPMN models for end-to-end workflow testing of an information system.

Decision tables for business rules in system testing.

Safety- or security-critical certification often requires linking software requirements to code and test cases.

Documentation for auditing or certification purposes may require models annotated accordingly.

2.3

Good Practices for MBT Modeling Activities K1–K2K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

2.3.1

Quality Characteristics for MBT Models

Syntactic quality (correctness)

Consistent with the modeling language’s formal rules, so generation doesn’t hit syntax problems.

Semantic quality (validity)

The content correctly describes what it should; derived tests run against the test object without failing due to bad test design.

Pragmatic quality (suitability)

Fits the given test objective and test generator, so derived work products meet expectations.

Tools can check syntax and partly semantics; reviews check semantic and pragmatic quality; model simulators add dynamic checks. Best practice: develop the model incrementally and generate/execute derived tests repeatedly, checking the model, work products and test object early and often.

2.3.2

Typical Mistakes and Pitfalls in MBT Model Design

Common mistakes

Putting too many or too few details in a model (wrong abstraction level), and trying to build one model that covers everything. It’s better to write two focused models — e.g. a state transition diagram to verify implementation and a separate activity diagram to validate workflow — than one model that tries to cover every aspect.

2.3.3

Linking Requirements and Process Related Information to the MBT Model

Linking model elements to requirements is good practice. Benefits:

Facilitates model review, and lets generated tests link automatically to requirements.

Enables requirements-based test generation and priority-based execution ordering.

Makes requirements coverage measurable via generated tests.

Lets stakeholders analyze the impact of requirement changes and scope regression testing.

Test case generators can automatically produce traceability documentation. Testers can also attach other information to the model — test procedure detail, script segments, risks/hazards, priorities, duration, required equipment — to help integrate MBT with the wider test process.

2.3.4

Modeling Guidelines for MBT

Documented instructions for designing, writing and reading MBT models. They support understanding and review across stakeholders, conformance to syntactic requirements, a bounded/extended notation scope, consistent syntax and semantics across authors, good practice, and maintainability/reusability.

Projects without modeling guidelines take on extra risk — testers fall into the classic modeling mistakes more easily.

2.3.5

Reuse of Existing System Design or Requirements Models

Reusing existing design/requirements models directly (e.g. business process models, activity diagrams) is possible, but limited. A state machine from system design may suit testing a command-and-control system, but class diagrams don’t suit workflow-based testing.

Note

Reuse creates a single-source problem: any error in the original design model propagates into the MBT model, so testing isn’t independent from development. It’s recommended to write separate models by different authors for system design and MBT purposes.

If reused without modification, tests derived are verification tests only — checking implementation against the specified model, not validating it. For validation, the tester enriches an existing model with testing aspects (e.g. unforeseen transitions for error scenarios), and the resulting MBT model tends to grow beyond and away from the original design intent. Since the original author may not have been a tester, a reused model doesn’t necessarily follow MBT guidelines and may lead to test case explosion.

2.3.6

Tool Support for Modeling Activities

Model editors

A dedicated modeling tool, flowchart editor (graphical) or text/scripting editor (textual) — may offer predefined elements and syntax/semantic checks.

Model simulators

Execute different paths through the model to validate it.

Test case / data generators

Required to obtain test cases and/or test data from the model automatically.

Simple drawing tools (even pencil and paper) can work for documentation, but don’t support further processing of the model.

2.3.7

Iterative Model Development, Review and Validation

Complex behavior spanning multiple diagrams can outgrow what review alone can catch. Iterative development, model reviews, and frequent review of generated test work products — by the tester and by peers/other stakeholders — help testers validate their view with others, catch errors and missing parts early, identify incomplete/inconsistent requirements, let test managers manage risk, and reduce overall modeling time.

Iterative model development pairs with iterative test generation: each addition to the model triggers updated generation, which acts as a simulation providing feedback on behavior to be tested. In a visual ATDD approach, model review and validation happen as part of backlog refinement, with the model formulating acceptance criteria for user stories.

Language categories

Quality characteristics
Syntactic (correctness), semantic (validity), pragmatic (suitability).
Common mistakes

Reuse risk

Iterative development

Selection Criteria Classification Applying Criteria

Chapter 3 · CT-MBT

Selection Criteria for Test Case Generation

One MBT model can generate many different test suites. This chapter classifies the families of test selection criteria that pick a meaningful subset for a given objective, works through worked examples per modeling language, and covers how to apply, combine and choose between criteria in practice.

  • coverage itemAn attribute or combination of attributes derived from one or more test conditions by using a test technique.
  • model coverageThe coverage of model elements.
  • test case explosionThe disproportionate growth of the number of test cases with growing size of the test basis, when using a certain test design technique.
  • test selection criteriaThe criteria used to guide the generation of test cases or to select test cases in order to limit the size of a test.

3.1

Classification of MBT Test Selection Criteria K2–K3K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Test selection criteria help the tester pick a meaningful subset of test cases from everything a model could generate. Test case generators are what make this an efficiency win. This syllabus groups them into six families.

3.1.1

Test Selection Criteria

Coverage-based — requirements linked to the model

Full coverage means every selected requirement is covered by at least one test case.

Coverage-based — MBT model elements (model coverage)

Based on the model’s internal structure — states/transitions/decisions in state diagrams, activities/gateways in process models, conditions/actions in decision tables, statements/conditions in textual models.

Data-related

Relates to equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis, plus heuristics like pairwise/n-wise combinatorial generation.

Random / stochastic

A more or less random walkthrough of the model — random treats alternatives as equally probable, stochastic accounts for differing probabilities.

Scenario-based and pattern-based

Selection based on predefined scenarios (e.g. a use case or user story) or patterns (a partially defined scenario applicable across the model to produce multiple tests).

Project-driven

Based on project-related information added to the model — risks, priorities, required test equipment — e.g. selecting all tests that need specific equipment.

Most MBT tools support at least one of these criteria, but generally not all of them.

3.1.2

Test Case Selection in Practice

In practice, testers combine several criteria to fit the targeted objectives — e.g. requirements coverage with model coverage, or scenario/pattern with data-related criteria. Beyond the objective itself, application also depends on what the MBT tool supports, how the model is designed, and the tester’s experience with the criteria.

A formally correct model can still produce test case explosion purely from tool-specific generation algorithms.

3.1.3

Examples of Test Selection Criteria

Modeling languageExample coverage criteria
Activity diagrams / business process modelsActivity coverage; branch/gateway coverage; path coverage (with or without loops).
State transition diagramsState and transition coverage; transition pair coverage; path coverage (typically without loops).
Decision tablesEvery condition/decision; every action.
Data domainsEquivalence partition coverage; boundary value coverage.
Textual modelsStatement coverage; branch coverage.

3.1.4

Test Selection Criteria and ISTQB Foundation Level Test Techniques

MBT supports standard ISTQB Foundation Level test techniques — state transition testing, equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision table testing. The model itself may contain coverage items for those techniques directly (e.g. equivalence partitions or boundary values described in the model), or the model may be combined with other graphical/textual representations that contain them, such as decision tables or additional diagrams.

3.2

Applying Test Selection Criteria K1–K3K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

3.2.1

Degree of Automation in Test Generation

Manual

Test cases derived by hand, following model paths. Low maturity — doesn’t deliver the efficiency/effectiveness benefits of automated generation.

Automated

An MBT tool generates output work products automatically, usable as-is with no further post-processing.

Semi-automated

Tool-assisted, but with manual steps required in between or at the end — e.g. selecting specific test cases.

3.2.2

Pros and Cons of Specific Test Selection Criteria

CriterionProCon
Requirements coverageOften mandatory for regulatory reasons.Needs precise definition — e.g. is coverage achieved by covering all linked behaviors or just one?
Model coverageShows exactly where the model couldn’t be covered; a sense of completeness.Some structural criteria (e.g. all-path coverage) can cause test case explosion.
Data-relatedOften mandatory to cover equivalence partitions.Can be heavily combinatorial.
RandomGood for surfacing unexpected test cases.Can generate long tests with no business meaning.
Scenario/pattern-basedSupports use-case selection, e.g. for regression testing.Extra effort to define and maintain scenarios/patterns.
Project-drivenUseful for test management.Extra effort to link project information into the model.

3.2.3

Good Practices of MBT Test Selection

Often one criterion isn’t enough, so criteria get combined in one of two ways:

Composition (intersection)

The generated suite keeps only test cases that satisfy all applied criteria.

Addition (union)

The generated suite keeps all test cases that satisfy at least one criterion.

Note

Selection must be reproducible: the same model plus the same criteria should yield the same test cases. Small model changes can yield a completely different selection for some coverage criteria — the model is the master, generated tests are derived work products, so it’s essential to plan and document selection choices and reasoning. Selection criteria are also the main lever for taming test case explosion.

Chapter 3 in one screen

Requirements coverage, model coverage, data-related, random/stochastic, scenario/pattern-based, project-driven.
Combining criteria
Common in practice — e.g. requirements coverage + model coverage.
Automation degrees
Manual (low maturity), automated, semi-automated.
Composition vs. addition
Intersection of criteria vs. union of criteria.
Reproducibility
Same model + same criteria must yield the same tests; document the choices.
Explosion control
Selection criteria are the main tool for keeping generated suites manageable.

Implementation & Execution Test Adaptation

Chapter 4 · CT-MBT

MBT Test Implementation and Execution

Once test cases are generated, they still need to run. This chapter covers the difference between high-level and low-level generated test cases, offline versus online execution, how changes ripple through MBT work products, and the test adaptation work that bridges an abstract model to a concrete system under test.

  • offline MBTModel-based test approach in which test cases are generated into a repository for future execution.
  • online MBTModel-based test approach in which test cases are generated and executed simultaneously.Synonyms: on-the-fly MBT
  • test adaptation layerThe layer in a test automation architecture which provides the necessary code to adapt test scripts on an abstract level to the various components, configuration or interfaces of the SUT.

4.1

Specifics of MBT Test Implementation and Execution K2–K3K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Once a test suite is generated, the next step is running it — manually, or automated via a test execution environment. Either way, there must be a maintained connection between the MBT model and the resulting execution work products.

4.1.1

High-level and Low-level Test Cases in the MBT Context

High-level test cases

No concrete implementation-level values for input data or expected results, and no fine-grained test steps — e.g. abstract test actions, or equivalence partitions instead of concrete representative values. Good for review by business analysts.

Low-level test cases

Concrete implementation-level values for input data and expected results, with detailed step descriptions. Ready for testers to execute directly.

Moving from high-level to executable low-level test cases means adding fully defined test actions and concrete input/expected-result values — either inside the MBT model itself (as documented actions/data) or outside it (e.g. a data table mapping abstract to concrete values).

4.1.2

Different Kinds of Test Execution

MBT-generated tests may run manually or automatically. Manual execution needs test cases generated in a format usable by hand (ideally exportable to a test management tool). Automated execution needs tests generated in an executable form — sometimes convertible directly into scripts, sometimes needing a test adaptation layer: a wrapper around the test object (similar to keyword-driven testing) that separates test design from implementation details tied to the exact system version or configuration.

Offline MBT

Automated test scripts (including expected results) are generated first, then executed afterward.

Online MBT (“on-the-fly”)

Generation and execution happen simultaneously — each test step is generated after the previous one runs, and the execution result can influence the path taken through the model.

4.1.3

The Impact of Changes on the MBT Work Products

ChangeMay impact
Requirements, test object, or environmentThe MBT model (actions, conditions/expected results, data), the test selection criteria, and the adaptation layer (if any).
Interface only (no functional change)Just the adaptation layer, if one exists.
Test objective or test conditionsThe MBT model, the test selection criteria, and the adaptation layer (if any).

Change management for MBT work products should include impact analysis, exploring change options, applying the changes, and reviewing them.

4.2

Activities of Test Adaptation in MBT K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

For manual execution, test adaptation documents generated tests to bridge the model’s abstractions and the system’s concrete interfaces/data — e.g. supplying concrete representative values for boundary conditions — producing scripts complete and documented enough for direct manual use.

For automated execution, test adaptation integrates the model’s generated work products into the execution framework, supporting keyword-driven and/or data-driven testing:

Keyword-driven testing

Keywords defined in the model are used in generated test cases. Getting fully automated scripts requires: (1) exporting test cases into the execution tool’s scripting language, manually or via an exporter; (2) implementing the keywords in that language — done by the test automation engineer or the test object’s developer.

Data-driven testing

The model describes abstract input data and expected results (e.g. via equivalence partitioning); generated tests reference these abstractions. Getting fully automated scripts requires: (1) supplying concrete input data/results (e.g. in a table or spreadsheet); (2) linking the model’s formalized test data to the concrete data in the execution tool or test harness.

Chaining automated scripts requires correctly set preconditions before each run — either via post-conditions in one script feeding the next, or by explicitly setting up preconditions at the start of each script. Best practice: prepare test adaptation alongside MBT modeling, not after.

Chapter 4 in one screen

High-level vs. low-level
Abstract, review-friendly vs. concrete, execution-ready test cases.
Test adaptation layer
A wrapper isolating test design from implementation/configuration detail.
Offline vs. online MBT
Generate-then-execute vs. generate-and-execute simultaneously (“on-the-fly”).
Change impact
Requirement/object changes ripple into the model and criteria; interface-only changes stay in the adaptation layer.
Test adaptation
Supports keyword-driven and data-driven testing; best planned alongside modeling.
