Evaluate Deployment Manage & Monitor

Chapter 5 · CT-MBT

Evaluating and Deploying an MBT Approach

The closing chapter steps back from modeling technique to organizational adoption: the ROI factors that justify introducing MBT, matching its characteristics to what the organization actually needs, the metrics that track a deployment, and the good practices, costs, and tool integration that make the rollout stick.

5.1

Evaluate an MBT Deployment K1–K2K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

MBT deployment typically follows a classic product-adoption process:

  1. 1

    Awareness

    Establish test-process improvement objectives and identify MBT as a possible technology to address them — spotting the opportunity motivates teams to change how they work.

  2. 2

    Interest

    Learn more about MBT.

  3. 3

    Evaluation

    Analyze MBT’s principles and existing approaches against the given project context.

  4. 4

    Trial use

    Define KPIs and run a pilot project to measure improvements.

  5. 5

    Adoption

    Lead and reinforce the change — skill development and behavioral change across the organization.

Estimating ROI and evaluating MBT’s impact on testing performance (via KPIs) is part of this adoption cycle.

5.1.1

ROI Factors for MBT Introduction

MBT generates costs during both introduction and operation, which need to be counterbalanced by benefits — net financial balance over the long term, and test design quality with a positive impact on the whole development process.

Early requirements validation. MBT’s top-down approach allows design work even while requirements are still rough, validating them against current maturity and avoiding costly late bug fixes.

Reduced test design effort. All possible paths live in one redundancy-free work product, instead of redundancy across separate manual/automated test suites.

Reduced test implementation effort. Once the model exists, test cases generate automatically, cutting maintenance effort.

Earlier defect identification and improved time to market, from starting test design early with MBT’s efficiency.

Test management support. Generation strategies and filters let the test manager select the “ideal” set of test cases for the goal.

Potentially fewer test cases overall, thanks to optimized, systematic generation strategies — reducing what has to be executed.

Test-quality benefits: improved design methods, coverage and consistency; better prioritization and QA of the test design; improved traceability from better-organized test design content.

5.1.2

Organizational Objectives and their Relationship to the Characteristics of the MBT Approach

MBT can improve test quality, effort, and communication — but the organization has to prioritize which improvements matter, since the scope and impact depend heavily on how the MBT method is configured.

Organizational objectiveAchieved by
Improved quality of testingSeparate models for development and MBT (independent tester mindset); a well-defined abstraction level based on the test plan; high process automation including generation and execution; well-defined, adaptable test selection criteria.
Effort reductionShared, reusable MBT models; high process automation with automatically generated work products; test selection criteria tuned to generate the most efficient test-case set.
Improved communicationAn abstraction level suited to every stakeholder involved — high-level and business-oriented for business analysts, detailed and test-oriented for testers.

Combined organizational objectives can create contradicting requirements for the MBT approach — often resolved by developing different models for different test objectives (section 2.1.3).

5.1.3

Metrics and Key Performance Indicator

Introducing MBT should rest on clear objectives, metrics and KPIs to track progress and results. Possible metrics to monitor:

Requirements managed/traced into the model, and requirements coverage (%) by generated tests.

Size and complexity of the MBT model.

Number of generated test cases/scripts, including per person-day.

Defects found in requirements during modeling activities.

Reusability of model elements from one project to another.

Usage level of the models across business/development/testing stakeholders.

Efficiency gains vs. previous approaches — in productivity (cheaper tests) and defect detection (better tests).

5.2

Manage and Monitor the Deployment of an MBT Approach K1K1: RememberThe candidate will remember, recognize, and recall a term or concept.

5.2.1

Good Practices when Deploying MBT

The MBT-based process, its work products and tools should integrate closely with the existing development process, test process and tool chain — including application lifecycle management.

Configuration management

Version the test basis, MBT models and selection criteria, test cases/scripts, and the adaptation layer — just as release/deployment work products are versioned elsewhere in development.

Continuous integration

MBT tools, not just unit test tools, should be called by the CI server — especially when MBT drives continuous regression testing.

Requirements engineering and backlog integration

Backlog items need testing before they’re “done”; if MBT tests a backlog item, the corresponding work products should be traceable in the backlog tool — which test cases, from which model version, testing which objective.

5.2.2

Cost Factors of MBT

Initial — organization

Assessing existing resources/knowledge; evaluating approaches and tools; defining methods and processes; integrating with requirements/test management and CI; automating reporting; archiving; general modeling/process guidelines; coaching, training, tool licensing.

Initial — project

Creating project-specific guidelines and the initial model; transforming existing assets (e.g. textual test cases) into models; migrating models.

Test activityRe-occurring costs
GeneralTool licensing/maintenance; coaching and training of new team members.
Test planningAnalyzing the test basis for MBT testability; planning model development/enrichment/derivation.
Test analysis and designModeling; refactoring; validating and verifying models.
Test implementation and executionChoosing selection criteria; generating executable tests; developing the adaptation layer; executing tests.
Test monitoring and controlChecking model quality continuously; ensuring defect traceability; documenting completion criteria; combining MBT and other evaluations in one report.
Test completionArchiving work products; documenting lessons learned; transitioning to maintenance.

5.2.3

Integration of the MBT Tool

A key part of evaluating an MBT tool is how well it integrates with configuration management, requirements management, test management and test automation tools. A typical MBT-embedding tool chain supports:

Iterative model development, review and validation, using the modeling tool, the model simulator, and requirements traceability.

Test generation, applying selection criteria to the model via the test case generator.

Exporting generated test cases, scripts and traceability links to the test management tool and test automation framework.

Configuration management for MBT testware — the model and the adaptation layer.

Chapter 1 · CT-SEC

The Basis of Security Testing

Security testing starts with risk: what could go wrong, what it would cost, and how likely it is. This chapter covers security risk assessment and asset identification, the policies and procedures an organization relies on, and how security auditing surfaces the gaps that testing then has to prove or disprove.

  • data privacyThe protection of personally identifiable information or otherwise sensitive information from undesired disclosure.
  • ethical hackerA security tester using hacker techniques.
  • information securityThe protection of information and information systems from unauthorized access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification, or destruction.
  • penetration testingA testing technique aiming to exploit security vulnerabilities (known or unknown) to gain unauthorized access.
  • risk assessmentThe process of identifying and subsequently analyzing the identified project or product risk to determine its level of risk, typically by assigning likelihood and impact ratings.
  • risk exposureThe importance of a risk as defined by its characteristics impact and likelihood; can be expressed qualitatively (high, medium, low) or quantitatively.Synonyms: risk level
  • risk mitigationThe process through which decisions are reached and protective measures are implemented for reducing risks to, or maintaining risks within, specified levels.
  • security attackAn attempt to gain unauthorized access to a component or system, resources, or information, or an attempt to compromise system integrity.
  • security auditAn audit evaluating an organization’s security processes and infrastructure.
  • security policyA high-level document describing the principles, approach and major objectives of the organization regarding security.
  • security procedureA set of steps required to implement the security policy and the steps to be taken in response to a specific security incident.
  • security riskA quality risk related to security.

1.1.1

The Role of Risk Assessment in Security Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Security test objectives are grounded in security risks identified through a security risk assessment — a function of the adverse impact an event would cause and the likelihood of it occurring. Information security risks specifically arise from loss of confidentiality, integrity, or availability of information or information systems.

A risk assessment tells an organization which areas and assets are at risk and how large each risk is, giving security testers a rich source of information for planning and prioritizing tests: the highest rigor and coverage goes where risk exposure is greatest. This is what keeps security testing aligned with business security objectives — provided the assessment accurately reflects real threats, stakeholders and assets.

Note

A risk assessment is only a snapshot: it reflects limited information at a point in time and can miss risks if participants lack detailed knowledge. Since threats emerge continually, assessments should be repeated at regular intervals (commonly every three to twelve months) and should draw on input from a variety of people, ideally guided by an established methodology such as NIST SP 800-30.

1.1.2

Asset Identification K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

Not everything worth protecting is digital — printed contracts, handwritten notes and physical prototypes can carry as much value as a database. Identifying assets to secure means working through four questions.

Which assets are valuable?

Customer data, business plans, proprietary software, system documentation, intellectual property, financial spreadsheets, employee records — and intangibles like company reputation.

How valuable is the asset?

Future revenue it generates, its worth to a competitor, the effort to recreate it, and fines or penalties for its loss or unavailability.

Where is it located?

From old CDs and USB drives to secure enterprise servers, mobile devices and cloud storage — each location changes the exposure.

How is it accessed and secured?

LAN/Wi-Fi, VPN, physical media hand-offs, email — secured through encryption, authentication/tokens and authorization levels.

Example

A hard drive stolen from a secured government facility exposed payroll and bank details for over 100,000 current and former employees — a reminder that storage location and physical control matter as much as digital defenses.

1.1.3

Analysis of Risk Assessment Techniques K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

A security risk assessment follows the same shape as a standard risk assessment but focuses on security-related areas, and should incorporate the perspective of external stakeholders: customers and users, the public, and regulatory agencies.

PhaseKey tasks (after NIST SP 800-30)
PreparingIdentify the purpose, scope, assumptions/constraints, information sources, and the risk model/analytic approach to use.
ConductingIdentify relevant threat sources and events; identify exploitable vulnerabilities and predisposing conditions; determine likelihood and adverse impact.
CommunicatingShare the risk assessment results, and feed them into other risk management activities.

The output feeds a risk matrix combining likelihood and impact into an overall severity (e.g. Low/Medium/High/Critical), which in turn drives how urgently a risk needs mitigation and how much test rigor it deserves.

1.2.1

Understanding Security Policies and Procedures K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Security policies vary by organization, but share a common basis: a security risk assessment that examines specific threats and their impact. A wide range of policy types typically cover an organization’s security posture.

Acceptable use

Compliant vs. non-compliant behavior with digital resources.

Minimum access

Grants only the access needed to perform a task.

Network / remote / internet access

What is and isn’t permissible on LANs, VPNs and the internet.

User account management

Creation, maintenance, deletion and auditing of accounts.

Data classification

Public, confidential, highly confidential, private, secret — controls scaled to sensitivity.

Configuration & change management

Approval and rollback process for changes to secure devices/applications.

Server security

Baseline configuration, backup/recovery, minimal active services.

Mobile devices

Encryption, anti-malware, password requirements, loss/theft procedures.

Guest access, physical security, password policy

Guest onboarding; facility controls; password strength and rotation rules.

Malware protection, incident response, audit, licensing, monitoring

Defenses against malware; response playbooks; audit access rights; license compliance; electronic monitoring scope.

Security procedures sit beneath policies: they spell out the specific steps for implementing a policy or control, and the steps to take in response to an incident — e.g., exactly how to grant a user the correct access level.

1.2.2

Analysis of Security Policies and Procedures K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

Evaluating a set of policies and procedures starts with defining the objective of the evaluation and a set of criteria — sometimes drawn from standards such as COBIT, ISO 27001 or PCI DSS — along with the skills needed, what to measure, and a checklist to guide and standardize the assessment.

Review system documentation and technical control configuration (e.g. firewall, IDS)

Survey and interview personnel on perceived effectiveness

Witness systems and processes in action

Analyze previous audit results, logs and reports for trends

Sample data transactions for anomalies

Security controls are the technical or administrative safeguards that counteract threats acting on a vulnerability — categorized as administrative, technical or physical, and by function as preventive, detective, corrective or recovery. Security testing is what distinguishes a policy that merely exists on paper from one that is actually effective: a password policy can look reasonable until a password-cracking tool reveals it falls short in practice.

1.3

Security Auditing and Its Role in Security Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

A security audit is a manual examination that identifies weaknesses in an organization’s security processes and infrastructure. Procedural audits (e.g. reviewing internal controls) are often manual; architectural audits often use security audit tools. Auditing has a broader scope than testing — it also covers procedures, policies and controls that are hard to test directly — while security testing focuses more on the technologies (firewalls, authentication, encryption, user rights).

Assessment

Documents threats, assets, policies and management’s risk tolerance; repeated regularly as the environment changes.

Prevention

Administrative, operational and technical controls working together — no single defense stops every attack.

Detection

Identifying a breach or intrusion; without it, compromise can go unnoticed.

Reaction

Fast, well-prepared response minimizes exposure once an incident is detected.

Recovery

Restoring systems without recreating the original vulnerability, plus root-cause analysis to prevent recurrence.

1.3.1

Purpose of a Security Audit K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

A security audit is one more activity — alongside testing — for surfacing problem areas that need remediation. Typical findings include:

Inadequate physical security (e.g. sensitive reports discarded in unsecured trash — “dumpster diving”)

Inadequate password maintenance (e.g. users alternating between two passwords each rotation)

Inadequate controls on user rights and file sharing, especially for mobile/Wi-Fi users

Inadequate server-level security: port allocation, data protection, account protection, vendor update cadence

Inadequate intrusion detection and inadequate breach-response plans

1.3.2

Risk Identification, Assessment and Mitigation K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Once an audit surfaces problem areas, risk identification, assessment and mitigation planning follow. Risk exposure is the potential impact multiplied by the likelihood of that impact occurring; likelihood is typically assessed via NIST SP 800-30 or the OWASP Risk Rating Methodology.

Risk factorWhat it captures
ThreatAny circumstance or event with potential to adversely impact operations or assets, via unauthorized access, disclosure, modification, destruction or denial of service.
VulnerabilityA weakness in a system, procedure, control or implementation that a threat source could exploit — including emergent vulnerabilities that appear as environments and technologies evolve.
ImpactThe magnitude of harm from unauthorized disclosure, modification, destruction, or loss of availability.
LikelihoodThe probability that a threat event is initiated and succeeds — for adversarial threats, a function of intent, capability and targeting.

Likelihood and impact combine into an overall severity rating (e.g. via a 0–9 scored matrix), which determines how urgently a risk needs a response. A risk that is ongoing — not a one-time event — carries additional weight because the likelihood of eventual loss increases over time.

1.3.3

People, Process and Technology K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

An organization’s IT practice rests on three components — often called the “iron triangle” — and nearly every security incident can be traced to a deficiency in one of them.

People

End-users, administrators, data owners and managers, each with different skills, attitudes and agendas. Policies and controls fail if people don’t follow them.

Process

The procedures and standards protecting valuable assets; must be defined, current, consistent and aligned with best practice.

Technology

Hardware and software that automates and enforces controls — and, used incorrectly, that helps people make mistakes faster.

An auditor evaluates controls from an attacker’s perspective, anticipating how people, process or technology could be exploited. The only reliable way to know whether a security defense actually works is to test it from that same attacker perspective — commonly called ethical hacking or penetration testing. This is where auditing and testing meet most directly: auditing identifies what to test, and security testing proves or disproves whether the controls actually hold.

Example

A tax agency’s audit finds it possible to file a fraudulent return and collect another taxpayer’s refund. Security testing confirms the finding as “critical,” but the agency defers action — leaving it liable to defrauded taxpayers who followed every prescribed security procedure.

Chapter 1 in one screen

Security risk assessment
Identifies assets at risk and the magnitude of each risk; the primary basis for planning and prioritizing security tests.
Asset identification
What is valuable, how valuable, where it lives, how it’s accessed, how it’s secured — digital and physical.
Risk factors (NIST 800-30)
Threat, vulnerability, impact, likelihood, predisposing condition.
Risk exposure / risk level
Impact × likelihood; drives urgency of mitigation and test rigor.
Security policy vs. procedure
A policy states principles and objectives; a procedure spells out the steps to implement it.
Security controls
Administrative, technical, physical — each preventive, detective, corrective or recovery.
Security audit
Manual examination of processes/infrastructure; five pillars: assessment, prevention, detection, reaction, recovery.
People, process, technology
The “iron triangle” behind almost every security incident.
Ethical hacking / penetration testing
The only reliable way to prove whether a security defense is actually effective.

Chapter 2 · CT-SEC

Security Testing Purposes, Goals and Strategies

Before choosing techniques, a security tester needs to understand why testing exists, how it fits the organization, and what it’s meant to achieve. This chapter covers the purpose and organizational context of security testing, how to set and scope test objectives, how to choose and evaluate a testing approach, and how to keep improving practice over time.

  • cross-site scriptingA vulnerability that allows attackers to inject malicious code into an otherwise benign website.Abbreviation: XSS
  • data obfuscationData transformation that makes it difficult for a human to recognize the original data.
  • denial of serviceA security attack that is intended to overload the system with requests such that legitimate requests cannot be serviced.Abbreviation: DoS
  • information assuranceMeasures that protect and defend information and information systems by ensuring their availability, integrity, authentication, confidentiality, and non-repudiation, including restoration via protection, detection and reaction capabilities.
  • security policyA high-level document describing the principles, approach and major objectives of the organization regarding security.
  • security testingA test type to determine the security of a component or system.
  • security vulnerabilityA weakness in the system that could allow for a successful security attack.
  • software lifecycleThe period of time that begins when a software product is conceived and ends when it is no longer available for use — typically concept, requirements, design, implementation, test, installation/checkout, operation/maintenance and, sometimes, retirement phases.
  • test strategyA high-level description of the test levels to be performed and the testing within those levels for an organization or programme.Synonyms: organizational test strategy

2.1

Introduction K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Before applying specialized techniques, a security tester needs the broader context: why testing is needed, what it is meant to achieve, and how it fits the organization. Security testing differs from other functional testing in two significant ways: standard input-selection techniques can miss important security issues, and the symptoms of security defects look very different from ordinary functional defects.

Unauthorized copying of applications or data

Unauthorized access control (performing tasks the user lacks rights for)

Unintended side effects (e.g. a media player writing unencrypted temp files)

Cross-site scripting (XSS) — malicious code exercised by later users

Buffer overflow from over-long input strings

Denial of service, overloading a system with nuisance requests

Man-in-the-middle interception, mimicking or altering communications

Breaking encryption used to protect sensitive data

Logic bombs that activate malicious behavior under specific conditions

Security testing must be integrated with every other development and testing activity, shaped by the organization’s unique needs, existing policies, current skill sets and test strategy.

2.2

The Purpose of Security Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Security testing cannot guarantee immunity from attack, but it identifies risks and evaluates whether existing defenses actually work — complementing audits and security-practice reviews. It also demonstrates due diligence: if a breach leads to legal action, evidence of reasonable steps taken (including testing for vulnerabilities) can be a meaningful defense, and it reassures clients and customers that their information is being protected.

2.3

The Organizational Context K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Security testing is usually one type of testing competing for a limited testing budget, and is often treated as a specialist role — sometimes outsourced entirely. The extent of security testing scales with the organization’s security-based business risk: more risk exposure calls for more testing.

Like testing in general, information security is a lifecycle activity: security needs must be defined in requirements, expressed in design and implemented in code before testing can verify and validate them. Security cannot be effectively patched or tested into an application after the fact — it has to be built in. Limited time, resources, scope, risk levels, skill sets and lifecycle approach all shape how successful a security testing team can be.

2.4.1

The Alignment of Security Testing Goals K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

A security testing policy can only be written once senior management has approved the organization’s overall security policy, and its goals must stay aligned with that policy. Otherwise, tests may be performed without authorization, or may fail to achieve their intended purpose.

2.4.2

Identification of Security Test Objectives K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Security test objectives mirror functional test objectives but focus on security goals — there should be one or more per security feature. They must also reflect the attributes of the technology in play (web, mobile, cloud, LAN) and known vulnerabilities, both application-specific and generic.

Verify that password authentication applies the correct strength rule

Verify that all data-entry fields are validated to prevent SQL injection

Verify that customer data files are encrypted at the correct strength

2.4.3

The Difference Between Information Assurance and Security Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Information assurance (IA) is the broader, encompassing discipline of protecting and defending information and information systems; security testing is the narrower process of determining whether security features are implemented as designed and are adequate for the intended environment. The relationship mirrors that between Quality Assurance and software testing — IA is to security testing what QA is to testing.

2.5

The Scope and Coverage of Security Testing Objectives K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

The greater the need for integrity of sensitive digital and physical assets, the greater the need for coverage of security test objectives. Security test objectives essentially describe the scope of security testing — too small a scope leaves confidence gaps; too large a scope depletes resources before testing finishes. Objectives should tie directly to specific assets, protective measures, risks and the identification of vulnerabilities.

2.6.1

Analysis of Security Test Approaches K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

Every organization has unique business and mission concerns requiring a tailored security test strategy, alongside concerns common to many organizations. A project-level testing approach must stay consistent with the organization’s test policy and strategy, blending techniques, tools and skills to meet that project’s objectives. Analyzing a situation to define an approach means weighing factors such as:

The source of the system/application and any prior security testing

Security policy, security testing policy, and existing risk assessments

The technical environment (software, frameworks, languages, OS)

Team skills, structure and tool experience

Constraints (resources, time, environment access) and assumptions

Different technologies need different approaches: web applications face different vulnerabilities than mainframes, though some — like buffer overflows — recur across environments with different manifestations. Data-in-transit protection differs by channel, but the goal is constant: sensitive data must always be stored encrypted. A UK finance group once admitted losing two backup tapes with data for 1.4 million customers — a reminder that even “offline” data needs the same discipline.

2.6.2

Analysis of Failures in Security Test Approaches K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

An undetected vulnerability doesn’t automatically mean the testing approach failed — new vulnerabilities are discovered daily. But root-cause analysis can reveal genuine approach failures, commonly traced to:

Lack of executive leadership or resources for security testing

Ineffective implementation (missing skills) of the chosen approach

Lack of organizational or stakeholder support

Poor understanding of security risks or of the system’s purpose

Misalignment between the testing approach and the security/testing policy

Lack of effective tools or testing skills

2.6.3

Stakeholder Identification K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Making the business case for security testing to management means clearly defining the risk of lapses and the benefits of an effective approach — and different stakeholders value different benefits.

StakeholderWhat they value
Executive managementProtection of the business.
Senior managementDemonstrated due diligence.
Business customersProtection from fraud.
Compliance officersAssurance of internal policy compliance.
Regulatory officersConfirmation that external regulations are followed.
Privacy officersEvidence that private data is kept secure.

2.7

Improving the Security Testing Practices K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

Improving practice starts with an objective evaluation — from short-term and long-term perspectives, considering process and organization, and considering people, tools, systems and techniques. Key metrics include:

Coverage of security risks by tests

Coverage of security policies and practices by tests

Coverage of security requirements by tests

Effectiveness of past efforts, based on when/where vulnerabilities were found (pre- and post-release)

Chapter 2 in one screen

Why security testing differs
Standard input selection can miss issues; defect symptoms differ from ordinary functional bugs.
Purpose
Identifies risk, evaluates defenses, demonstrates due diligence — can’t guarantee safety.
Alignment
Security testing goals must align with the organization’s approved security policy.
Information Assurance vs. security testing
IA is broader — like QA is to testing.
Scope & coverage
Scaled to the need for integrity of the assets being protected.
Approach analysis
Weighs prior testing, policy, tech environment, skills, constraints and assumptions.
Approach failure causes
Usually leadership, resourcing, skills, understanding or alignment gaps — not “missed one bug.”
Stakeholders
Each sees a different benefit: protection, due diligence, fraud prevention, compliance, privacy.
Improving practice
Coverage of risks/policies/requirements, plus effectiveness of past efforts.

Chapter 3 · CT-SEC

Security Testing Processes

Security testing follows the same shape as the general ISTQB test process, with a security-specific lens at every step. This chapter walks through process definition and lifecycle alignment, planning, test design (including secure coding, DoS/DDoS and policy-based tests), execution and environment requirements, evaluation, and ongoing maintenance of the process itself.

  • account harvestingThe process of obtaining user account information based on trial and error with the intention of using that information in a security attack.
  • password crackingA security attack recovering secret passwords stored in a computer system or transmitted over a network.
  • social engineeringAn attempt to trick someone into revealing information (e.g., a password) that can be used to attack systems or networks.
  • test approachThe implementation of the test strategy for a specific project — the decisions following from the project’s goal and risk assessment: starting points, test design techniques, exit criteria and test types.
  • test planA document describing the scope, approach, resources and schedule of intended test activities.
  • test processThe fundamental test process comprises test planning and control, test analysis and design, test implementation and execution, evaluating exit criteria and reporting, and test closure activities.

3.1.1

ISTQB Security Testing Process K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Security testing is a lifecycle activity: failing to test security defenses throughout a project can leave severe defects unresolved. The security test process aligns with the general ISTQB test process, adding a security-specific focus to each step.

ISTQB test process stepSecurity testing focus
Planning and controlDefine scope matching security risks; identify objectives, resources, estimates/schedules, metrics and entry/exit criteria; monitor progress.
Analysis and designUnderstand specific threats and risks from assessments, audits and known-vulnerability sources; define test conditions from objectives, risks, standards and existing defenses.
Implementation and executionTranslate conceptual tests into executable ones from multiple perspectives — internal user, external user, malicious user; set up the test environment.
Evaluating exit criteria and reportingDetermine vulnerabilities from outcomes; evaluate risk levels; report interim and final results promptly to authorized parties.
Test closureConfirm all planned tests ran and deliverables were produced; archive testware and results securely; feed results back into development improvement.

This process is not strictly sequential — security test activities happen alongside other lifecycle activities, and the exact tasks depend on the organization’s chosen strategy and approach, not on a prescriptive checklist.

3.1.2

Aligning the Security Testing Process to a Particular Application Lifecycle Model K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Every lifecycle model carries its own security testing concerns.

Sequential

Needs defined early and documented in requirements; late-project changes may not be reflected; tests are commonly (and riskily) left until late; findings are hard to address near the end.

Iterative / incremental

Needs emerge continuously across iterations, in user stories, models, acceptance criteria or prototypes; tests run continuously; some risks can’t be fully mitigated in one short cycle.

Commercial off-the-shelf (COTS)

Often black-box, frequently needing security patches; no code access, so structural testing isn’t possible.

Open source

Like COTS but with visible code — once a vulnerability is public, unpatched users of that version are immediately at risk.

In a sequential project, a security tester has work at every phase: requirements (define the security test approach), analysis and design (identify major test objectives), detailed design (first model-based tests), coding (structural tests, static analysis, code review), system testing (transaction and infrastructure-level security), acceptance testing (business-process-level scenarios), deployment (verifying no new vulnerabilities from configuration) and maintenance (regression and ongoing monitoring). In an iterative example — four-week releases built from a prioritized backlog — core security features (login, TLS, password reset, lockout) are typically built in an early iteration because later features depend on them, and the tester works alongside developers each sprint to confirm no regressions.

3.2.1

Security Test Planning Objectives K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

Security testing focuses on two aspects: verifying that designed defenses are implemented and function correctly, and verifying that no vulnerabilities were introduced during development. Since defenses should already be grounded in a risk analysis, that analysis is the natural starting point for test planning — supplemented by an assessment of development practices, since many unintended vulnerabilities can be avoided through QA activities during architecture, design and coding.

3.2.2

Key Security Test Plan Elements K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

Each element of a security test plan can be pinned down by asking a set of framing questions.

Plan elementFraming questions
ScopeWhat is in/out of scope? What is achievable given resources, risk and time?
Who performs testingDo we have the right skills in-house? Is outsourcing acceptable? Who’s responsible for vendor-supplied components?
ScheduleWhat must be tested before other testing can start (e.g. logins)? When are security features testable? How long will testing take?
Tasks and timeHow long to design tests, evaluate/report results, run regression, and stand up the environment?
Test environment(s)What’s the extent of the environment? Is it new? Which tools need installing?
AuthorizationsWho must approve testing, by when, and is budget sufficient?

Like any deliverable, the plan should be reviewed — often via a technical review given its technical content — ideally with IT auditors and security administrators present, since they know the relevant policies and procedures well.

3.3.1

Security Test Design K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Detailed security tests can start from a risk analysis, an available threat model, or an origin-based categorization of security risks, and should be prioritized by risk, traced to requirements, tailored to their audience (developers, functional testers, security testers), and automated where practical. The basic flow runs from approach → risks/threat models/requirements → design techniques → test cases and scenarios.

Functional security controls

Verify transaction-level controls work and are effective, e.g. a bank teller needing head-teller approval above a threshold.

Functional access controls

Username/password policy enforcement, appropriate access levels, resistance to password cracking; e.g. verifying an error message doesn’t reveal whether the username or the password was wrong (defending against account harvesting).

Structural access controls

User rights created and enforced correctly at the system/DB level — test accounts at each access tier to confirm no privilege leakage.

Secure coding practices

Mostly static verification that developers followed practices such as: session IDs are random; authorization decisions happen server-side; no sensitive info in error messages or HTTP GET; input is sanitized and strongly typed; least-privilege service accounts.

Operating system access

Once OS access is gained, an attacker can control data, network access and plant malware — tests probe for rootkit-planting and similar.

Language and platform vulnerabilities

Vulnerability rates are broadly similar across popular languages (.NET, Java, PHP, ASP, ColdFusion, Perl) — the deciding factor is how code is written, not which language is used.

Note

New security risks and vulnerabilities emerge quickly. Security test planners need to stay current with standards and threat lists (see Chapter 9) rather than relying on a fixed checklist.

Denial of service (DoS) overloads system or application resources so legitimate users can’t get through; a distributed DoS (DDoS) launches the attack indirectly through a botnet or amplification technique (e.g. spoofed DNS/NTP requests that multiply traffic toward a victim). Resource-exhaustion and logical DoS attacks abuse desired functionality itself — e.g. locking out predictable usernames after repeated failed logins to lock many accounts at once.

DDoS test levelFocus
1Confirm hosts aren’t infected with known malware.
2Confirm the IDS can quickly spot multiple requests from one source.
3Identify configurations open to abuse (SSL renegotiation, webserver, DNS).
4Identify logic defects that enable a DoS.

Other external intrusion methods include social engineering, injection attacks, account compromise, exploiting known vulnerabilities, malware, insecure configuration, authorization defects, and application-logic abuse (e.g. replaying an e-commerce checkout out of order to gain an unintended discount). Internal threats — often the greatest risk — include corporate espionage by trusted staff, information carried out by departing outsourced personnel, theft of physical storage, and disgruntled employees.

3.3.2

Security Test Design Based on Policies and Procedures K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Designing tests to validate policies and procedures makes the policy itself the test basis — a form of security auditing through testing. The goal is to understand the policy’s purpose and scope, assess its testability, and build tests directly against it.

Example

A lockout procedure (“three failed logins triggers a lock-out; recovery requires IT verification”) translates directly into a six-step test: fail login three times → confirm lockout → contact support → log in with the temporary password → set a new, policy-conformant password → log out and back in with it. Not every policy is this testable — a broad audit-logging requirement needs a sample of triggered events checked for completeness and accuracy, rather than one clean pass/fail.

3.4.1

Key Elements and Characteristics of an Effective Security Test Environment K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Security testing carries risks that call for a more segregated test environment than most other testing — especially against untrusted, third-party or open-source code.

Isolated

Separated from other systems, scaled to the malware risk.

Complete

Reflects the production target: OS/config, networking, middleware, hardware, databases, access rights, browsers/plug-ins, co-existing apps, and realistic (or safely obfuscated) data.

Restorable

Repeatable and recoverable if corruption occurs.

3.4.2

The Importance of Planning and Approvals in Security Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Security testing routinely brushes against laws around unauthorized access — in some countries even against possessing security testing tools — so testers need a waiver from the system/data owner and management approval before starting. Tests can also trigger intrusion-detection alerts (making the tester look like a malicious insider) or cause outright system failures.

Name of the authorizing entity, and of testing personnel/entity

Statement of work and authorization dates (from/to)

Originating IP addresses, user accounts and other relevant details

Attestations: system ownership, authority to authorize, backups taken and verified as restorable, risks understood

A hold-harmless clause and signatures of authorized representatives

Testing without this authorization risks violating security policy and can expose the tester to termination or prosecution.

3.5

Security Test Evaluation K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

Security test evaluation happens alongside execution, as each test runs. When a vulnerability is found, an incident report should record at minimum: the tester’s name, the test environment, the steps performed (to enable re-creation), the nature and extent of the vulnerability, its potential impact, and a suggested remediation.

Because security incidents carry higher sensitivity than ordinary defects, reports may need extra restriction — e.g. when independent testers use a tool with loose viewing permissions, when a vulnerability is known but not yet resolved, or when internal personnel could exploit it themselves. The IT auditor typically decides whether to restrict access to results, and a final report may be issued at the conclusion of a major testing effort such as system testing.

3.6

Security Test Maintenance K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Maintaining the security testing process often just means adding new test types as new threat types emerge — but targets and threats change daily, so the process itself needs to be designed to change easily. New tools also keep appearing; testers should track advances that might add power or flexibility to their testing.

Chapter 3 in one screen

ISTQB Security Testing Process
Maps 1:1 onto the general ISTQB test process, adding a security lens at every step; not strictly sequential.
Lifecycle alignment
Sequential, iterative, COTS and open-source projects each carry distinct security testing concerns.
Planning objectives
Verify defenses work as designed; verify no new vulnerabilities were introduced.
Test plan elements
Scope, who tests, schedule, tasks/time, environment, authorizations — each answered by framing questions.
Test design bases
Risk analysis, threat model, or origin-based risk categorization.
Control test types
Functional security, functional access, structural access, secure coding practice, OS access.
DoS/DDoS
Overload, amplification/botnet, resource exhaustion, and logic-abuse variants — each needs its own test level.
Policy-based test design
Turns a testable policy statement directly into a step-by-step test procedure.
Test environment
Isolated, complete, restorable.
Authorization
Required before testing — legal, IDS-trigger and system-failure risk all demand sign-off.
Test evaluation
Incident reports record tester, environment, steps, nature/extent/impact and remediation.
Test maintenance
Add new test types as threats emerge; process must be built to change easily.

Chapter 4 · CT-SEC

Security Testing Throughout the Software Lifecycle

Security can’t be tested or patched into a finished application — it has to be designed and verified at every stage. This chapter follows security testing through requirements, design, implementation (component and integration testing, with coverage measures), system and acceptance testing, and maintenance.

  • abuse caseA use case in which some actors with malicious intent are causing harm to the system or to other actors.
  • fuzz testingA software testing technique used to discover security vulnerabilities by inputting massive amounts of random data, called fuzz, to the component or system.Synonyms: fuzzing

4.1.1

The Lifecycle View of Security Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Security is not tested or patched into an already-built application — it comes from security-oriented design and verification throughout construction. A lifecycle process provides checkpoints so security activities happen at the right time: a prescribed point for security-related work (e.g. asking what levels of access are needed while capturing user needs), review checkpoints, testing checkpoints, and entry/exit criteria (e.g. no component enters integration testing until its security activities are complete).

4.1.2

Security-Related Activities in the Software Lifecycle K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

PhaseSecurity objectives & activities
RequirementsIdentify security needs from every perspective (including outside the organization, e.g. customer privacy); document them unambiguously so implementation and testing can trace back to them.
DesignTranslate security requirements into a workable, secure design approach; document it in a way that fits the lifecycle (whiteboard sessions or formal models).
ImplementationWrite code that meets security requirements and implements needed procedures/technology (firewalls, tokens); verify via component testing and code review.
System testingEnd-to-end functioning and performance of the full assembled system; verify security requirements at the system level.
Acceptance testingUsers or their agents test against security-related acceptance criteria in an operational-like environment.
MaintenanceConfirmation and regression testing after corrective, adaptive or perfective changes, to ensure no new vulnerabilities and that existing defenses still hold.

4.2

The Role of Security Testing in Requirements K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

Requirements are often the weakest link: many organizations struggle to write clear, unambiguous, testable requirements at all, and quality characteristics like security are easily crowded out by pure functionality. A checklist keeps the security perspective from being overlooked.

Privacy needs

Are user groups and their data-privacy needs identified? Are access rights defined?

Compliance needs

Are relevant security policies (and exceptions) identified and documented?

Common vulnerabilities

Are known vulnerabilities for the feature captured as risks?

Testability

Can tests be written from the document? Are vague terms like “processing must be secure” made specific?

Usability

Is the security process appropriately balanced against usability — e.g. a login flow so confusing customers abandon it?

Performance

Is security efficiency (e.g. encryption overhead) appropriately scoped?

4.3

The Role of Security Testing in Design K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

Test-related activities help recognize designs likely to be vulnerable and steer toward strong, identifiable security properties. The IEEE Computer Society Center for Secure Design recommends design approaches worth checking for during design review:

Earn or give, but never assume, trust

Use an authentication mechanism that cannot be bypassed or tampered with

Authorize only after authenticating

Strictly separate data and control instructions; never process control instructions from untrusted sources

Explicitly validate all data

Use cryptography correctly

Identify sensitive data and how it should be handled

Always consider the users

Understand how integrating external components changes the attack surface

Stay flexible for future changes to objects and actors

4.4.1

Security Testing During Component Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Component-level security testing starts with static evaluation (inspection, walkthrough, audit, technical review) and adds dynamic testing of behavior against valid and invalid inputs.

White-box / glass-box

Tests designed with visibility into the code, able to target specific controls and measure structural coverage (statements, decisions, paths). Structural testing (including fuzz testing, which floods a component with random data) can surface memory buffer overflows, malicious insider code, and undocumented “backdoor” access.

Black-box (functional)

Stimulus-response testing without structural visibility, confirming satisfaction of specified security requirements plus creative probing for what developers may have overlooked.

4.4.2

Security Test Design at the Component Level K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

A well-known high-level checklist (CERT’s “Top 10 Secure Coding Practices”) anchors component-level test design: validate input, heed compiler warnings, architect and design for security policies, keep it simple, default deny, adhere to least privilege, sanitize data sent to other systems, practice defense in depth, use effective QA techniques, and adopt a secure coding standard. Tests against this checklist should be grounded in a documented risk analysis and realistic threat modeling — focusing effort on the highest probability, highest consequence violations.

4.4.3

Analysis of Security Tests at the Component Level K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

Coverage typeTypical measures
Requirements-based% requirements tested, % use/abuse cases tested, % critical scenarios tested.
Data-drivenEquivalence classes; pairwise/N-wise coverage of input combinations.
Model-basedCause-effect and postcondition-disjunct coverage (pre/post models); axiom coverage (algebraic models).
Transition-based% nodes/states, % transitions, % transition-pairs, % cycles.
Structural% packages/classes/methods/decisions/statements exercised.

Cyclomatic complexity measures the number of independent paths through code; the strongest control-flow criterion, path coverage, is rarely feasible due to loops, so testers fall back to critical-path or branch (decision-outcome) coverage.

4.4.4

Security Testing During Component Integration Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

As components combine into subsystems and the full system, new attack vectors emerge from the interactions between components — not just the sum of each component’s individual vulnerabilities. Some interactions can also mitigate risks that existed in isolation. Testers again need to be creative about what integration might expose that unit-level testing couldn’t. The integration approach (top-down vs. bottom-up) affects when security concerns surface.

4.4.5

Security Test Design at the Component Integration Level K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Like component testing, integration security tests should rest on documented risk analysis and threat modeling. Scaffolding (stubs and drivers) may stand in for incomplete paths through the system; as it’s progressively replaced by real components, fuller functional assessment becomes possible — along with newly exposed paths to vulnerabilities.

4.5.1

The Role of Security Testing in System Testing K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

System testing is the first end-to-end exercise of the fully integrated system, and can reveal emergent properties invisible before integration. Security requirements are usually paired with functional ones (“in the process of doing X, the system should not allow Y”), so as functional tests run, the tester should also probe for ways security constraints could be violated. Use cases, abuse cases, process models and state transition models all describe procedures that can shape end-to-end security test scenarios.

4.5.2

The Role of Security Testing in Acceptance Testing K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Acceptance testing runs in a realistic operational environment and evaluates the system against documented acceptance criteria — ideally defined before development or purchase even began, though criteria commonly evolve and need re-analysis for security impact. Criteria can be global (e.g. authentication, user rights, encryption strength and audit trails applying across all functions) or function-specific (e.g. requiring dual approval for large payments).

4.6

The Role of Security Testing in Maintenance K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Regression testing confirms that previously acceptable behavior — including resistance to known attacks — still holds after a change, which matters especially because usability or efficiency enhancements are prone to quietly sacrificing security controls. Individual-function regression tests are often insufficient for security; end-to-end regression scenarios give a stronger guarantee that complete transactions remain secure after changes to hardware, configuration, OS, databases, networking or software.

Example

Confirming that users can still complete a purchase securely without exposing personal data, and that a payroll clerk who can add a new employee still cannot view that employee’s banking details, after any given maintenance change.

Chapter 4 in one screen

Lifecycle view
Security is designed and verified across the lifecycle, never patched in at the end.
Requirements checklist
Privacy, compliance, common vulnerabilities, testability, usability, performance.
Secure design principles
Never assume trust; authenticate then authorize; validate all data; use cryptography correctly.
Component testing
White-box (structural, incl. fuzzing) + black-box (functional) together.
Coverage measures
Requirements-based, data-driven, model-based, transition-based, structural.
Integration testing
New attack vectors emerge from component interactions, not just summed component risk.
System/acceptance testing
Pairs security constraints with functional requirements; acceptance uses documented, evolving criteria.
Maintenance
End-to-end regression scenarios catch security regressions that function-level tests miss.

Chapter 5 · CT-SEC

Testing Security Mechanisms

Every organization layers multiple lines of defense, and none of them is sufficient alone. This chapter covers the mechanisms a security tester needs to understand and probe: system hardening, authentication and authorization, encryption, firewalls and network zones, intrusion detection, malware scanning, data obfuscation, and security training.

  • anti-malwareSoftware that is used to detect and inhibit malware.
  • authenticationA procedure determining whether a person or a process is, in fact, who or what it is declared to be.
  • authorizationPermission given to a user or process to access resources.
  • demilitarized zoneA physical or logical subnetwork that contains and exposes an organization’s external-facing services to an untrusted network, commonly the Internet.Abbreviation: DMZ
  • encryptionThe process of encoding information so that only authorized parties can retrieve the original information, usually by means of a specific decryption key or process.
  • firewallA component or set of components that controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on predetermined security rules.
  • hashingTransformation of a variable length string of characters into a usually shorter fixed-length value or key, commonly used in table/database lookups; cryptographic hash functions secure data.
  • insider threatA security threat originating from within the organization, often by an authorized system user.
  • intrusion detection systemA system which monitors activities to detect violations of the security policy.Abbreviation: IDS
  • malwareSoftware that is intended to harm a system or its components.
  • malware scanningStatic analysis aiming to detect and remove malicious code received at an interface.
  • network zoneA sub-network with a defined level of trust — for example, the Internet or a public zone would be considered untrusted.
  • pharmingA security attack intended to redirect a website’s traffic to a fraudulent website without the user’s knowledge or consent.
  • phishingAn attempt to acquire personal or sensitive information by masquerading as a trustworthy entity in an electronic communication.
  • saltingA cryptographic technique that adds random data (salt) to the user data prior to hashing.
  • system hardeningThe step-by-step process of reducing the vulnerabilities of a system by applying a security policy and different layers of protection.
  • vulnerability scannerA tool that automates the assessment of a system or application for known vulnerabilities, easing the workload of a manual vulnerability audit.

5.1.1

Understanding System Hardening K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

As systems grow more complex, their attack surface keeps growing. Vulnerabilities come from design errors (“by design”), source code defects (“by construction”) or configuration slips (“by configuration”). System hardening is the step-by-step process of reducing that attack surface through a security policy and layers of protection, applied at any level — a component, a product, a system, or a system of systems.

Remove

Unnecessary software, libraries, developer tools, accounts, applications, network services, and peripherals/ports.

Patch & configure

Prompt patching, automatic updates, current configurations, coding rules that avoid by-construction defects, remote logging so an attacker can’t erase evidence.

Layer defenses

Strong authentication and least-privilege authorization, encryption, firewalls and security zones, intrusion detection, anti-malware, and obfuscation.

Note

Hardening must be balanced against usability — over-restrictive protections that block productivity tend to get disabled, which defeats the purpose.

5.1.2

Testing the Effectiveness of System Hardening Mechanisms K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Tests should confirm hardening is applied in the right places, in the right ways — and isn’t so restrictive that it’s excessive relative to the actual risk. Some tests are review/audit-based; others check what specific user groups can actually do or access.

Audit server/application configuration for unchanged default passwords

Audit configuration for unnecessary services and open network ports

Verify components, libraries and application versions aren’t obsolete or vulnerable

A vulnerability scanner automates much of this work, especially for complex, multi-site environments; static analysis tools detect coding-rule violations that introduce construction vulnerabilities.

5.2.1

The Relationship Between Authentication and Authorization K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Authentication answers “who is this user, and are they really who they claim?” via a login/token — implementations range from weak-password detection to one-time passwords, fingerprinting, software or hard-token certificates, local/server/network authentication, and Single Sign-On. Authorization then answers whether the authenticated user has rights to a given action or resource. The two are tightly linked: an unauthenticated user has no rights (or only minimal ones) — e.g. a merchant site lets anyone browse products, but only an authenticated account can purchase, and even then cannot perform administrative actions.

5.2.2

Testing the Effectiveness of Authentication and Authorization Mechanisms K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Attackers exploit coding errors (missing input filtering), outdated libraries, configuration errors (default passwords/rights left in place), and simple weak passwords (“123456” still tops the charts). Password rules alone don’t help if users aren’t diligent, or if the rules themselves don’t reflect current good practice (e.g. SANS’ Password Construction Guidelines).

Brute-force and dictionary attacks against common/weak passwords

Exploiting missing input filtering, e.g. SQL injection to bypass login entirely

Manipulating URIs/URLs (path traversal, guessing admin routes) to reach restricted data

Exploiting an unpatched vulnerability for unintended behavior, gaining control and privilege escalation

5.3.1

Understanding Encryption K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Encryption encodes plain text into cipher text using an algorithm and a shared secret, so only authorized parties — who hold the decryption mechanism — can recover the original. It underpins confidentiality, integrity, availability and non-repudiation of sensitive assets. Hashing and salting are companion techniques often used alongside encryption.

Protocol typeUse
SymmetricA single shared secret key, protecting data at rest (ciphered databases, drives) or in transit.
AsymmetricA private/public key pair, commonly used in communication protocols like SSL/TLS and ciphered email.

5.3.2

Testing the Effectiveness of Common Encryption Mechanisms K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Design vulnerabilities

Right symmetric mode in use; adequate key size (a 2015-era RSA key <2048 bit is already insecure); certificate validity and alerting on self-signed certs; replay-attack resistance (e.g. WEP); protocol-strength attacks.

Construction vulnerabilities

Code review for weak random-number seeding; fuzzing for unexpected behavior; timing attacks (measuring execution time); power analysis on hardware devices.

Configuration vulnerabilities

TLS server- and client-side protocol configuration; cipher order and downgrade/renegotiation resistance.

Aging

Mechanisms that were strong when deployed but have since become crackable as compute power and cryptanalysis advance.

5.4.1

Understanding Firewalls K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

A firewall restricts access between a protected network and the internet, or between other network sets, enforcing a policy of authorized and forbidden communication. It can be host-based (monitoring one host’s traffic) or network-based (monitoring traffic between networks), filtering primarily on source/target address and protocol, protocol options, and data size — while Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) add filtering by user/connection and data patterns.

A network zone is a sub-network with a defined trust level: the untrusted internet/public zone, one or more demilitarized zones (DMZs) with intermediate trust, and the most-trusted internal/private network(s) — the zone map is itself part of the firewall configuration, defining what traffic is authorized between zones.

5.4.2

Testing Firewall Effectiveness K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Port scanning to verify the security policy is correctly implemented

Malformed packets and network fuzzing to trigger unexpected behavior (e.g. a DoS)

Fragmentation attacks to bypass filtering and carry an attack behind the firewall

Encoding/compressing/obfuscating payloads to hide malicious content from a WAF

Given the sheer number of protocols, options and network complexity, efficient firewall configuration is genuinely hard — which is exactly why these tests matter.

5.5.1

Understanding Intrusion Detection Tools K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

An intrusion detection system (IDS) monitors activity from network to application layer to detect security policy violations, raising alerts for further action (traffic blocking, virtual patching) when it spots a deviation. IDS design follows two models.

Negative / signature-based (blacklist)

“All that is not explicitly forbidden is allowed.” Detection is based on a list of known attacks or patterns.

Positive / behavior-based (whitelist)

“All that is not explicitly allowed is rejected.” Detection is based on the specified normal behavior of the protected system; trusted traffic can be used to build that specification.

A firewall looks outward to stop intrusions before they happen; an IDS looks inward, analyzing suspicious activity and raising alerts once it’s confirmed.

5.5.2

Testing the Effectiveness of Intrusion Detection Tools K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Against signature-based (evasion)

Character encoding/modification, IP fragmentation, TCP segmentation, encryption/obfuscation, URL encoding — all designed to slip past known-pattern matching.

Against behavior-based

Complementary tests can gradually shift the IDS’s notion of “normal” using malicious traffic, so genuinely intrusive behavior ends up classified as authorized — alongside checking for the high false-positive/false-negative rates typical of this approach.

5.6.1

Understanding Malware Scanning Tools K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Malicious code reaches its target via infected email attachments, fake URLs, client-side code execution and similar vectors. An anti-malware application analyzes, detects and removes malicious code aimed at malware, phishing and pharming targets — primarily via signature-based detection (matching known patterns), sometimes supplemented with heuristics to catch slight variations of known malware.

5.6.2

Testing the Effectiveness of Malware Scanning Tools K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Exploiting system library functions the malware relies on (e.g. closing the anti-malware application itself)

String obfuscation (encryption, compression such as UPX) to hide behavior from static signatures

Dynamic loading of functions/libraries to limit what static analysis can see

Auto-updating malware, or offloading decompression to the GPU so it’s never fully in analyzable memory

Functional testing can use a harmless test file such as EICAR instead of real malicious code. Before rolling out a new or upgraded anti-malware tool organization-wide, test it on a representative platform first — there are real cases of anti-malware software quarantining legitimate OS files and taking down an organization’s entire computing capability.

5.7.1

Understanding Data Obfuscation K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Data obfuscation (sometimes “data masking” or “anonymization”) makes data and source code non-understandable to a human, protecting against unlicensed copying and reverse-engineering, and letting staff such as support or functional testers work with non-sensitive stand-ins. Techniques include base64-encoding, XORing, random renaming, method overriding, whitespace stripping and shuffling; encryption is also usable as an obfuscation technique, though ciphered data remains fully viewable to anyone holding a valid key.

Note

Obfuscation is a double-edged tool — attackers routinely use the same techniques to hide their own malicious code and attacks.

5.7.2

Testing the Effectiveness of Data Obfuscation Approaches K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Tight configuration control between obfuscated data and the keys used to obfuscate it is essential, or the data can’t be recovered for legitimate use. Since production data often can’t be shown to testers as-is (e.g. patient records in a health system), obfuscation is also used to anonymize test data.

Brute-force or dictionary attacks attempting to recover plain data from obfuscated data

Reverse-engineering byte code (e.g. decompiling Java or .NET) to test code-level obfuscation

Brute-force attacks against known-weak obfuscation mechanisms (e.g. unXOR-style tools)

In theory, code can never fully protect itself against de-obfuscation — debugging is always available to a determined attacker — so anti-decompilation tools reduce risk rather than eliminate it.

5.8.1

The Importance of Security Training K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Humans are consistently the weakest link in security. Continuous training reminds people why established policies exist and keeps them current with new policies and threats — it should run throughout the software lifecycle and specifically cover recognizing social engineering attacks and insider threats.

5.8.2

How to Test the Effectiveness of Security Training K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Social engineering: attempt to extract a password over the phone posing as technical support

Physical sweep for passwords on sticky notes (especially under keyboards)

Password audit tools to identify weak passwords (noting the tool itself exposes them to whoever runs it)

Injecting SQL into an unvalidated field to see if a developer needs secure-coding training

Attempting unauthorized physical access to view documents left in the open

Chapter 5 in one screen

System hardening
Reduce the attack surface: remove unneeded software/accounts/services, patch promptly, layer defenses — balanced against usability.
Authentication vs. authorization
Who are you, and are you who you claim (authN); what are you allowed to do (authZ) — authZ presumes authN.
Encryption
Symmetric (shared key) vs. asymmetric (public/private key); tested for design, construction, configuration and aging weaknesses.
Firewalls & network zones
Filter traffic between trust zones (public / DMZ / internal); tested via port scans, fuzzing, fragmentation, WAF-evasion.
IDS
Signature-based (blacklist, evadable) vs. behavior-based (whitelist, false-positive prone).
Malware scanning
Mostly signature-based; malware counters with obfuscation, dynamic loading and auto-update; test with tools like EICAR.
Data obfuscation
Masks data/code from humans; keys must be tightly controlled; attackers use the same techniques offensively.
Training
The human layer — tested with social engineering, physical sweeps, password audits and injection probes.
