Human Behavior & Risk Attacker Mentality Attack Motivations Attack Scenarios & Forensics Social Engineering Security Awareness Increasing Awareness

Chapter 6 · CT-SEC

Human Factors in Security Testing

Technology alone never secures a system — people do, or fail to. This chapter covers how attackers think and what motivates them, the basics of computer forensics, how social engineering exploits human trust, and how to build and sustain security awareness across an organization.

  • attackerA person or process that attempts to access data, functions or other restricted areas of the system without authorization, potentially with malicious intent.
  • botnetA network of compromised computers, called bots or robots, which is controlled by a third party and used to transmit malware or spam, or to launch attacks.
  • computer forensicsThe practice of determining how a security attack has succeeded and assessing the damage caused.
  • hackerA person or organization who is actively involved in security attacks, usually with malicious intent.
  • reconnaissanceThe exploration of a target area aiming to gain information that can be useful for an attack.Synonyms: footprinting
  • script kiddieA person who executes security attacks that have been created by other hackers rather than creating one’s own attacks.

6.1.1

The Impact of Human Behavior on Security Risks K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

In information security, the human being is both the largest threat and the weakest point of defense. Every attack begins with reconnaissance — gathering information about the target. Anything published about an organization, deliberately or not, will eventually be found and used; it’s never a question of “if” but “when.” Employees add to this constantly through their own social media activity, so the information available to an attacker keeps shifting after a security policy is written — meaning security tests that were valid when created may lose coverage as that public information changes.

6.1.2

Understanding the Attacker Mentality K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

During reconnaissance (“footprinting”), an attacker uses passive and active means to build a picture of the target. Passive sources need no direct connection to the target system.

Passive

Search engines (including Google Hacking Database queries), Shodan, social networks, Whois, RIPE, DNS lookups — IP addresses, org structure, email conventions, OS/application fingerprints.

Active

Pinging, TCP/UDP port scanning, OS detection and service fingerprinting (e.g. via Nmap) — the attacker directly touches the system.

Because unauthorized access is illegal in most jurisdictions, attackers typically try to erase evidence afterward — via log tunneling/alteration, hide tools, rootkits or file streaming — both to avoid detection and to preserve continued access, including turning a compromised system into part of a botnet.

6.1.3

Common Motivations and Sources of Computer System Attacks K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Many breaches originate inside the organization: insider attackers — authorized users turned malicious, often motivated by revenge or increasingly by economic espionage. External attackers are responsible for the minority of attacks and are motivated by curiosity, prestige, notoriety, challenge, boredom or revenge (considered the most dangerous, highest-motivation case).

Attackers range across a spectrum: script kiddies run attacks others created; at the top are professional, well-resourced organizations engaged in hacktivism or government-sponsored activity. Motivation similarly spans from playing around for fun to deliberately taking down a system for political, ideological, economic or terrorist reasons. Understanding this spectrum helps an organization scope both its defenses and its security test strategy.

6.1.4

Understanding Attack Scenarios and Motivations K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

A security incident is a security-relevant event in which the system’s security policy is disobeyed or breached. Computer forensics investigates what happened and who was responsible, through three phases.

1. Acquire & authenticate

Snapshot the system, authenticate the copy as genuine and complete, store it safely, then eradicate the cause and recover the system to its normal state. Watch for suspicious log entries, unexplained accounts, modified files, unusual services, and unsuccessful logins as early symptoms.

2. Analyze

Examine log files and active connections, trace originating IP addresses (harder when attackers chain proxies or Tor); tools such as Netstat and Tracert/traceroute help. Botnet-based attacks are especially difficult to trace — the owners of the compromised machines are often unaware they’re part of the attack.

3. Report

Feeds into security test evaluation and reporting (Chapter 7).

6.2

Social Engineering K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Every technical defense still depends on employees getting legitimate access to do their work — and it is human behavior, not technology, that is the greatest threat to security. Social engineering exploits people’s natural willingness to trust and help strangers, manipulating them into revealing access, authorization details, or other sensitive information.

Direct human interaction

Tailgating/piggybacking into a restricted area; eavesdropping; shoulder surfing; phone pretexting (posing as a manager or support technician).

Computer-based

Malware-laden email, chat/instant-messaging abuse, fake pop-ups prompting re-entry of credentials, spam with malicious links, and phishing (including highly targeted spear phishing) toward infected websites.

There is no single defense — least-privilege access, separation of duties and rotation of duties limit the damage, but education and awareness at every level remain the primary defense.

6.3.1

The Importance of Security Awareness K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

The threat model keeps shifting: networks evolve, new applications and interfaces appear, and new vulnerabilities are constantly introduced and discovered. Risks that were once flagged but never materialized get forgotten and their safeguards quietly withdrawn — opening the door to both hacking and social engineering. Regular awareness training keeps administrators and staff alert to changes in the threat model, tailored to distinct groups: developers, operations, management and general staff.

6.3.2

Increasing Security Awareness K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Effective training builds on real case studies — incidents discovered through security testing or actual breaches — structured around a common set of questions that make the lesson concrete and actionable.

How did they (we) do it?

What were the business consequences?

What did it cost to investigate and process the incident?

What did it cost to repair the problem?

How could the incident have been avoided?

Which changes will be implemented?

Chapter 6 in one screen

Human factor
The largest threat and weakest point of defense in any security posture.
Reconnaissance
Passive (search engines, social media, Whois, DNS) and active (scanning, fingerprinting) information gathering.
Attacker types
Insiders (often revenge/espionage) vs. external (curiosity to professional/hacktivist); script kiddies to well-resourced organizations.
Computer forensics
Acquire & authenticate → analyze → report.
Social engineering
Exploits trust via direct human interaction or computer-based channels; countered mainly through education.
Security awareness
Must be continuous, group-tailored, and built on real case studies to stay ahead of a shifting threat model.

Chapter 7 · CT-SEC

Security Test Evaluation and Reporting

Security test results carry more sensitivity than ordinary defects, and expectations shift as a project unfolds. This chapter covers evaluating results against evolving criteria, keeping security test results appropriately confidential, and structuring reports so each audience gets what it actually needs.

  • acceptance criteriaThe exit criteria that a component or system must satisfy in order to be accepted by a user, customer, or other authorized entity.
  • attack vectorA path or means by which an attacker can gain access to a system for malicious purposes.
  • dashboardA representation of dynamic measurements of operational performance for some organization or activity, using metrics represented via metaphors such as visual dials, counters, and other devices resembling an automobile dashboard.
  • exit criteriaThe set of generic and specific conditions, agreed upon with stakeholders, for permitting a process to be officially completed — used to report against and to plan when to stop testing.Synonyms: test completion criteria, completion criteria, definition of done

7.1

Security Test Evaluation K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Measuring results against security expectations, exit criteria and acceptance criteria is what determines test completion. It’s rarely possible to know every security risk at a project’s outset, and stakeholder expectations shift — a newly disclosed threat can suddenly demand a higher level of security than originally planned. This is why security risk assessments need to be revisited throughout a project, feeding their results back into ongoing test planning and execution rather than being treated as a one-time gate.

7.2.1

Confidentiality of Security Test Results K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

A thorough security tester often ends up knowing more about a system’s weaknesses than its own developers or designers do. The general rule — share information only with those who need to know — applies with particular force to security test results, where being conservative about distribution is simply good practice, since the same information that helps a defender helps an attacker.

7.2.2

Creating Proper Controls and Data Gathering Mechanisms for Reporting Security Test Status K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Security vulnerabilities are typically judged more sensitive than comparable functional defects, and are usually assigned higher severity in the incident-tracking system as a result. That heightened sensitivity demands more precise, accurate and timely reporting of both the nature of the defect and its implied risk — and it’s good practice to agree explicitly with management on how and when they want access to security defect reports (e.g. via a security test dashboard), rather than assuming a default cadence.

7.2.3

Analyzing Interim Security Test Status Reports K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

Reports can be produced throughout the security testing process, or only at its conclusion (e.g. end of system testing, or end of acceptance-phase security testing). Early reporting is generally preferred: it leaves more time to remediate before release.

Report identifier

Summary (executive summary + key findings)

Variances (process followed, deviations from plan, methods/tools used)

Comprehensive assessment (coverage evaluation; explanation for anything untested)

Summary of results (resolved vulnerabilities and resolutions; unresolved vulnerabilities)

Evaluation (status against exit criteria; classified risks and impact of what’s unresolved)

Summary of activities

Approvals

A report’s effectiveness rests on its timing, content, recipients, and how well the content is tuned to what each recipient actually needs — an executive summary and a system architect’s technical detail are rarely the same document, so multiple tailored reports are often warranted.

Chapter 7 in one screen

Evaluation
Measured against expectations, exit criteria and acceptance criteria; risk assessments must be revisited as scope evolves.
Confidentiality
Share security test results on a need-to-know basis — a conservative default.
Reporting controls
Security defects get higher severity than comparable functional ones; agree the reporting cadence with management explicitly.
Report structure
Identifier, summary, variances, comprehensive assessment, results, evaluation, activities, approvals.
Effectiveness factors
Timing, content, recipients, and tuning content to each audience — often several tailored reports, not one.

Tool Types & Purposes Documenting Tool Needs Open Source Issues Vendor Evaluation

Chapter 8 · CT-SEC

Security Testing Tools

Security testing tools trace their history to the hacking community itself, and the market today is vast and non-standardized. This chapter covers the types and purposes of security testing tools, and how to select them — documenting real needs, weighing open-source trade-offs, and evaluating vendor capability.

8.1

Types and Purposes of Security Testing Tools K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Security testing tools trace their lineage straight back to the hacking community: early exploit tools, shared and improved within that community, became the basis for legitimate security testing tools used by administrators and testers. John the Ripper, originally a hacker tool for cracking Unix passwords, is now a standard tool for detecting weak passwords defensively — and frameworks like Nessus and Metasploit followed a similar path from open-source hacker tooling to broadly used, GUI-friendly security platforms.

Today the field is huge: nearly any environment or task has a dedicated tool, open source or licensed. The core challenge is that most of these tools are non-standardized — developers broadly agree on how to test for a given defense or vulnerability, but differ in test data, implementation and interpretation of results, so the same target tested with two tools can yield two different pictures.

Testing styleCharacteristics
Static analysisPerformed very early in the lifecycle, while the object under test is not running; available for most languages and usually reports on security aspects directly.
Dynamic analysisProbes a running system — though in security testing the line blurs: a “dynamic” tool that performs a static scan of a database is really acting as a static tool in that moment. If the entire system is the object under test, the tool is genuinely dynamic.

The Web Application Security Consortium and OWASP maintain categorized tool lists, and penetration-testing distributions such as Kali Linux offer their own classification. The advanced security tester is expected to maintain their own current list, since the tool market changes quickly and no single resource stays comprehensive for long.

8.2.1

Analyzing and Documenting Security Testing Needs K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

Tool selection starts from documenting what needs testing, drawing on multiple sources as the test basis.

The organization’s security policy and test policy

Threat and risk analysis results for the actual system/project

Requirements and other system specifications

System architecture and design; security (test) strategy

Known security threats, exploits and vulnerabilities; user profiles

These sources reveal what interfaces need testing, which protocols and standards to verify, which secure-coding guidelines apply, and which component configurations need hardening — and whether security testing here is a development activity or an operations/maintenance one. All of it shapes the requirements for the tool set.

8.2.2

Issues with Open Source Tools K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Many security testing tools live in the open-source domain, distributed under licenses that permit free use and modification — though some organizations, especially under regulatory compliance obligations, are restricted to commercial or certified tools only. Open source tools can be free to acquire but still carry real cost: technical capacity for support and configuration, learning time, time invested in community forums, upgrade cadence, and risk that the tool’s direction changes or it goes commercial.

Limited functional scope of any one tool

Time to learn to administer, configure and use it

Time invested in user forums and community groups

Time needed for updates/upgrades, and the internal upgrade policy

The tool’s future direction, and how responsive its support community is

8.2.3

Evaluating a Tool Vendor's Capabilities K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

For a purchased tool, the vendor should offer services that let the security testing practice start and grow internally.

Types of licenses offered (fixed / desk / floating / token)

License scalability (per functional area, per number of licenses)

Helpdesk/support facilities and hours

Forum or user community

Update frequency

Administration and user manuals

Support and maintenance contracts

Chapter 8 in one screen

Tool origins
Many legitimate security tools began as hacker tools (e.g. John the Ripper).
Non-standardization
Tools agree broadly on what to test for but differ in data, implementation and result interpretation.
Static vs. dynamic
Static = object under test isn’t running; dynamic = it is — but the line blurs when a “dynamic” tool performs a static scan.
Documenting needs
Security/test policy, risk analysis, requirements, architecture, strategy, known threats, user profiles.
Open source trade-offs
Free to acquire, but costs support capacity, learning time, upgrade effort and community dependency.
Vendor evaluation
License model/scalability, support, community, update cadence, documentation, contracts.

Standards Benefits Regulatory vs. Contractual Standard Selection Applying Standards Industry Trends Evaluating Practices

Chapter 9 · CT-SEC

Standards and Industry Trends

Standards give security testing a shared vocabulary and a starting framework, but only if applied correctly. This chapter covers the benefits and selection of security testing standards, how to apply mandatory versus optional clauses correctly, and where to track industry trends as the threat landscape keeps evolving.

  • consensus-based standardThe considered opinion of a knowledgeable body of experts, made available for voluntary use (in whole or in part) in contractual agreements between suppliers and customers.

9.1.1

The Benefits of Using Security Testing Standards K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Standards give visibility into professional consensus or regulatory obligation. A consensus-based standard reflects the considered opinion of knowledgeable experts, offered for voluntary use in contractual agreements; lesser, self-identified or vendor-specific “standards” also exist and carry correspondingly less weight. In regulated industries — medical, financial, transportation, energy — agencies may mandate compliance with their own regulations or their interpretation of otherwise-voluntary standards.

Provide a framework for security testing, eliminating the need to start from a blank page

Describe effective defenses and how to test for the most common attacks

Can be tailored to a project’s or organization’s specific needs

Let an organization demonstrate due diligence by following a recognized standard

9.1.2

Applicability of Standards in Regulatory Versus Contractual Situations K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

In regulated activities, every party must understand its compliance obligations — failing to comply can delay or block product approval, or in extreme cases lead to financial or criminal sanctions. In contractual situations, standards give both parties a reasonable, convenient starting point for negotiating requirements rather than beginning from nothing, letting consensus best practice be adopted or adapted as needed.

Unless a regulator imposes a standard unilaterally, or a contract is non-negotiable, standards form the basic framework for a negotiated agreement or can be self-imposed on one’s own work. Once a contract commits to specific standards, the entity is obligated to follow them strictly and document any deviation.

9.1.3

Selection of Security Standards K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Not every security standard applies to every situation. It’s an organization’s responsibility to research the standard(s) most appropriate to its systems, applications, sensitive assets, risk level and compliance requirements — and to remember that most standards are designed to be tailored to an organization’s specific needs, not adopted verbatim.

9.2

Applying Security Standards K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Precise language matters in any standard: shall identifies a mandatory requirement for conformance, while should and may mark optional tasks not required for conformance. A common misuse is blurring this distinction — treating an optional item as required, or an obligatory item as optional. Where a project or organization needs to deviate from a standard’s strict wording, that deviation — omission, modification or addition — needs to be documented and agreed by all parties.

9.3.1

Where to Learn of Industry Trends in Information Security K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

Both general-purpose and industry-specific news services (publications, sites, mailing lists) and events (conferences, trade shows, professional society meetings) surface new and growing concerns. Belonging to a focused professional community typically delivers more timely, targeted updates than general media — and given how fast new exploits appear, electronic alerts offer the most immediate actionable warning.

Widely-publicized exploits reveal broad trends, but issues specific to one’s own industry, application area or product are more likely to surface in specialized publications, technical conferences and professional events than in general news.

9.3.2

Evaluating Security Testing Practices for Improvements K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic.

New technologies, or novel uses of existing ones, typically open a window of misuse before their risks and limits are well understood — location-aware mobile services are one example, where convenience has led people to accept minute-by-minute tracking of their movements.

The range of motivated actors keeps expanding: criminal, hacktivist, economic and political agents with growing resources; extortion schemes moving from physical threats into digital ones; large ad hoc networks of ideologically driven individuals mobilized on short notice; well-funded corporate espionage; and nation-states pursuing economic or military advantage who may consider themselves immune to consequences. Because the threat keeps evolving, security testers need to stay ready for the next one — industry awareness, tracking security trends, and acquiring the right tools are the best available defense.

Chapter 9 in one screen

Standards
Consensus-based (expert opinion, voluntary) vs. lesser self-identified/vendor-specific variants.
Benefits
Ready-made framework, documented effective defenses, tailorable, demonstrates due diligence.
Regulatory vs. contractual
Regulatory = mandatory compliance with sanctions for failure; contractual = negotiated starting point.
Shall / should / may
Shall = mandatory for conformance; should/may = optional — don’t blur the distinction.
Selection
No standard fits every situation — research and tailor to the organization’s actual context.
Industry trends
Professional communities and electronic alerts beat general media for timely, targeted updates.
Evolving threat landscape
New tech opens misuse windows; criminal, hacktivist, economic and nation-state actors keep expanding in reach and resources.
