CTAL-TM · Chapter 1

Managing the Test Activities

The test manager plans, monitors, and controls the test process end to end — test planning, test monitoring and control, and test completion — while tailoring that work to the project’s stakeholders, its software development lifecycle model, and its test levels and test types. This chapter covers how risk-based testing focuses test effort where it matters most, how a project test strategy is chosen and justified, how test processes are improved over time, and how test tools are introduced, evaluated, and retired.

  • hybrid software development modelA type of software development lifecycle model that combines elements of different software development lifecycle models.
  • IDEALAn organizational improvement model that serves as a roadmap for initiating, planning, and implementing improvement actions.
  • incremental development modelA type of software development lifecycle model in which the component or system is developed through a series of increments.
  • iterative development modelA type of software development lifecycle model in which the component or system is developed through a series of repeated cycles.
  • product riskA risk that impacts the quality of a product.
  • quality riskA product risk or a project risk impacting quality management.
  • retrospectiveA regular event in which team members discuss results, review their practices, and identify ways to improve.Synonyms: project retrospective, retrospective meeting, post-project meeting
  • risk analysisThe overall process of risk identification and risk assessment.
  • risk assessmentThe process to examine identified risks and determine the risk level.
  • risk identificationThe process of finding, recognizing and describing risks.
  • risk impactThe damage that will be caused if a risk becomes an actual outcome or event.Synonyms: impact
  • risk levelThe measure of a risk defined by risk impact and risk likelihood.Synonyms: risk exposure
  • risk likelihoodThe probability that a risk will become an actual outcome or event.Synonyms: likelihood
  • risk managementThe process for handling risks.
  • risk mitigationThe process through which decisions are reached and protective measures are implemented for reducing or maintaining risks to specified levels.
  • risk monitoringThe activity that checks and reports the status of known risks to stakeholders.
  • risk-based testingA test approach in which the management, selection, prioritization, and use of test activities and resources are based on corresponding risk types and risk levels.
  • S.M.A.R.T. goal methodologyA framework for the clear formulation of management objectives by requiring goals to be specific, measurable, attainable, relevant, and timely.Abbreviation: SMART
  • sequential development modelA type of software development lifecycle model in which a complete system is developed in a linear way of several discrete and successive phases with no overlap between them.
  • software development lifecycleThe activities performed at each phase in software development, and how they relate to one another logically and chronologically.Abbreviation: SDLCSynonyms: lifecycle model
  • test completionThe activity that makes testware available for later use, leaves test environments in a satisfactory condition and communicates the results of testing to relevant stakeholders.Synonyms: test closure
  • test controlThe activity that develops and applies corrective actions to get a test project on track when it deviates from what was planned.
  • test levelA specific instantiation of a test process.Synonyms: test stage
  • Test Maturity Model integrationA five-level staged framework for test process improvement, related to the Capability Maturity Model Integration (CMMI), that describes the key elements of an effective test process.Abbreviation: TMMi
  • test monitoringThe activity that checks the status of testing activities, identifies any variances from planned or expected, and reports status to stakeholders.
  • test planDocumentation describing the test objectives to be achieved and the means and the schedule for achieving them, organized to coordinate testing.
  • test planningThe activity of establishing or updating a test plan.
  • test process improvementA program of activities undertaken to improve the performance and maturity of the organization’s test processes.
  • test strategyA description of how to perform testing to reach test objectives under given circumstances.
  • test typeA group of test activities based on specific test objectives aimed at specific characteristics of a component or system.
  • TPI NextA continuous business-driven framework for test process improvement that describes the key elements of an effective and efficient test process.

1.1

The Test Process K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

The ISTQB® Foundation Level Syllabus describes a test process with seven activities: test planning, test monitoring and control, test analysis, test design, test implementation, test execution, and test completion — often implemented iteratively or in parallel depending on the SDLC model and project context. This syllabus focuses on three key test management activities, which the ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-2 standard defines as test management processes applicable at different levels — project, program, or portfolio — each with its own test plan aligned to the higher-level plan.

1.1.1Test PlanningDefine objectives, approach, scope, resources, schedule, deliverables, participants
→
1.1.2Test Monitoring & ControlTrack progress, results, deviations; act corrective; report status
→
1.1.3Test CompletionFinalize and archive testware, evaluate the process, communicate closure

1.1.1 Test Planning Activities K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Test planning can target different scopes — the entire project, a test level, a test type, or a release/iteration/sprint in Agile — so its start and end points shift with scope. It identifies the activities and resources needed to achieve the test objectives set in the test policy, should start as early as possible (preferably before requirements are identified), and is often iterative, requiring re-planning as the project progresses.

The following tasks are part of test planning, similar to those in ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-2:

Understand the context and organize test planning

Understand the organization’s context (test policy, organizational test strategy), the test scope, and the test item. Organize the plan’s development and obtain stakeholder approval of activities and schedule.

Identify and analyze product risks

Identify and assess the potential impact and likelihood of product risks as part of test planning (see Section 1.3, Risk-Based Testing).

Identify risk treatment approaches

Based on the risk analysis, select and document appropriate preventive, corrective, or mitigating actions in the test plan.

Define test approach and estimate/allocate resources

Define the test approach for the current scope based on the organizational test strategy, regulatory standards, and project constraints (see Section 1.4). Estimate required resources — staff, tools, environments, data — and allocate them.

Establish the test plan

The test plan must be accepted by all stakeholders, so disagreements between them should be settled.

1.1.2 Test Monitoring and Control Activities K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Efficient test control requires a testing schedule and monitoring framework that enables tracking of status and progress, including the detailed measures and targets needed to relate test work products and resources to the plan and strategic objectives. Small, less complex projects can relate work products and activities to objectives fairly easily, but larger projects generally need more detailed measures and targets covering test objectives and test basis coverage. Above all, the status of test work products and activities must be related in a way that is understandable and relevant to project and business stakeholders. Test monitoring and control are ongoing activities.

Test control

Compares actual progress against the test plan and implements corrective actions as needed. It guides testing to meet the test strategies and objectives (Section 1.4) and revisits test planning when necessary; control data requires detailed test planning information for appropriate reactions.

Test monitoring

Collects and records test results, identifies deviations from planned testing, identifies and analyzes new risks that require testing, and monitors changes for identified risks.

Test control activity involves:

Implementing the test plan and control directives.

Managing deviations from planned testing.

Treating newly identified and changed risks.

Establishing readiness to begin testing.

Granting and obtaining approval for test completion based on the exit criteria.

1.1.3 Test Completion Activities K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Test completion usually occurs at project milestones — a release, the end of an iteration, or test level completion. Unresolved defects become change requests or product backlog items. Once exit criteria are met, key outputs should be captured, archived, and provided to relevant stakeholders.

Create and approve the test completion report

Ensure all testing has been accomplished and all test objectives met, by collecting and summarizing information from test plans, test results, test progress reports, and defect reports. The report is approved and communicated to relevant stakeholders.

Archive testware

Identify testware useful for future reuse (typically test cases), make it accessible and understandable, and temporarily archive test results, logs, reports, and other testware in the configuration management system.

Handover testware

Deliver valuable work products to those who need them — for example, communicating deferred or accepted known defects to those who will use or support the testware.

Clean and restore the test environment

Remove test data, tools, drivers, stubs, and scripts from the test environment, and restore it to its original or desired state so it is ready for the next testing cycle or project.

Perform/collect/document lessons learned

Discuss and document important lessons learned during the test process in retrospectives, potentially covering the entire SDLC. These feed test process improvement (Section 1.5).

1.2

The Context of Testing K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

The context of testing encompasses the unique conditions and constraints that shape decisions and strategies for planning, designing, and executing tests. Test managers must grasp this context to align testing with the specific needs of the project — a context that can differ by product type, industry, regulatory requirements, and, crucially, the SDLC being employed. Test managers apply established test strategies and choose test techniques rather than developing them, and play a key role in tailoring test plans to the project’s context.

1.2.1 Test Stakeholders K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Test stakeholders are individuals or groups with a direct or indirect interest in the product’s quality. This is a typical, non-exhaustive list — test managers must conduct a stakeholder analysis when creating the test strategy and test plan, considering the test scope to identify the specific stakeholders for their project.

Stakeholder groupInterest in testing
Developers, dev leads, dev managersImplement the system under test and act on test results; also involved in unit testing and contribute to the testing process.
Testers, test leads, test managersPrepare testware, develop test plans, and contribute through requirements analysis, test design, execution, defect tracking/reporting, test automation, and progress reporting.
Project managers, product owners, business usersSpecify requirements, define required quality, recommend coverage based on perceived risks; review work products, participate in UAT, and decide based on test results.
Operations teamEngaged in operational acceptance testing; ensure production readiness and help define non-functional requirements.
Customers and usersCustomers purchase the product, users use it directly; both help define requirements and should be involved in UAT to confirm the product meets their needs.

1.2.2 Importance of Stakeholders’ Knowledge in Test Management K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

The stakeholder matrix (also called the power-interest matrix) guides test managers in prioritizing stakeholder engagement and managing expectations. It utilizes stakeholders’ expertise (end-users and technical teams give feedback on performance and security), supports risk management by highlighting interest and influence, and values diverse perspectives. It is composed of four quadrants:

Promoters — high influence, high interest

Key collaborators, vital for shaping the test strategy and plan.

Latents — high influence, low interest

Not strongly interested in day-to-day tasks, but their decisions are critical for resource allocation and high-level direction.

Defenders — low influence, high interest

Often provide qualitative feedback; keep engaged through regular updates and involvement in specific discussions.

Apathetics — low influence, low interest

Not closely involved, but updating them on significant milestones and seeking input on particular issues can yield unique insights.

The test manager compiles a detailed stakeholder list and understands each one’s connection to the testing activities, using the stakeholder matrix to make test management practices more effective.

1.2.3 Test Management in a Hybrid Software Development Model K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

A hybrid software development model integrates elements of both traditional sequential approaches and Agile practices to suit specific project needs or organizational transitions.

Hybrid as a transition to Agile

Moving from traditional to Agile methods can be challenging given fundamental changes in workflow, culture, and team dynamics; a hybrid model eases the transition by combining traditional structure with Agile flexibility.

Hybrid as fit for purpose

Some organizations or projects cannot move fully to Agile — high-risk projects may need sequential tasks for some things and Agile practices for others, so a hybrid model fits their purpose.

In a hybrid setting, test management activities may include:

Evaluating the team’s understanding and capability to transition seamlessly between traditional and Agile methodologies.

Identifying strengths and weaknesses in adapting to a hybrid approach.

Ensuring the team is adept at combining structured processes with Agile flexibility.

Enhancing collaboration between the test team and stakeholders to manage testing within sprints and traditional test phases.

Participating in coordinated efforts, such as a scrum-of-scrums for testers, to maintain testing focus while contributing to overall objectives.

Tracking and reviewing test efforts and cases within sprints to keep them aligned with Agile practices.

1.2.4 Test Management Activities for Various Software Development Lifecycle Models K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

To properly align testing within the SDLC model, a test manager must understand the various SDLC models used in their organization and use that knowledge to align testing with development activities.

AspectSequential (e.g., V-model)Iterative (e.g., Scrum)
EstimationEarly detailed estimation for each test level.Iterative estimation, part of story planning per iteration.
TestwareStrategy, plan, cases, schedule, and reports.Acceptance criteria and definition of done; minimal documentation.
RolesTest manager oversees decisions and team management.Roles integrated; facilitator or coach replaces the traditional test manager.
ToolsPredominantly test management tools suited for phase-based testing.CI/CD and automation tools are central, supporting continuous testing.
Testing approachScheduled in advance, corresponding to project phases.Embedded within iterations, focused on adaptability and feedback.
Test automation, monitoring & reportingImplemented strategically, can occur at various stages.Built in from inception, emphasizing automated regression in CI/CD.
MetricsMilestone-based reporting, with optional automated dashboards; traditional test metrics and defect management (e.g., test execution, defect rates).Continuous reporting with real-time dashboards and daily status updates; Agile metrics (e.g., team velocity, burndown charts) alongside traditional metrics.

1.2.5 Test Management Activities at Various Test Levels K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Component testing

Define scope, objectives, and completion criteria for component (unit) testing; involve testers in activities beyond traditional testing, such as code reviews; coordinate with development for issue resolution and unit test contribution.

Component integration testing

Determine integration sequences and test combinations with the development team, factoring in the SDLC model, tools, and processes; oversee progress against system and acceptance testing strategies; manage cooperatively with developers, including component (unit) integration testing.

System integration testing

Ensure scope and objectives are clear and attuned to risk assessment and quality targets; maintain oversight of progress, outcomes, and issue management.

System testing

Tailor planning to the SDLC model — resource allocation, tool selection, scheduling. In Agile, integrate system testing with iterative story testing rather than distinct phases, keeping testing continuous; in sequential models, testing may follow planned stages.

Acceptance testing

Collaborate with stakeholders to review and confirm acceptance criteria and plan testing, including managing UAT; coordinate acceptance testing logistics (e.g., at the customer’s site); facilitate resolution of UAT issues and guide stakeholders through sign-off once acceptance criteria are met.

1.2.6 Test Management Activities for Different Test Types K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Effective test management requires an integrated approach considering the unique demands of functional, non-functional, black-box, and white-box testing.

Functional testing management

Strategic planning & progress tracking: craft a test strategy aligned with functional requirements and project objectives, and monitor progress. Resource coordination: allocate human and technical resources to cover all functional aspects.

Non-functional testing management

Performance benchmarking: establish benchmarks and manage testing against them. Compliance verification: oversee tests ensuring the system meets non-functional standards such as security, usability, and reliability.

Black-box testing management

Test coverage analysis: ensure black-box tests cover all user scenarios and business requirements. Feedback incorporation: manage gathering stakeholder feedback to refine black-box approaches and defect fixing.

White-box testing management

Code coverage optimization: use code coverage tools to identify gaps and direct resources accordingly. Technical insight integration: incorporate technical insights into test planning so tests reflect the application’s internal workings.

1.2.7 Test Management Activities to Plan, Monitor, and Control K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

Effective test management is the cornerstone of any successful testing effort, requiring careful planning, vigilant monitoring, and strategic control tailored to the project’s unique demands.

Comprehensive scope definition

Craft the test plan with a thorough definition of scope, including all functional and non-functional requirements and both black-box and white-box implications, so test cases validate the system from all angles.

Risk assessment & mitigation plan

Undertake detailed risk analysis to pinpoint vulnerabilities and challenges affecting the project and product, then develop mitigation strategies to circumvent or minimize those risks.

Resource allocation strategy

Define team structure, roles, and communication protocols beyond mere allocation — especially significant for distributed (onsite/offsite) teams needing synchrony and seamless collaboration.

Execution oversight

Continually review test execution against the plan, track progress of test cases, and manage defects; adjust priorities based on risk assessments and real-time developments to stay focused on critical areas.

Tool & environment optimization

Select and use test tools and environments judiciously, continuously monitoring their integration within the CI/CD pipeline to support continuous testing and immediate feedback, vital for Agile.

Development collaboration

Maintain a close working relationship with the development team, leveraging both white-box and black-box perspectives to preemptively address potential issues.

Adaptive process management

Dynamically adjust the testing process in response to new insights, challenges, and evolving project dynamics, staying responsive and flexible.

Quality gate management

Take a structured approach to defining what constitutes a quality gate in the testing lifecycle and make informed decisions on progressing the testing phase, instrumental to maintaining product integrity.

1.3

Risk-Based Testing K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

Risk-based testing involves the identification, assessment, monitoring, and mitigation of risks to drive testing. Risks are identified by diverse stakeholders and used to select and prioritize tests: the higher the risk level, the earlier testing should begin, and the more intense and prolonged the test effort should be.

1.3.1 Testing as a Risk Mitigation Activity K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

A product risk is a potential situation where quality problems may exist in a product. When tests reveal defects, testing has helped mitigate product risk by exposing defects and opportunities to deal with them before release; when tests find no defects, testing indicates the product risk level is lower than expected. The test manager is responsible for delivering a correct and reliable evaluation of product quality, requiring active involvement in project risk management focused on quality-assurance-related project risks (e.g., ambiguous requirements causing major late-validation issues, insufficient test environments obstructing execution).

Risk-based testing follows the generic risk management process, whose main activities — logically sequential but able to overlap — are:

Risk analysis

Risk identification and risk assessment. To be most effective it should include diverse stakeholders; the test manager, a principal stakeholder, should understand, monitor, and be able to moderate these activities.

Risk control

Risk monitoring and risk mitigation. Test monitoring should include monitoring the evolution of known quality risks, analyzing new ones, and adjusting the risk register.

Note

Risk mitigation is distributed across several test activities: quality risk analysis results shape test planning (focusing testing on the right areas with the right techniques); risk levels guide test condition selection in test analysis; and risk-based prioritization governs execution sequence during test execution.

1.3.2 Identification of Quality Risks K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

The test manager gathers risks from stakeholders, who can identify quality risks through techniques such as:

Expert interviews

Independent assessments

Retrospectives

Risk workshops

Brainstorming

Checklists

Referring to past experience

Involving the broadest possible sample of stakeholders helps identify most significant product risks; it is essential the list of participating stakeholders is comprehensive and agreed with the project manager, since missing key stakeholders can be very problematic. If they cannot participate, they should at least delegate the task; a kick-off meeting can help determine whether key stakeholders are missing.

Risk is not uniformly distributed within test objects — for example, customer-facing components of a self-service application may carry very different usability risks than administration components — so identifying the individual risks of the various test items is an important test planning task.

Note

Risk identification often produces by-products that are not product risks — general questions or issues about the product/project, or problems in referenced documents such as requirements and design specifications. Project risks are also often identified as a by-product but are not the focus of risk-based testing. The test manager can highlight these by-products, making clear that quality is everyone’s concern; poor or missing requirements often indicate a more fundamental planning and preparation problem.

1.3.3 Quality Risk Assessment K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Once identified, risks can be assessed. Quality risk assessment categorizes risks by type (product or project risk) and by the quality characteristics impacted. Determining risk level involves assessing, for each risk item, risk likelihood and risk impact.

Factors influencing risk likelihood

Complexity of technology/tools/architecture; organizational maturity; personnel skills, availability, motivation, or autonomy (including SDLC knowledge); team conflict; supplier contractual problems; geographically distributed teams; weak managerial or technical leadership; time/resource/budget/management pressure; lack of early QA activities; high change rates of the test basis, product, or personnel.

Factors influencing risk impact

Frequency of use and criticality of the affected feature; criticality of the affected business goal; damage to reputation; loss of business income; potential financial, ecological, or social losses, or liability; civil or criminal legal sanctions; interfacing/integration issues; lack of reasonable workarounds; safety needs.

The test manager combines risk likelihood and risk impact to determine the risk level. With extensive, statistically valid risk data, a quantitative assessment is appropriate — likelihood as a percentage, impact as an amount, risk level as their product. More typically, likelihood and impact can only be ascertained qualitatively on ordinal scales (very high, high, medium, low, very low), combined through a risk matrix into an aggregate, relative risk level — based on stakeholders’ subjective perceptions unless extensive statistical data exists.

1.3.4 Quality Risk Mitigation Through Appropriate TestingK4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

Testing is the most important quality risk mitigation activity, reducing the likelihood of failures; other measures include contingency plans (e.g., workarounds), risk transfer to a third party (e.g., a component vendor), or risk acceptance. In test planning, effort should be proportional to risk level: higher risk starts earlier and uses more rigorous techniques, lower risk can start later with less rigorous techniques. To best mitigate overall risk, the test manager analyzes:

The test items

Different test items within a test object may carry different levels of the same risk type, so uniform rigor is not required.

The quality characteristics

Risks affecting specific quality characteristics should be mitigated by associated test types needing specific effort, environments, and skills.

The test levels and test types

Some risks are only testable dynamically at particular test levels; others by static testing (e.g., static analysis/code review for maintainability), or a combination (e.g., architecture review plus dynamic security testing of the integrated system). Testing every item as early as possible mitigates finding critical defects late, which raises internal failure costs and delays.

The SDLC

Test activities have their own entry criteria, fulfilled at different times by different SDLCs.

The test team

The most qualified people should test the items with the highest risk levels.

The regulatory requirements

Some safety-related standards (e.g., IEC 61508) prescribe test techniques and required coverage based on integrity level; the test manager must ensure they are followed.

Risk level should also influence quality control decisions: reviews of work products such as test cases, the level of independence of testing from development, and the extent of regression testing performed.

During test monitoring and control, risk-based testing supports reporting progress in terms of residual risk level at any point, helping stakeholders make release decisions — which requires reporting results in risk terms stakeholders can understand. During test implementation, prioritization is risk-based; during test execution, this ensures early coverage of the most critical areas.

Depth-first

Tests are prioritized in strict descending order of the risk levels they cover, starting with the highest — appropriate when mitigating the highest-level risks as early as possible matters most.

Breadth-first

At least one test per risk gets highest priority; all other tests are prioritized by risk level covered — appropriate when stakeholders want an early overall view of product quality. In practice, testing often starts depth-first, then switches to breadth-first as time runs short, testing all remaining risk items at least once.

Whichever approach is used, the time allocated for testing may run out before all planned tests are run. At that point, risk-based testing helps provide a justified recommendation to management on whether to extend testing or accept the remaining risk.

1.3.5 Techniques for Risk-Based Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Techniques for implementing risk-based testing vary in formality; suitability depends on project, process, and product considerations. There are two basic types — heavyweight, common in safety-critical systems, and lightweight, common elsewhere.

Heavyweight techniques

Formal, using defined procedures and detailed documentation, involving broad groups of stakeholders. Risk assessment uses detailed likelihood/impact factors and mathematical formulas. Examples: hazard analysis (identifies the hazards underlying each risk), cost of exposure (failure likelihood, cost of a typical loss, and cost of testing for it), FMEA and variants (identifies risks, causes, and likely effects, then assigns severity/priority/detection rates), and fault tree analysis (relates failures to the defects and errors that cause them, down to root causes).

Lightweight techniques

Less thorough, less effort from the test team and stakeholders, though still stakeholder-driven; risk factors are usually reduced to impact and likelihood on an ordinal scale. Some, like Systematic Software Testing (SST), need requirements specifications; others, like PRAM and PRISMA, use requirements/specifications as input but can also run entirely on stakeholder input.

1.3.6 Success Metrics and Difficulties Associated with Risk-Based Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

In a retrospective, the test team should measure how far it realized the benefits of risk-based testing, typically by answering questions such as:

Were the relevant stakeholders involved or represented in the risk analysis, and was that involvement appropriate?

If critical incidents in production indicate escaped critical defects, have they been resolved?

Were most high-priority defects found early in test execution?

Was the test team able to explain results to stakeholders in terms of risk, and did skipped tests carry lower risk than executed ones?

Successful risk-based testing usually answers all of these affirmatively; in the long term, process improvement goals for success metrics should be set, along with efforts to improve the efficiency of quality risk analysis itself. Managing risk also encounters recurring difficulties:

Difficulty assessing the risk level

Estimating impact and likelihood can be very hard. Solution: use historical data and ask key stakeholders for their assessment.

Keen beginnings

Setting up and maintaining a proper risk-based approach is often neglected under short-term pressure to succeed. Solution: regular monitoring and reporting of risk to stakeholders.

Déjà vu

The same risks are raised on every project, breeding complacency. Solution: involve the right people in risk identification and mitigate only the risks deemed important.

Key risks are missed

Usually caused by involving inexperienced or inappropriate people. Solution: involve appropriate people and train them.

Stakeholder churn

Stakeholders change over time and new risks appear, so risk analysis is an ongoing, iterative activity — not a one-time exercise at the start.

1.4

The Project Test Strategy K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

This syllabus takes the organizational test strategy as given — its development and maintenance is covered by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3 (as an “organizational test practice”) and by the ISTQB® Expert Level Test Management and Agile Test Leadership at Scale syllabi. If none exists, or it doesn’t cover the required aspects, test management must clarify the missing details with stakeholders.

A project test strategy (a “test strategy” in ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3) describes the approach to testing in a specific context — a project, release, product, or other initiative — so the organization’s objectives, particularly product quality and test activities, can be met; a strategy may also cover a single test level or test type. It is the main outcome of test planning, typically documented in a test plan or other document. Documentation is recommended but need not be a formal test plan — the need depends on the context of testing (Section 1.2). Sequential projects usually document the strategy, preferably in the test plan; contracts, agreements, regulatory bodies, or laws often also require documentation.

1.4.1 Choosing a Test Approach K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

The project test strategy guides all testing activities within a project, detailing objectives, resources, schedules, and responsibilities, tailored to the project’s unique requirements. Key decisions include selecting test levels, test types, and test techniques for static and dynamic testing and other practices (e.g., scripted testing, manual testing, back-to-back testing).

In theory, any test type can be performed at any test level, and any technique applied to any type at any level. In practice, the right selection and combination significantly affects testing’s effectiveness and efficiency — for example, code maintainability is often better evaluated with static code analysis or code review, performance efficiency by scripted system tests due to component interaction, and the usefulness of functionality by collaboratively developed manual acceptance tests with users. Choosing the best approach is a complex process, influenced by the organizational test strategy, project context, and other aspects.

1.4.2 Analyzing the Organizational Test Strategy, Project Context and Other Aspects K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

To choose the appropriate test approach, the following factors typically must be analyzed:

Domain

Domain-specific regulations, standards, and practices can change the rigor of testing and required documentation — e.g., pharmaceuticals emphasize intensive UAT focused on patient-health risks, while web-based insurance UAT might focus on usability and A/B-testing to increase new contracts.

Organizational goals & quality characteristics

Goals such as demonstrating testing’s value, increasing test automation, or improving test process maturity or defect-detection efficiency can determine required test levels and types.

Project goals and type

Budget/time/quality goals and project type (customer-specific vs. market-oriented) carry constraints, risks, and opportunities — e.g., tight budgets demand rigorous risk-based prioritization, while customer-specific products need tests covering contractual acceptance criteria.

Test resources

Constraints on tools, infrastructure, technology, environment, and staff skills must be considered — e.g., experience-based testing needs good domain knowledge, mobile apps need a limited device set, and tool licenses may be limited.

The SDLC model used

Determines appropriate test levels, effort, and entry/exit criteria; continuous integration needs more automated testing than one-off waterfall development, calling for different test types and techniques.

Interfaces with other systems

In a system of systems, aligning with other teams and selecting appropriate levels, especially for system integration testing, is essential — risk-based testing helps prioritize and scale it.

Availability of test data

Constraints such as anonymized production data, or hard-to-provide, hard-to-validate data (e.g., for AI testing) must be considered; model-based testing can support test data creation and management.

The test manager determines which combination of test techniques, test levels, and test types best satisfies the organizational test strategy, project context, and other constraints.

1.4.3 Definition of Test Objectives K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

A test plan should be defined for each test project, containing (among other things) test scope, test objectives, and exit criteria. It may be set up at release level as a project test plan (master test plan) and, if required, as a level test plan per test level; plans for different quality characteristics (e.g., security, performance) can also be defined. In Agile and hybrid projects, an iteration test plan can be agreed. For each release and iteration, the scope of functional features and non-functional characteristics to be delivered is defined and agreed with stakeholders.

Project test objectives and exit criteria can be defined using the S.M.A.R.T. goal methodology:

S — Specific

Clear and unambiguous.

M — Measurable

Quantifiable, with specific criteria for measuring progress.

A — Achievable

Feasible given available resources, timeframe, and capabilities.

R — Relevant

Aligned with overall project objectives.

T — Timely

A specific timeframe and defined deadline.

Test objectives should address all targeted aspects of quality and quantity that are measurable or evaluable. Examples include:

Reaching the specified exit criteria within the defined timeframe.

Meeting the organization’s quality goals (e.g., a KPI for customer claims about a product).

Complying with the industry’s rules and regulations.

Ensuring data is available to authorized users only (e.g., via access rights).

Checking functional completeness/correctness, performance, efficiency, portability, and security of data migration.

Enhancing the level of test automation (e.g., for regression or performance tests by a defined percentage).

Refactoring code successfully without introducing new defects, proven by a regression test.

Proving the security of interfaces (e.g., validating XML messages against their schema to reject malicious data).

Checking usability of a user interface (e.g., measuring time to complete a task in an online shop).

Beyond counting and measuring test objectives, the assessment of quality level by domain experts and stakeholders should also be considered. Depending on the project context, multiple test environments and resources or tools may be required and may not all be available at once — a factor to weigh when formulating achievable test objectives and exit criteria, alongside the other contextual factors from Section 1.2, The Context of Testing.

1.5

Improving the Test Process K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Testing often accounts for at least 30–40% of total project costs, and alongside the many technical challenges software projects face — growing complexity and size, new technologies, diverse devices and operating systems, security vulnerabilities — there is a constant need to improve test process effectiveness and efficiency. Learning from best practices and one’s own errors makes projects more successful. Improvement at the organizational level is typically more useful than at project or team level, but project/team-level improvement, tailored to that scope, is also possible and beneficial. A test improvement can be triggered by dissatisfaction with current results, unexpected defects, changing circumstances, a benchmark result, or a lack of communication. The techniques below apply to both sequential and Agile/incremental development models.

1.5.1 The Test Improvement Process (IDEAL) K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Once test process improvement is agreed upon, the implementation activities can be defined per the IDEAL model, based on ideas similar to the plan-do-check-act (PDCA) cycle. IDEAL stands for Initiating, Diagnosing, Establishing, Acting, and Learning. Though originally defined for the organizational level, it also applies at project or Agile team level — mainly with a much smaller initiating phase, and a lighter diagnosing/establishing step, while acting and learning remain relevant at any scope.

InitiatingStakeholders agree the objectives and scope of the process improvements.
→
DiagnosingAssess the current test process against a standard framework (model-based) or by analyzing metrics (analytical-based).
→
EstablishingList and prioritize detailed actions in a test process improvement plan, by ROI, risk, strategic alignment, or measurable benefit.
→
ActingImplement the plan — typically training and piloting changed processes, then full deployment.
→
LearningVerify which planned or unexpected benefits were received, and act on the lessons before the next improvement cycle.

1.5.2 Model-Based Test Process Improvement K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Model-based and analytical-based improvement share the premise that product quality is highly influenced by the quality of the processes used. Model-based improvement uses a test improvement model — based on testing best practices and organized in a stepwise manner. It can also be applied at project level, focusing on project-level test processes (e.g., test planning and design) and largely omitting organizational-level ones (e.g., test policy and organization), or by appropriately tailoring the organizational-level practices to the project’s context.

Test Maturity Model integration (TMMi®)

Composed of five maturity levels; each level except level 1 contains test process areas and improvement goals, plus practices, sub-practices, and examples to support implementation. Initially developed to complement CMMI®, now widely used independently. A specific guideline explains its beneficial use in Agile software development.

TPI NEXT®

Defines 16 key areas, each covering a specific aspect of the test process (e.g., test strategy, test metrics, test tools and environment), with four maturity levels defined for each. Specific checkpoints assess each key area at each maturity level; results are summarized and visualized in a maturity matrix covering all key areas.

1.5.3 Analytical-Based Test Process Improvement Approach K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Where model-based improvement compares a project or team’s test approach to external best practices, analytical approaches identify problems from the project or team’s own data, then derive improvements from that analysis — the two can be combined to verify results and add diversity. Data analysis is important for objective improvement and a valuable complement to purely qualitative assessments, which can otherwise yield imprecise, data-unsupported recommendations. Applying an analytical approach usually means a quantitative analysis of the test process to identify problem areas and set project-specific goals, requiring definition and measurement of key parameters.

Root cause analysis

Studies problems to identify their root causes rather than just their symptoms — e.g., selecting a set of defects, identifying clusters, and using cause-effect (Ishikawa/fishbone) diagrams to find root causes of important clusters, then deriving improvements to prevent recurrence.

Measures, metrics, and indicators

Used quantitatively to assess how well the test process is performed, typically across effectiveness, efficiency, and predictability, with one or more metrics selected per attribute to identify key areas needing improvement.

The GQM (Goal-Question-Metric) approach

A framework to define and analyze metrics tailored to stakeholders’ information needs: measurement goals define a quality aspect to measure, refined into questions from the stakeholder viewpoint, which select the metrics whose data answers the questions and satisfies those information needs.

1.5.4 Retrospectives K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

A retrospective is a meeting in which a team reviews its methods and collaboration, captures lessons learned (good and bad), and decides on changes and actions for improvement — covering process, people, organization, collaboration, and tools, for testing and non-testing issues alike. In sequential models, retrospectives are part of test completion, generating lessons learned for future projects; in Agile, they are generally held at the end of each iteration to incorporate improvements into the next one. They are performed by the entire team, supporting a whole-team approach, though dedicated retrospectives are sometimes needed for testing issues specifically.

IntroductionReview the goal and agenda; build an atmosphere of mutual trust for blame-free discussion.
→
Collect dataGather qualitative data (a timeline of key events, how people feel) and quantitative data (test progress, defect detection, effectiveness, efficiency, predictability).
→
Derive improvementsAnalyze the data to understand the situation and generate ideas — e.g., root cause analysis plus brainstorming for root-cause resolutions.
→
Decide on improvement actionsDerive and prioritize actions, define an improvement plan and responsibilities, and set goals/metrics to evaluate impact — without overloading on too many changes at once.
→
Close retrospectiveReview the retrospective itself for strengths and improvements — continuous improvement applies to the practice too.

Documenting results appropriately matters: in sequential models, findings, conclusions, and recommendations should be distributed and communicated understandably across the organization; in Agile, problems and actions should be documented to allow reviewing their impact in the next iteration. Testers, as part of the team, bring a unique perspective — raising testing-related problems and stimulating the team to think about possible improvements.

1.6

Test Tools K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

There are three types of business tools — commercial, open-source, and custom — and selecting one requires considering all organizational and stakeholder requirements and regulations. Technical tools such as test automation, test management, and many others also exist; examples of their use appear in the ISTQB® Foundation Level Syllabus V.4.

1.6.1 Good Practices for Tool Introduction K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

A test manager may be involved in introducing a tool or may foster or facilitate that process; test managers typically own a dedicated test tool, or any tool related to testing (e.g., requirements management, defect management, monitoring).

Evaluating and selecting a tool

Identify process-improvement opportunities the tool could support; understand the organization’s technologies and select a compatible tool; understand how it integrates technically and organizationally into the SDLC; evaluate it against clear requirements and objective criteria; evaluate the vendor (commercial) or support (open source); identify internal coaching/mentoring/training needs; weigh pros and cons of licensing models; finish with a proof-of-concept evaluation.

Adopting and rolling out a tool

Run a pilot project to validate selection criteria and see how the tool fits existing processes; adapt processes to the tool (and the tool to processes, if needed); define usage guidelines; provide training, coaching, and mentoring; roll out in increments; gather feedback from actual use for further improvement; define tool ownership.

1.6.2 Technical and Business Aspects for Tool Decisions K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Regulations and security

Organizations building safety- or mission-critical software, or subject to regulatory compliance, may prefer commercial tools, which more often meet required standards and hold appropriate certification.

Financial aspects

Open-source tools usually cost less initially thanks to community support; commercial tools may combine a purchase price with recurring license costs; a custom tool’s initial cost is hard to pin down. Training and maintenance costs over the tool’s lifetime must also be calculated — all tools can carry high maintenance and support costs.

Stakeholder requirements

Gathering requirements from all stakeholders is essential to evaluating and identifying the right tool; commercial and open-source tools may not fulfill every requirement in detail, making a custom tool the best choice where no other tool provides the needed functionality.

Existing landscape and tool strategy

The existing composition of tools and the associated tool strategy must be evaluated, given preferred or locked vendors, integrated systems with dependencies, or a full-service support model with specific regulations.

1.6.3 Selection Process Considerations and Return on Investment Evaluation K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

Test tools can be a long-term investment across many iterations or projects, so a prospective tool must be considered from several viewpoints: senior management needs a positive ROI; support and operations teams want a limited number of tools that aren’t costly or time-consuming to license and maintain; project leads need measurable value; users need usability (support for the task, learnability, operability); operational staff need maintainability. The tool owner ensures features are analyzed from each interested perspective — test management, (technical) test analysis, test automation, development — and that all these points are considered.

All tools introduced should ensure a positive ROI; the test manager (or, in Agile, the whole development team) is responsible for calculating and evaluating it. A cost-benefit analysis, covering both recurring and non-recurring costs, should precede acquiring or building a tool.

Cost categoryIncludes
Non-recurringDefining tool requirements; evaluating/selecting the tool and vendor and running a proof of concept; purchasing, adapting, or developing the tool; defining usage guidelines; initial training; integrating the tool into the existing landscape; procuring supporting hardware/software.
RecurringLicensing and support fees; maintenance costs; ongoing training costs; porting the tool to different environments.

Opportunity costs also count: time spent evaluating, administering, training on, and using the tool could otherwise go to test tasks, so more test resources may be needed before the tool delivers value.

ROI risks

Organizational immaturity leading to inefficient use; vendor maintenance-policy changes increasing workload; higher costs than expected; lower benefit than expected.

Potential benefits

Reduced manual repetitive work (e.g., regression testing); faster test cycle time through automation; lower execution costs from fewer manual activities; increased coverage for supported test types; fewer human errors; quicker access to information about tests.

Note

A test organization rarely uses a single tool — total ROI is usually a mix across all tools used for testing, which need to share information and work cooperatively. A long-term, comprehensive strategy for test tools covering risks, costs, and benefits is advisable.

1.6.4 Tool Lifecycle K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

A tool administrator must be appointed to define, carry out, and manage the activities of the tool’s four lifecycle stages:

AcquisitionA tool is selected and a tool owner assigned, who decides on naming conventions and where work products are stored — upfront decisions that shape eventual ROI.
→
Support & maintenanceThe tool owner is accountable for maintenance, usually carried out by an administrator or dedicated tools group; interoperability, data interchange, and backup/restore decisions are required.
→
EvolutionChanging environments, business needs, or vendor decisions require tool changes; the more complex the operating environment, the more disruptive a change can be.
→
RetirementThe tool is retired, usually replaced, with data preserved and/or archived — driven by a vendor decision or by a new tool’s benefits outweighing its costs and risks.

1.6.5 Tool Metrics K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Objective metrics from tools are designed and collected based on the needs of the test team and other stakeholders. Test tools mostly capture real-time data and reduce data collection effort, used to manage the overall test effort and identify areas for optimization. Different tools focus on different data:

Tool typeTypical metrics
Test management toolsAvailable test items, tests, planned tests, and current/passed execution status (passed, failed, skipped, blocked, planned).
Requirements management toolsTraceability of requirements coverage by passed and failed test cases.
Defect management toolsDefect status, severity, priority, and defect density; other data such as defect detection percentage and introduction/detection test level and lead time may need additional sources.
Static analysis toolsMetrics related to code complexity.
Performance testing toolsResponse times and failure rates under peak loads.
Code coverage toolsWhich parts of the test object have been exercised by testing.

Test tools should also monitor themselves — measuring the quality of the test process itself (e.g., defects found with and without tools, requirements coverage) and test efficiency (e.g., execution duration, number of tests executed). More detail on collecting and using metrics is in Section 2.1 of this syllabus, Test Metrics.

Chapter 1 in one screen

Key test management activities
Test planning, test monitoring and control, test completion — per ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-2, applicable at project, program, or portfolio level.
Test planning tasks
Understand context and organize planning; identify/analyze product risks; identify risk treatment approaches; define test approach and estimate/allocate resources; establish the test plan.
Test control vs. test monitoring
Control compares progress to plan and applies corrective actions; monitoring collects/records results and identifies deviations and new risks.
Test completion tasks
Create/approve the completion report, archive testware, handover testware, clean/restore the test environment, and perform/document lessons learned.
Test stakeholders
Developers, testers/test leads/test managers, project managers/product owners/business users, operations, customers and users — identified via stakeholder analysis.
Stakeholder matrix
Power-interest quadrants: Promoters (high/high), Latents (high influence/low interest), Defenders (low influence/high interest), Apathetics (low/low).
Hybrid SDLC
Combines sequential and Agile elements as a transition to Agile, or because it’s fit for purpose.
Risk-based testing
Identification, assessment, monitoring, and mitigation of risks driving test selection and prioritization; higher risk means earlier, more intense testing.
Risk analysis vs. risk control
Risk analysis = identification + assessment; risk control = monitoring + mitigation; sequential but overlapping.
Risk level factors
Risk likelihood (complexity, maturity, personnel, pressure, etc.) combined with risk impact (frequency/criticality of use, business criticality, damage, legal/safety needs).
Depth-first vs. breadth-first
Depth-first executes tests in strict descending risk order; breadth-first gives at least one test per risk top priority for an early overall quality view.
Risk-based testing technique weight
Heavyweight (hazard analysis, cost of exposure, FMEA, fault tree analysis) for safety-critical systems; lightweight (SST, PRAM, PRISMA) elsewhere.
Project test strategy
The approach to testing in a specific context, the main outcome of test planning; documentation need depends on the context of testing.
Test approach factors
Domain, organizational goals, project goals/type, test resources, SDLC model, interfaces with other systems, availability of test data.
S.M.A.R.T. goals
Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Timely — for defining test objectives and exit criteria.
IDEAL model
Initiating, Diagnosing, Establishing, Acting, Learning — a PDCA-like test process improvement cycle usable at organizational, project, or team level.
Model-based improvement
Compares the test process to an external model such as TMMi® (5 maturity levels) or TPI NEXT® (16 key areas, 4 maturity levels each).
Analytical-based improvement
Root cause analysis, measures/metrics/indicators, and the GQM approach — derived from the project’s own data.
Retrospective steps
Introduction, collect data, derive improvements, decide on improvement actions, close retrospective.
Tool introduction
Evaluate against clear criteria and a proof of concept; roll out via pilot, guidelines, training, incremental rollout, and defined ownership.
Tool decision factors
Regulations/security, financial aspects, stakeholder requirements, existing software landscape and tool strategy.
Tool ROI
Weighed against non-recurring costs (selection, purchase, training, integration), recurring costs (licenses, maintenance), and opportunity costs.
Tool lifecycle
Acquisition, support and maintenance, evolution, retirement — overseen by a tool administrator.
Tool metrics
Test management, requirements management, defect management, static analysis, performance, and code coverage tools each surface different metrics; tools should also monitor their own process impact.
