✦ Study Hub
Test Metrics Test Estimation Defect Management

CTAL-TM · Chapter 2

Managing the Product

The test manager tracks and steers testing through test metrics — for planning, monitoring/control and completion, and for building reports that empower stakeholder decisions — and through test estimation, choosing between metric-based and expert-based techniques for a given context. The chapter closes with defect management: the defect lifecycle and workflow, the cross-functional process and committee behind it, its Agile and hybrid-development variations, what a defect report should capture, and how that data feeds process improvement.

  • anomalyA condition that deviates from expectation.
  • defectAn imperfection or deficiency in a work product where it does not meet its requirements or specifications or impairs its intended use.Synonyms: bug, fault, flaw
  • defect reportDocumentation of the occurrence, nature, and status of a defect.Synonyms: bug report
  • defect workflowThe state transition model of a defect lifecycle, including responsibilities.
  • failureAn event in which a component or system does not meet its requirements within specified limits during its execution.Synonyms: malfunction
  • metricA measurement scale and the method used for measurement.
  • planning pokerA consensus-based estimation technique, mostly used to estimate effort or relative size of user stories in Agile software development. It is a variation of the Wideband Delphi method using a deck of cards with values representing the units in which the team estimates.
  • test estimationAn approximation related to various aspects of testing.
  • test objectiveThe purpose for testing.Synonyms: test goal
  • test progressThe progress of testing against a baseline.
  • three-point estimationAn expert-based technique, three estimations are made by the experts: the most optimistic estimation (a), the most likely estimation (m) and the most pessimistic estimation (b). The final estimate (E) is their weighted arithmetic mean.
  • Wideband DelphiAn expert-based test estimation technique that aims at making an accurate estimation using the collective wisdom of the team members.

2.1

Test Metrics

There’s a saying in management: “What gets measured, gets done.” What is not measured is easy to ignore. Test objectives answer why we test; test metrics are the indicators that tell us whether those objectives have been met. Metrics fall into three categories: project metrics measure progress against exit criteria (e.g. percentage of tests executed, passed, failed); product metrics measure product attributes such as how well the product meets user quality expectations; process metrics measure the capability of the testing process and the effectiveness of testing.

2.1.1 Metrics for Test Management Activities K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Test management must define a set of test metrics for test monitoring, test control and test completion as part of test planning. Each metric needs to be defined, measured, monitored and reported. Metrics used during monitoring and control track the progress of test activities; metrics used at completion assess whether test objectives were achieved — one or more metrics can combine into a test exit criterion.

MetricTest monitoring & controlTest completion
Requirements coverageXX
Product risk coverageXX
Code coverageX–
Actual vs. planned estimation (hours)X–
Executed test cases per status vs. plannedXX
Accumulated resolved vs. total defectsX–
Actual vs. planned automated test cases–X
Actual vs. planned cost of testingX–

Metrics marked in both columns are reported either in a test progress report (monitoring/control) or a test completion report, or both. There are also metrics for monitoring test effectiveness, such as defect detection percentage (DDP).

Formula

DDP = defects found by a level ÷ (defects found by that level + defects it could have detected that escaped to later phases)

This syllabus doesn't spell out the calculation — definition per Roman & Hamburg, Practical Software Test Analysis.

2.1.2 Monitoring, Control and Completion K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Test metrics indicate how far testing has progressed and whether exit criteria or related test tasks have been achieved.

Test monitoring

Collecting data about the test and evaluating/assessing it, to check fulfillment of exit criteria or associated test activities. Exit criteria derive from the test objectives.

Test control

Uses monitoring data to guide corrective actions — e.g. re-prioritizing tests when a risk becomes an issue, re-evaluating entry/exit criteria after rework, adjusting the schedule for an environment delay, adding resources.

Test completion

Collects data from completed test activities to consolidate lessons learned, testware and other information — at milestones such as a test level, iteration, project completion/cancellation, release, or maintenance release.

Common metrics for these activities cover progress against schedule and budget, current test item quality, and testing effectiveness against test or iteration objectives.

2.1.3 Test Reporting K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

For higher test levels (system, system integration, acceptance, security), the test basis is typically requirement specifications, use cases, user stories and product risks. Structural coverage metrics (e.g. statement or interface coverage) suit lower levels such as component and component integration testing. Even 100% structural coverage at those lower levels leaves defects and quality risks to address at higher levels. Metrics can be reported as a snapshot at a point in time or as a trend over time.

Product risk metrics

Percentage of risks with all tests passed; with some/all tests failed; not yet completely tested — assess test-basis quality and how well test cases cover product risks.

Defect metrics

Accumulated resolved vs. total defects; breakdowns by component, source, release, level/iteration of introduction-detection-removal, priority/severity, root cause, and status.

Test progress metrics

Execution status — planned, implemented, executed, passed, failed, blocked, skipped; test effort — actual vs. planned resource hours.

Coverage metrics

Requirements coverage, product risk coverage, and code coverage (statements, branches, paths or conditions executed).

Cost & effort metrics

Residual risk for untested components (impact/likelihood of undiscovered defects); actual vs. planned cost of testing.

Note

Combining metrics across categories is useful — e.g. correlating trends of open defects against executed tests, or relating requirement defect counts to test-basis quality. When execution continues and fewer defects surface, that trend (against agreed exit criteria) can justify ending testing.

2.2

Test Estimation

Project management has established best practices for estimating resources — cost, people, time. Test estimation applies these practices to the testing associated with a project or operation.

2.2.1 Estimating What Activities Testing Will Involve K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Effort

Usually person hours or story points needed to finish test tasks. Effort and duration (elapsed time) can differ — how many person hours will it take?

Time

A critical, constrained resource. Test planning estimates effort in calendar and working days against project milestones and deadlines — how long will it take?

Cost

The project budget: test resources, tools and infrastructure — what will the test project cost?

To estimate, first identify the test levels, activities and tasks, then divide the project into its main test activities within the test process. In Agile projects, testing is often estimated within development work rather than separately. Next, estimate the effort to finish the tasks or work products and their expected cost.

Key distinction

Testing is a sub-activity of a project and is bound by the same natural constraints — the time-cost-quality triangle: three interdependent values that cannot be manipulated arbitrarily without affecting one another.

2.2.2 Factors Which May Influence Test Effort K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Test effort estimation predicts the work needed to meet test objectives for a project, release or iteration. Influencing factors fall into five characteristic groups:

Product

Quality of the test basis; size of the test object; complexity of the product domain; requirements for quality characteristics such as security or reliability.

Development process

Stability and maturity of development processes; the development model in use (Agile, sequential, hybrid); availability of automation, tools and environments.

People

People satisfaction (holidays, benefits); skills and experience, especially with similar projects and products — the most necessary resource, so instability matters.

Test results

Number and severity of defects found during execution; the amount of rework required. Historical statistics support more accurate estimates.

Test context

Distribution across subsidiaries, team composition/location, project complexity (e.g. multiple sub-systems); the type of work (virtual or on-site).

2.2.3 Selection of Test Estimation Techniques K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

Estimated cost, effort and especially execution duration matter most to test management because they affect the project, yet execution estimates are hard to generate when overall software quality is low or unknown. A common practice is estimating the number of test cases derived from the test basis. Techniques or approaches are categorized as metric-based or expert-based; assumptions made should always be documented.

Selection factorWhat it means
Estimation errorSome techniques calculate a standard deviation as a measure of uncertainty — e.g. three-point estimation, from optimistic/likely/pessimistic values.
Data availabilitySome techniques need historical data from similar projects — e.g. estimation based on ratios and extrapolation.
Expert availabilitySome rely on the judgment of experts or team members — e.g. the Delphi method and planning poker.
Knowledge in modelingSome require mathematical models or formulas — e.g. extrapolation and three-point estimation.
Time constraintsSome take more time and effort than others — e.g. planning poker is quick, extrapolation can be slower.

Selection criteria are highly dependent on the context of testing (SDLC, stakeholders, test levels and types). The test manager coordinates and applies estimation techniques across different SDLC models within one project.

Formula

E = (a + 4m + b) ÷ 6 — three-point estimation's final estimate (E) as a weighted arithmetic mean of the optimistic (a), most likely (m), and pessimistic (b) expert estimates.

The syllabus names the three inputs and calls E their “weighted arithmetic mean” without spelling out the weights; this is the standard PERT (Program Evaluation and Review Technique) weighting used for that calculation.

Example

Determine topic complexity first: low complexity favors metric-based techniques, high complexity favors expert-based ones. A sequential development model favors the Wideband Delphi technique; an Agile development model favors planning poker.

2.3

Defect Management

Defect management covers the activities that begin once actual results are observed to differ from expected results (also called incident or anomaly management, since the cause may not yet be known to be a defect). It gives the test team and stakeholders insight into project state throughout the SDLC, and decides which defects get fixed so effort targets the right ones. Collecting and analyzing defect data over time helps locate improvement areas for testing and other SDLC processes.

2.3.1 Defect Lifecycle K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Each SDLC phase should detect and remove potential defects; the earlier a defect is caught, the lower the overall cost of quality — ideally within the same phase it was introduced (perfect phase containment). During dynamic testing, a defect reveals itself as a failure — a discrepancy between actual and expected results, i.e. an anomaly. An observed anomaly typically triggers a defect report, though not every failed test does (e.g. in test-driven development, tests are expected to fail until the component is complete).

1OPENInitial state when the defect report is created (may be called NEW).
→
2IN PROGRESSThe team analyzes and/or fixes the defect — or diverts to REJECTED.
→
3RESOLVEDA confirmation test checks whether the fix resolved the defect (may be called FIXED).
→
4CLOSEDTerminal state, reached after a successful confirmation test or to acknowledge a rejection.

A basic workflow is often extended with further states relevant to context (e.g. RE-OPENED, ACCEPTED, CLARIFICATION, DEFERRED); it is typically simpler in Agile software development than in sequential models, and should always be adapted to context. Good practice guidelines for designing a defect workflow:

One workflow, org-wide

Define it organization-wide where possible, for unified defect management across projects.

Separate duplicate/false-positive state

Represent these with their own state or a REJECTED reason — useful data for further process improvement analysis.

One terminal state

Use a single state such as CLOSED; require a closure reason, useful for process assessment.

Consistent state names

Reuse the same state names as for other entities (user stories, test tasks) to simplify working across them.

Different roles per consecutive state

Consecutive states should usually belong to different responsible roles, unless there's a good reason (e.g. to measure time in a state).

More than one outgoing transition

Every non-terminal state should offer the responsible role a decision on the next step, with justified exceptions.

2.3.2 Cross-functional Defect Management K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Though the test organization and test manager often own the overall defect management process and tool, a cross-functional defect management committee is generally responsible for managing defects on a project — often including the test manager, development, suppliers, project management, and product management/owner. As anomalies are entered into the tool, the committee decides whether each report is a valid defect and whether it should be fixed (by which party), rejected, or deferred, weighing benefits, risks and costs — often in a triage meeting. If fixed, the team sets its priority relative to other tasks; the test manager and team provide objective input on relative importance. On very large projects a full-time defect manager, possibly shared across projects, may be justified. Neither the tool nor the committee substitutes for the other — both, plus good communication and a well-defined workflow, are necessary.

2.3.3 Specifics of Defect Management in Agile Teams K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Defect management in Agile software development is often lighter-weight than in sequential models; co-located, well-communicating teams may exchange defect information informally. Defect reports should still be created when a defect:

Blocks current sprint activities

And could not be fixed immediately within the Agile team.

Cannot be resolved within the iteration

Some teams create a report if a defect can't be resolved the same day it was found.

Needs another team

Must be resolved by or in cooperation with other teams in multi-team organizations.

Is a supplier's responsibility

Must be solved by a supplier.

Is explicitly requested

E.g. when a developer can't work on a fix immediately.

Defects unresolved within the iteration commonly go to the product backlog for later prioritization. The level of formality — triggers for reports, attributes captured — is often left to team agreement, reflecting co-location, time-zone distribution, number of cooperating teams, team maturity and size, product risk, and regulatory/contractual requirements. The team's final decisions should always be documented.

2.3.4 Defect Management Challenges in Hybrid Software Development K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Multiple teams often collaborate on delivery — e.g. an Agile customer with a sequential-model supplier, or vice versa. This multi-team environment poses several challenges:

Tool & attribute alignment

Ideally all teams share one defect management tool; in practice, different tools are common, so synchronizing them (preferably automatically) matters.

Prioritization

Product owner(s) should join defect management meetings; Agile-paced projects need more frequent (though shorter) meetings, sometimes with a smaller stakeholder group holding final say.

Plan alignment & transparency

All teams' work, including defect fixes, must align to the same project plan — improved by shared participation in planning and shared visibility (dashboards, product backlog).

2.3.5 Defect Report Information K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Defect report information should support: managing the report through its lifecycle, assessing overall project status (especially product quality and test progress), assessing a product increment's quality, and assessing process capability. Because every additional attribute costs reporting time and can add confusion, the test manager should collect only what is needed for the given context and for process improvement.

Mandatory in most environments

Title, a detailed description (ideally with reproduction steps), severity, and priority.

Usually tool-generated

Unique ID, creation date/time, reporter, project/SDLC phase, current state, current owner, change history, and references (e.g. to test cases, related defects).

Further information groups by intended purpose:

To help resolution

The subsystem/component, test item and release, or the test environment where the anomaly was observed.

To assess project status

Risks, costs, opportunities, benefits of fixing (or not), available workarounds, affected requirements.

To assess increment quality

Defect type (per a taxonomy), the work product where it was introduced, and the affected quality characteristic.

To assess process capability

SDLC phase of introduction, detection and removal; defect root cause.

2.3.6 Defining Process Improvement Actions Using Defect Report Information K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Defect data, discussed during retrospectives, can drive process improvement. Examples include:

Phase containment / cost of quality

Using introduction/detection/removal phase data to improve per-phase detection effectiveness and minimize defect cost.

Defect prevention

Using introduction-phase data to target improvements where most defects are introduced.

Root cause analysis

Using root cause data to determine underlying causes and reduce total defects.

Defect clustering

Using defect location data to understand technical risk for risk-based testing and target refactoring.

Re-opened defects

Assessing the quality of debugging implementations.

Duplicate/rejected defects

Assessing the quality of defect report creation itself.

Watch out

Teams that skip tracking defects during some SDLC phases — often for efficiency — lose visibility into process capability, making these improvements hard to justify without reliable supporting data.

Chapter 2 in one screen

Test metrics
Project, product and process metrics measure whether test objectives are met; defined during test planning, applied in monitoring/control and completion.
Test monitoring, control, completion
Monitoring collects and evaluates progress data; control turns it into corrective action; completion consolidates lessons learned at milestones.
Test reporting
Structural coverage suits lower test levels; higher levels report against requirements, use cases, user stories and product risks. Metrics span risk, defect, progress, coverage and cost categories.
Test estimation
Estimates effort, time and cost, bound by the time-cost-quality triangle; metric-based or expert-based techniques.
Factors influencing test effort
Product, development process, people, test results, and test context.
Selecting an estimation technique
Weigh estimation error, data availability, expert availability, modeling knowledge and time constraints against the context — e.g. planning poker for Agile, Wideband Delphi for sequential.
Defect lifecycle
OPEN → IN PROGRESS → RESOLVED → CLOSED, with a REJECTED branch; workflow design should stay organization-wide, single-terminal-state, and role-aware.
Cross-functional defect management
A defect management committee (test manager, development, suppliers, product management) triages, prioritizes and decides fix/reject/defer.
Agile defect management
Lighter-weight; formal reports mainly for blocking, cross-iteration, cross-team, supplier, or explicitly requested defects.
Hybrid development challenges
Aligning tools/attributes, prioritizing across paces, and keeping plans and transparency aligned across teams.
Defect report information
Mandatory title/description/severity/priority plus tool-generated data, grouped by purpose: resolution, project status, increment quality, process capability.
Process improvement from defects
Phase containment, defect prevention, root cause analysis, clustering, re-opened and duplicate/rejected defect data all feed improvement — but only if defects are consistently tracked.

The Test Team Stakeholder Relationships

CTAL-TM · Chapter 3

Managing the Team

A test team's success rests on its people. This chapter looks at the four areas of competence a test team needs, how the test manager analyzes, assesses and develops the required skills, and the management skills — and motivating or demotivating factors — needed to lead the team itself. It closes with stakeholder relationships: quantifying cost of quality and using a cost-benefit calculation to make the case for testing's added value.

  • appraisalThe activities of measuring and monitoring the quality of a system.
  • cost of qualityThe total costs incurred on quality activities and defects, consisting of the costs of defect prevention, appraisal, internal failure, and external failure.
  • defectAn imperfection or deficiency in a work product where it does not meet its requirements or specifications or impairs its intended use.Synonyms: bug, fault, flaw
  • defect preventionThe measures that reduce the likelihood of recurrence of defects in work products and limit the propagation of defects in subsequent work products.
  • external failureA failure that occurs during the regular operation of a system after its delivery to the end users.
  • failureAn event in which a component or system does not meet its requirements within specified limits during its execution.Synonyms: malfunction
  • internal failureA failure that occurs during the operation of a system before its delivery to the end users.

3.1

The Test Team

Any team performing test tasks combines individuals with different competencies; some teams self-organize, others are recruited and developed by a test manager. The right skill mix is critical to completing testing tasks, and skills required can change over time — people outside the test team may also supply specific skills. This section covers analyzing and developing test team skills, the skills needed to lead or coach the team, and the factors that motivate or demotivate its members.

3.1.1 Typical Skills within Four Areas of Competence K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

A person's skills can be classified into four areas of competence. As the methodological, social and personal areas aren't specific to testing, ISTQB® focuses on developing professional competence — managing test tasks, analyzing the test basis, designing tests, identifying and analyzing risks, and developing/configuring/maintaining test data, environments and scripts.

Professional competence

Skills to perform specialized tasks — test techniques, technological and business/domain expertise, project management skills.

Methodological competence

General skills used independently to perform complex or novel tasks — analytical, conceptual, and judgmental skills.

Social competence

Communication, cooperation and conflict management in intra- and intercultural contexts, enabling shared and individual goals to be achieved — e.g. conflict resolution, teamwork, adaptability, assertiveness.

Personal competence

Ability and willingness to develop oneself, one's talent, motivation and attitudes — e.g. self-management, personal responsibility, resilience, confidence, discipline, openness to change, willingness to help and learn, ability to delegate.

3.1.2 Analyze Required Test Team Member Skills K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

Staffing — identifying the roles and skills a test strategy requires — is a test planning activity, needing a detailed context analysis to determine what a project requires.

Test activitySkills required
Test planningConceptual knowledge for developing a test strategy.
Test monitoring & controlProject management skills to manage all test tasks.
Test analysisAnalytical skills for the test basis and product risks.
Test designTest technique skills and conceptual knowledge for test environment design.
Test implementationJudgment for test selection; technical expertise for scripting and environment setup.
Test executionTechnical expertise for automation, exploratory testing, and evaluating results.
Test completionAbility to communicate outcomes and personal responsibility for decisions made.

Different test types and levels need different skills (e.g. domain expertise for functional suitability, technical expertise for maintainability). The project context also shapes required professional competence:

System domain

Business expertise in the application area — e.g. IT, automotive, gambling.

Architecture & technology

Technical expertise — e.g. programming languages, interface technology, security vulnerabilities.

SDLC

Knowledge of test levels, testing roles, and specific test techniques used.

Social competence lets team members relate appropriately to others and reach test objectives — communication, cooperation, conflict resolution — and demands may be higher in Agile or offsite testing than in document-centric sequential models. Personal competence affects effectiveness through self-management and discipline (higher in self-organized Agile teams), ability to delegate (needed by managers of hierarchical teams), and reliability/resilience, especially under time pressure.

3.1.3 Assessing Test Team Member Skills K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Since test teams often form from existing staff, test management assesses their existing skills against required skills, often via a skills matrix. Models such as Belbin's Team Roles, DISG, or PCM help teams recognize what skills they have and lack — Belbin holds that teams work best with a mix of personality and role types.

Professional and methodological competence can be assessed by having team members demonstrate typical test tasks:

Strategy & review

Outlining a test strategy and discussing feedback; reviewing the test basis and communicating findings (which can also reveal communication skills).

Technique application

Determining and applying appropriate test techniques for a given project context and objectives.

Reporting

Writing a test completion report including an assessment of the test results.

External evidence

Certifications, credentials, work experience, and degrees.

Agile teams often identify skills through regular retrospectives and feedback; experienced coaches or mentors help resolve knowledge gaps.

3.1.4 Developing Test Team Member Skills K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

A test team rarely has every required skill at project start; a strong team balances individual strengths and weaknesses. Comparing required against available skills in a skills matrix identifies development needs and the approach to take:

Training and education

Predefined knowledge and practices, usually in a (virtual) classroom — courses, in-house sessions, custom training, live e-learning.

Self-study

Learning alone rather than in a classroom — books, recorded videos, internet research.

Peer learning

Colleagues sharing knowledge, ideas and experiences, learning with and from each other.

Mentoring or coaching

Individual guidance from a coach, or knowledge/skills/experience from an experienced mentor acting as an ongoing resource.

Training on the job

A mixture of self-study, peer learning and mentoring/coaching applied in the flow of work.

Note

Self-study and training suit developing professional and methodological competence (e.g. ISTQB® training sessions or self-study on the syllabi). Social and personal competence develop better through training and coaching — social exchange, feedback and reflection are key success factors there.

3.1.5 Management Skills Required to Manage a Test Team K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Leading a test team needs professional and methodological competence in fundamental management activities (planning, monitoring, controlling, reporting) plus specific test management knowledge (test approaches, strategy development, technique and SDLC use). Social and personal competence — resilience, delegation, being accepted by the team, asserting test interests, promoting testing's benefits, resolving conflict with stakeholders — are essential success factors. Acquiring people for the team also needs skill in analyzing social, team and working conditions, so the team fits (or working conditions adapt to) it. Test teams undergo dynamic development, requiring situational skills matched to the Tuckman model:

1FormingWillingness to help members join the test team.
→
2StormingThe ability to resolve conflicts within the team.
→
3NormingDiscipline and target-oriented leadership to secure agreed values and rules.
→
4PerformingThe ability to delegate, giving the team personal responsibility.
→
5AdjourningThe ability to act with appreciation and confidence toward departing members.

3.1.6 Motivating or Demotivating Factors for a Test Team in Certain Situations K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Satisfied, motivated team members raise productivity and performance — and enable informal cross-training and self-managed workloads, freeing test management to handle external issues. The motivation-hygiene theory distinguishes two factor types:

Motivators

Perceived consciously, driving growth and satisfaction — recognition and appreciation, increased responsibility and autonomy, interesting/meaningful/challenging tasks, and professional advancement.

Hygiene factors

Usually taken for granted; meeting them doesn't add satisfaction, but their absence demotivates — fair remuneration, appreciative management style, pleasant working conditions, safety, and good interpersonal relationships.

Test management should continuously eliminate demotivating factors while creating and strengthening motivating ones.

3.2

Stakeholder Relationships

Test management must optimize testing to deliver business value: excessive testing causes unreasonable delay and cost, insufficient testing risks delivering low quality. The test manager helps stakeholders understand this balance and the added value of testing in achieving it, within the project's time constraints.

3.2.1 Cost of Quality K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Testing's benefits are offset by quality costs. Cost of quality quantifies total quality-related effort and defect costs across four categories:

Defect prevention costs

Planned, proactive activities — e.g. developer training in maintainable/secure code, reviewing the test basis early, good team communication.

Appraisal costs

Activities aimed at detecting defects — static and dynamic testing, reviewing work products.

Internal failure costs

Reactive activities before release — fixing defects found in testing, providing workarounds.

External failure costs

Non-value-added reactive activities after release — lost revenue/assets/health/life, legal costs, fixing field defects flagged by customers.

Appraisal and internal failure costs together are usually significantly less than external failure costs — making a strong case for testing's value. Determining costs in these four categories lets test managers build a convincing business case.

Key distinction

The ISTQB® syllabi support two cost-of-quality approaches: this syllabus follows Feigenbaum's approach, treating quality as a customer-oriented, company-wide process; the Foundation Level syllabus presents Boehm's approach, which focuses on the trade-off between prevention cost and failure cost.

3.2.2 Cost-benefit Relationship of Testing K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Most organizations sense testing is valuable, but few managers can quantify or articulate that value — often because they focus on operational testing details rather than the tactical and strategic issues other stakeholders care about. Testing delivers benefits both qualitatively and quantitatively:

Qualitative benefits

Improved reputation for quality, smoother and more predictable releases, increased confidence, protection from legal liability, reduced risk of loss of missions or lives.

Quantitative benefits

Defects found, prevented, or fixed before release; known-but-undocumented defects tracked; cost benefits; reduced risk level from running tests; information on project, process and product status.

Testing gives stakeholders the information to decide whether product quality is sufficient to go live, with or without known defects — a call that depends heavily on a defect's probability of occurrence and severity.

FormulaDefinition
Average savings per defectAverage external failure costs − (average appraisal costs + average internal failure costs)
Total cost of qualityDefect prevention costs + (appraisal costs × defects found before release) + (internal failure cost × defects found before release) + (external failure costs × defects found after release)
Example

With defect prevention costs $180, average appraisal cost $500/defect, average internal failure cost $200/defect, and average external failure cost $4,000/defect: average savings per defect = $4,000 − ($500 + $200) = $3,300.

Boehm's curve shows the cost of fixing a defect rising the later it's found in the SDLC — supporting earlier testing to reduce fix cost. The test manager should find the optimal balance between prevention cost and internal/external failure cost: too much testing costs more than the risk reduction it buys; too little risks costlier missed defects than the omitted tests would have cost. Risk-based testing supports this balance by investing test effort proportional to risk level and prioritizing tests by risk. Test managers should understand which benefits and costs apply to their organization, project or operation, and communicate testing's added value in these terms.

Chapter 3 in one screen

Four areas of competence
Professional, methodological, social, and personal — ISTQB® focuses on professional competence as testing-specific.
Analyzing required skills
Staffing during test planning maps test activities and project context (domain, architecture/technology, SDLC) to required skills.
Assessing skills
A skills matrix compares required vs. available skills; models like Belbin, DISG, and PCM help; demonstrated tasks, credentials, and retrospectives reveal gaps.
Developing skills
Training/education and self-study suit professional/methodological competence; training and coaching suit social/personal competence.
Managing the team
Needs fundamental management skills plus social/personal competence, matched situationally to the Tuckman stages: forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning.
Motivators vs. hygiene factors
Motivators (recognition, autonomy, challenge, advancement) drive satisfaction; hygiene factors (pay, management style, conditions, safety, relationships) demotivate only when absent.
Cost of quality
Four categories — defect prevention, appraisal, internal failure, external failure — quantify testing's value; this syllabus follows Feigenbaum's approach.
Cost-benefit of testing
Qualitative and quantitative benefits; average savings and total cost-of-quality formulas quantify value; Boehm's curve and risk-based testing guide the optimal test effort level.

Introduction Risk-Based Testing Tasks

CTAL-TTA · Chapter 1

The Technical Test Analyst’s Tasks in Risk-Based Testing

The Test Manager owns the risk-based testing strategy; the Technical Test Analyst works within that framework and contributes technical knowledge of product risks (security, reliability, performance) and of project risks tied to test environments. This chapter covers the three risk-based tasks — risk identification, risk assessment and risk mitigation — and the generic project and product risk factors the Technical Test Analyst typically considers.

  • product riskA risk that impacts the quality of a product.
  • project riskA risk that impacts project success.
  • risk assessmentThe process to examine identified risks and determine the risk level.
  • risk identificationThe process of finding, recognizing and describing risks.
  • risk mitigationThe process through which decisions are reached and protective measures are implemented for reducing or maintaining risks to specified levels.
  • risk-based testingTesting in which the management, selection, prioritization, and use of testing activities and resources are based on corresponding risk types and risk levels.

1.1

Introduction

The Test Manager has overall responsibility for establishing and managing a risk-based testing strategy. The Test Manager will usually request the involvement of the Technical Test Analyst to ensure the risk-based approach is implemented correctly.

Technical product risks

Technical Test Analysts work within the risk-based testing framework established by the Test Manager for the project. They contribute their knowledge of the technical product risks inherent in the project, such as risks related to security, system reliability and performance.

Project risks for test environments

They should also contribute to the identification and treatment of project risks associated with test environments, such as the acquisition and set-up of test environments for performance, reliability, and security testing.

1.2

Risk-based Testing Tasks K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

Technical Test Analysts are actively involved in the following risk-based testing tasks:

1.2.1Risk identification
→
1.2.2Risk assessment
→
1.2.3Risk mitigation

These tasks are performed iteratively throughout the project to deal with emerging risks and changing priorities, and to regularly evaluate and communicate risk status.

1.2.1 Risk Identification

By calling on the broadest possible sample of stakeholders, the risk identification process is most likely to detect the largest possible number of significant risks. Because Technical Test Analysts possess unique technical skills, they are particularly well-suited for conducting expert interviews, brainstorming with co-workers, and analyzing their experiences to determine where the likely areas of product risk lie.

In particular, Technical Test Analysts work closely with other stakeholders, such as developers, architects, operations engineers, product owners, local support offices, technical experts, and service desk technicians, to determine areas of technical risk impacting the product and project. Involving other stakeholders ensures that all views are considered and is typically facilitated by Test Managers.

Note

Risks that might be identified by the Technical Test Analyst are typically based on the [ISO 25010] product quality characteristics listed in Chapter 4 of this syllabus.

1.2.2 Risk Assessment K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

While risk identification is about identifying as many pertinent risks as possible, risk assessment is the study of those identified risks to categorize each risk and determine the likelihood and impact associated with it.

The likelihood of a product risk is usually interpreted as the probability of the occurrence of the failure in the system under test. The Technical Test Analyst contributes to understanding the probability of each technical product risk, whereas the Test Analyst contributes to understanding the potential business impact of the problem should it occur.

Project risks that become issues can impact the overall success of the project. Typically, the following generic project risk factors need to be considered:

Conflict between stakeholders regarding technical requirements

Communication problems resulting from the geographical distribution of the development organization

Tools and technology (including relevant skills)

Time, resource, and management pressure

Lack of earlier quality assurance

High change rates of technical requirements

Product risks that become issues may result in higher numbers of defects. Typically, the following generic product risk factors need to be considered:

  • Complexity of technology
  • Code complexity
  • Amount of change in the source code (insertions, deletions, modifications)
  • Large number of defects found relating to technical quality characteristics (defect history)
  • Technical interface and integration issues
Who decides

Given the available risk information, the Technical Test Analyst proposes an initial risk likelihood according to the guidelines established by the Test Manager. The initial value may be modified by the Test Manager when all stakeholder views have been considered. The risk impact is normally determined by the Test Analyst.

1.2.3 Risk Mitigation

During the project, Technical Test Analysts influence how testing responds to the identified risks. This generally involves the following:

Design

Designing test cases for those risks addressing high risk areas and helping to evaluate the residual risk.

Execute and act

Reducing risk by executing the designed test cases and by putting into action appropriate mitigation and contingency measures as stated in the test plan.

Re-evaluate

Evaluating risks based on additional information gathered as the project unfolds, and using that information to implement mitigation measures aimed at decreasing the likelihood of those risks.

The Technical Test Analyst will often cooperate with specialists in areas such as security and performance to define risk mitigation measures and elements of the test strategy. Additional information can be obtained from ISTQB® Specialist syllabi, such as the Security Testing syllabus [CT_SEC] and the Performance Testing syllabus [CT_PT].

Chapter 1 in one screen

Technical Test Analyst’s role
Works within the Test Manager’s risk-based framework; contributes knowledge of technical product risks (security, reliability, performance) and project risks around test environments.
Three tasks
Risk identification, risk assessment, risk mitigation — performed iteratively throughout the project.
Risk identification
Broadest possible stakeholder sample; expert interviews, brainstorming, analysis of experience; risks typically based on ISO 25010 quality characteristics.
Risk assessment
Categorize risks and determine likelihood and impact. The Technical Test Analyst proposes the initial likelihood; the Test Manager may modify it; the Test Analyst normally determines the impact.
Project risk factors
Stakeholder conflict on technical requirements; distributed development communication; tools, technology and skills; time, resource and management pressure; lack of earlier quality assurance; high change rate of technical requirements.
Product risk factors
Technology complexity; code complexity; amount of code change; defect history for technical quality characteristics; interface and integration issues.
Risk mitigation
Design test cases for high-risk areas and help evaluate residual risk; execute tests and apply mitigation and contingency measures from the test plan; re-evaluate risks as information arrives; cooperate with security and performance specialists.

Introduction Statement Testing Decision Testing MC/DC Testing Multiple Condition Basis Path (Removed) API Testing Selecting a Technique

CTAL-TTA · Chapter 2

White-Box Test Techniques

White-box test techniques apply to code and other structures with a control flow, such as business process flow charts. This chapter covers statement testing, decision testing, modified condition/decision testing, multiple condition testing and API testing — what each one measures, where it is applicable, and its limitations — and how to select a white-box technique for non-safety-related and safety-related systems.

  • API testingTesting performed by submitting requests to the test object using its application programming interface.
  • atomic conditionA condition that does not contain logical operators.
  • control flowThe sequence in which operations are performed by a business process, component or system.
  • decision testingA white-box test technique in which test cases are designed to execute decision outcomes.
  • modified condition/decision testingA white-box test technique in which test conditions are outcomes of atomic conditions that independently affect a decision outcome.Synonyms: condition determination testing, modified multiple condition testing, MC/DC testing
  • multiple condition testingA white-box test technique in which test conditions are outcome combinations of atomic conditions.Synonyms: branch condition combination testing, condition combination testing
  • safety integrity levelThe level of risk reduction provided by a safety function, related to the frequency and severity of perceived hazards.Abbreviation: SIL
  • statement testingA white-box test technique in which test conditions are based on executable source statements.
  • white-box test techniqueA test technique based on the internal structure of a component or system.Synonyms: white-box test design technique, structure-based test technique

2.1

Introduction

This chapter describes white-box test techniques. These techniques apply to code and other structures with a control flow, such as business process flow charts.

Each specific technique enables test cases to be derived systematically and focuses on a particular aspect of the structure. The test cases generated by the techniques satisfy coverage criteria which are set as an objective and are measured against. Achieving full coverage (i.e. 100%) does not mean that the entire set of tests is complete, but rather that the technique being used no longer suggests any useful further tests for the structure under consideration.

Test inputs are generated to ensure a test case exercises a particular part of the code (e.g., a statement or decision outcome). Determining the test inputs that will cause a particular part of the code to be exercised can be challenging, especially if the part of the code to be exercised is at the end of a long control flow sub-path with several decisions on it. The expected results are identified based on a source external to this structure, such as a requirements or design specification or another test basis.

The following techniques are considered in this syllabus:

SectionTechniqueFocus
2.2Statement testingExercises the executable statements in the code.
2.3Decision testingExercises the decision outcomes.
2.4Modified condition/decision testingChecks that each atomic condition independently affects the decision outcome.
2.5Multiple condition testingExercises combinations of atomic condition outcomes.
2.7API testingA type of testing performed through an application programming interface.

The Foundation Syllabus [CTFL] introduces statement testing and decision testing. Statement testing focuses on exercising the executable statements in the code, whereas decision testing exercises the decision outcomes.

The modified condition/decision and multiple condition techniques are based on decision predicates containing multiple conditions and find similar types of defects. No matter how complex a decision predicate may be, it will evaluate to either TRUE or FALSE, which will determine the path taken through the code. A defect is detected when the intended path is not taken because a decision predicate does not evaluate as expected.

Reference

Refer to [ISO 29119] for more details on the specification, and examples, of these techniques.

2.2

Statement Testing K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Statement testing exercises the executable statements in the code. Coverage is measured as the number of statements executed by the tests divided by the total number of executable statements in the test object, normally expressed as a percentage.

statement coverage = statements executed by the tests ÷ total executable statements in the test object × 100%

Applicability

Achieving full statement coverage should be considered as a minimum for all code being tested, although this is not always possible in practice.

Limitations/Difficulties

Achieving full statement coverage is not always possible in practice due to constraints on the available time and/or effort. Even high percentages of statement coverage may not detect certain defects in the code’s logic. In many cases achieving 100% statement coverage is not possible due to unreachable code. Although unreachable code is generally not considered good programming practice, it may occur, for instance, if a switch statement must have a default case, but all possible cases are handled explicitly.

2.3

Decision Testing K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Decision testing exercises the decision outcomes in the code. To do this, the test cases follow the control flows from a decision point:

IF statement

One control flow for the true outcome and one for the false outcome.

CASE statement

There may be several possible outcomes.

LOOP statement

One control flow for the true outcome of the loop condition and one for the false outcome.

Coverage is measured as the number of decision outcomes exercised by the tests divided by the total number of decision outcomes in the test object, normally expressed as a percentage. Note that a single test case may exercise several decision outcomes.

decision coverage = decision outcomes exercised by the tests ÷ total decision outcomes in the test object × 100%

Compared to the modified condition/decision and multiple condition techniques described below, decision testing considers the entire decision as a whole and evaluates only the TRUE and FALSE outcomes, regardless of the complexity of its internal structure.

Branch testing

Branch testing is often used interchangeably with decision testing, because covering all branches and covering all decision outcomes can be achieved with the same tests. Branch testing exercises the branches in the code, where a branch is normally considered to be an edge of the control flow graph. For programs with no decisions, the definition of decision coverage above results in a coverage of 0/0, which is undefined, no matter how many tests are run, while the single branch from entry to exit point (assuming one entry and exit point) will result in 100% branch coverage being achieved. To address this difference between the two measures, ISO 29119-4 requires at least one test to be run on code with no decisions to achieve 100% decision coverage, so making 100% decision coverage and 100% branch coverage equivalent for nearly all programs. Many test tools that provide coverage measures, including those used for testing safety-related systems, employ a similar approach.

Applicability

This level of coverage should be considered when the code being tested is important or even critical (see the tables in section 2.8.2 for safety-related systems). This technique can be used for code and for any model that involves decision points, like business process models.

Limitations/Difficulties

Decision testing does not consider the details of how a decision with multiple conditions is made and may fail to detect defects caused by combinations of the condition outcomes.

2.4

Modified Condition/Decision Testing K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

Compared to decision testing, which considers the entire decision as a whole and evaluates the TRUE and FALSE outcomes, modified condition/decision testing considers how a decision is structured when it includes multiple conditions (where a decision is composed of only one atomic condition, it is simply decision testing).

Each decision predicate is made up of one or more atomic conditions, each of which evaluates to a Boolean value. These are logically combined to determine the outcome of the decision. This technique checks that each of the atomic conditions independently and correctly affects the outcome of the overall decision.

This technique provides a stronger level of coverage than statement and decision coverage when there are decisions containing multiple conditions. Assuming N unique, mutually independent atomic conditions, MC/DC for a decision can usually be achieved by exercising the decision N + 1 times. Modified condition/decision testing requires pairs of tests that show a change of a single atomic condition outcome can independently affect the result of a decision. Note that a single test case may exercise several condition combinations and therefore it is not always necessary to run N+1 separate test cases to achieve MC/DC.

Applicability

This technique is used in the aerospace and automotive industries, and other industry sectors for safety-critical systems. It is used when testing software where a failure may cause a catastrophe. Modified condition/decision testing can be a reasonable middle ground between decision testing and multiple condition testing (due to the large number of combinations to test). It is more rigorous than decision testing but requires far fewer test conditions to be exercised than multiple condition testing when there are several atomic conditions in the decision.

Limitations/Difficulties

Achieving MC/DC may be complicated when there are multiple occurrences of the same variable in a decision with multiple conditions; when this occurs, the conditions may be “coupled”. Depending on the decision, it may not be possible to vary the value of one condition such that it alone causes the decision outcome to change. One approach to addressing this issue is to specify that only uncoupled atomic conditions are tested using modified condition/decision testing. The other approach is to analyze each decision in which coupling occurs.

Short-circuiting

Some compilers and/or interpreters are designed such that they exhibit short-circuiting behavior when evaluating a complex decision statement in the code. That is, the executing code may not evaluate an entire expression if the final outcome of the evaluation can be determined after evaluating only a portion of the expression. For example, if evaluating the decision “A and B”, there is no reason to evaluate B if A has already been evaluated as FALSE. No value of B can change the final result, so the code may save execution time by not evaluating B. Short-circuiting may affect the ability to attain MC/DC since some required tests may not be achievable. Usually, it is possible to configure the compiler to switch off the short-circuiting optimization for the testing, but this may not be allowed for safety-critical applications, where the tested code and the delivered code must be identical.

2.5

Multiple Condition Testing K3K3: ApplyThe candidate can carry out a procedure when confronted with a familiar task, or select the correct procedure and apply it to a given context.

In rare instances, it might be required to test all possible combinations of atomic conditions that a decision may contain. This level of testing is called multiple condition testing. Assuming N unique, mutually independent atomic conditions, full multiple condition coverage for a decision can be achieved by exercising it 2N times. Note that a single test case may exercise several condition combinations and therefore it is not always necessary to run 2N separate test cases to achieve 100% multiple condition coverage.

Coverage is measured as the number of exercised atomic condition combinations over all decisions in the test object, normally expressed as a percentage.

Applicability

This technique is used to test high risk software and embedded software which are expected to run reliably without crashing for long periods of time.

Limitations/Difficulties

Because the number of test cases can be derived directly from a truth table containing all the atomic conditions, this level of coverage can easily be determined. However, the sheer number of test cases required for multiple condition testing makes modified condition/decision testing more feasible for situations where there are several atomic conditions in a decision. If the compiler uses short-circuiting, the number of condition combinations that can be exercised will often be reduced, depending on the order and grouping of logical operations that are performed on the atomic conditions.

TechniqueTests needed for N atomic conditionsWhat is exercised
Decision testingIndependent of N: only the TRUE and FALSE outcomes of the whole decisionThe decision as a whole
Modified condition/decision testingusually N + 1Each atomic condition independently affecting the outcome
Multiple condition testing2NAll combinations of atomic conditions

2.6

Basis Path Testing (Removed from v4.0)

Removed

This section has been removed from version v4.0 of this syllabus. Learning objective TTA-2.6.1 has been removed from version v4.0 of this syllabus, so there is nothing to study here.

2.7

API Testing K2K2: UnderstandThe candidate can select the reasons or explanations for statements related to the topic, and can summarize, compare, classify, and give examples for the concept.

An application programming interface (API) is a defined interface that enables a program to call another software system, which provides it with a service, such as access to a remote resource. Typical services include web services, enterprise service buses, databases, mainframes, and Web UIs.

API testing is a type of testing rather than a technique. In certain respects, API testing is quite similar to testing a graphical user interface (GUI). The focus is on the evaluation of input values and returned data.

Negative testing

Negative testing is often crucial when dealing with APIs. Programmers that use APIs to access services external to their own code may try to use API interfaces in ways for which they were not intended. That means that robust error handling is essential to avoid incorrect operation.

Combinatorial testing

Combinatorial testing of many interfaces may be required because APIs are often used in conjunction with other APIs, and because a single interface may contain several parameters, where values of these may be combined in many ways.

Recovery and reliability

APIs frequently are loosely coupled, resulting in the very real possibility of lost transactions or timing glitches. This necessitates thorough testing of the recovery and retry mechanisms. An organization that provides an API interface must ensure that all services have a very high availability; this often requires strict reliability testing by the API publisher as well as infrastructure support.

Applicability

API testing is becoming more important for testing systems of systems as the individual systems become distributed or use remote processing as a way of off-loading some work to other processors. Examples include:

Operating systems calls

Service-oriented architectures (SOA)

Remote procedure calls (RPC)

Web services

Software containerization results in the division of a software program into several containers which communicate with each other using mechanisms such as those listed above. API testing should also target these interfaces.

Limitations/Difficulties

Testing an API directly usually requires a Technical Test Analyst to use specialized tools. Because there is typically no direct graphical interface associated with an API, tools may be required to setup the initial environment, marshal the data, invoke the API, and determine the result.

Coverage

API testing is a description of a type of testing; it does not denote any specific level of coverage. At a minimum, the API test should include making calls to the API with both realistic input values and unexpected inputs for checking exception handling. More thorough API tests may ensure that callable entities are exercised at least once, or all possible functions are called at least once.

Representational State Transfer is an architectural style. RESTful Web services allow requesting systems to access Web resources using a uniform set of stateless operations. Several coverage criteria exist for RESTful web APIs, the de-facto standard for software integration [Web-7]. They can be divided into two groups: input coverage criteria and output coverage criteria.

Input criteria (among others)

May require the execution of all possible API operations, the use of all possible API parameters, and the coverage of sequences of API operations.

Output criteria (among others)

May require the generation of all correct and erroneous status codes, and the generation of responses containing resources exhibiting all properties (or all property types).

Types of defects

The types of defects that can be found by testing APIs are quite disparate. Interface issues are common, as are data handling issues, timing problems, loss of transactions, duplication of transactions and issues in exception handling.

2.8

Selecting a White-Box Test Technique K4K4: AnalyzeThe candidate can separate information related to a procedure or technique into its constituent parts for better understanding, and can distinguish between facts and inferences — typically to analyze a document, software, or project situation and propose appropriate actions.

The selected white-box test technique is normally specified in terms of a required coverage level, which is achieved by applying the test technique. For instance, a requirement to achieve 100% statement coverage would typically lead to the use of statement testing. However black-box test techniques are normally applied first, coverage is then measured, and the white-box test technique only used if the required white-box coverage level has not been achieved. In some situations, white-box testing may be used less formally to provide an indication of where coverage may need to be increased (e.g., creating additional tests where white-box coverage levels are particularly low). Statement testing would normally be sufficient for such informal coverage measurement.

Specify only 100%

When specifying a required white-box coverage level it is good practice to only specify it at 100%. If lower levels of coverage are required, the parts of the code not exercised are typically the most difficult to test, and these parts are normally also the most complex and error-prone. So, by requesting and achieving for example 80% coverage, the code that includes the majority of the detectable defects may be left untested. For this reason, when white-box coverage criteria are specified in standards, they are nearly always specified at 100%. Strict definitions of coverage levels have sometimes made this impracticable; however, those given in ISO 29119-4 allow infeasible coverage items to be discounted from the calculations, thus making 100% coverage an achievable goal.

Specify a single criterion

When specifying the required white-box coverage for a test object, it is only necessary to specify this for a single coverage criterion (e.g., it is not necessary to require both 100% statement coverage and 100% MC/DC). With exit criteria at 100% it is possible to relate some exit criteria in a subsumes hierarchy, where coverage criteria are shown to subsume other coverage criteria.

Different levels for different parts

It is quite normal to define different levels for different parts of the system, because different parts of a system contribute differently to risk. For instance, in an avionics system, the subsystems associated with in-flight entertainment would be assigned a lower level of risk than those associated with flight control. Testing interfaces is common for all types of systems and is normally required for all integrity levels for safety-related systems (see section 2.8.2). The level of required coverage for API testing will normally increase based on the associated risk (e.g., the higher level of risk associated with a public interface may require more rigorous API testing).

Subsumes

One coverage criterion is said to subsume another if, for all components and their specifications, every set of test cases that satisfies the first criterion also satisfies the second. For example, branch coverage subsumes statement coverage because if branch coverage is achieved (to 100%), then 100% statement coverage is guaranteed.

Coverage criterionSubsumes (for the techniques in this syllabus)
Branch coverage and decision coverageStatement coverage
MC/DCDecision and branch coverage
Multiple condition coverageMC/DC

If we consider branch and decision coverage to be the same at 100%, then we can say that they subsume each other.

The selection of which white-box test technique to use is generally based on the nature of the test object and its perceived risks. If the test object is considered to be safety-related (i.e. failure could cause harm to people or the environment) then regulatory standards are applicable and will define required white-box coverage levels (see section 2.8.2). If the test object is not safety-related then the choice of which white-box coverage levels to achieve is more subjective, but should still be largely based on perceived risks, as described in section 2.8.1.

2.8.1 Non-Safety-Related Systems

The following factors (in no particular order of priority) are typically considered when selecting white-box test techniques for non-safety-related systems:

FactorWhy it matters
ContractIf the contract requires a particular level of coverage to be achieved, then not achieving this coverage level will potentially result in a breach of contract.
CustomerIf the customer requests a particular level of coverage, for instance as part of the test planning, then not achieving this coverage level may cause problems with the customer.
Regulatory standardFor some industry sectors (e.g., financial) a regulatory standard that defines required white-box coverage criteria applies for mission-critical systems. See section 2.8.2 for regulatory standards for safety-related systems.
Test strategyIf the organization’s test strategy specifies requirements for white-box code coverage, then not aligning with the organizational strategy may risk censure from higher management.
Coding styleIf the code is written with no multiple conditions within decisions, then it would be wasteful to require white-box coverage levels such as MC/DC and multiple condition coverage.
Historical defect informationIf historical data on the effectiveness of achieving a particular coverage level suggests that it would be appropriate to use for this test object, it would be risky to ignore the available data. Such data may be available within the project, organization or industry.
Skills and experienceIf the testers available to perform the testing are not sufficiently experienced and skilled in a particular white-box technique, it may be misunderstood and may introduce unnecessary risk if that technique was selected.
ToolsWhite-box coverage can only be measured in practice by using coverage tools. If such tools are not available that support a given coverage measure, then selecting that measure to be achieved would introduce a high risk level.

When selecting white-box testing for non-safety-related systems, the Technical Test Analyst has more freedom to recommend the appropriate white-box coverage than for safety-related systems. Such choices are typically a compromise between the perceived risks and the cost, resources and time required to treat these risks through white-box testing. In some situations, other treatments, which might be implemented by other software testing approaches or otherwise (e.g., different development approaches) may be more appropriate.

2.8.2 Safety-Related Systems

Where the software being tested is part of a safety-related system, then a regulatory standard which defines the required coverage levels to be achieved will normally have to be used. Such standards typically require a hazard analysis to be performed for the system and the resultant risks are used to assign integrity levels to different parts of the system. Levels of required coverage are defined for each of the integrity levels.

IEC 61508 (functional safety of programmable, electronic, safety-related systems [IEC 61508]) is an umbrella international standard used for such purposes. In theory, it could be used for any safety-related system; however, some industries have created specific variants (e.g., ISO 26262 [ISO 26262] applies to automotive systems) and some industries have created their own standards (e.g., DO-178C [DO-178C] for airborne software). Additional information regarding ISO 26262 is provided in the ISTQB® Automotive Software Tester syllabus [CT_AuT].

IEC 61508 defines four safety integrity levels (SILs), each of which is defined as a relative level of risk-reduction provided by a safety function, correlated to the frequency and severity of perceived hazards. When a test object performs a function related to safety, the higher the risk of failure means that the test object should have higher reliability. The following table shows the reliability levels associated with the SILs. Note that the reliability level for SIL 4 for the continuous operation case is extremely high, since it corresponds to a mean time between failures (MTBF) greater than 10,000 years.

IEC 61508 SILContinuous operation (probability of a dangerous failure per hour)On-demand (probability of failure on demand)
110−6 to <10−510−2 to <10−1
210−7 to <10−610−3 to <10−2
310−8 to <10−710−4 to <10−3
410−9 to <10−810−5 to <10−4

The recommendations for white-box coverage levels associated with each SIL are shown in the following table. Where an entry is shown as “Highly recommended”, in practice achieving that level of coverage is normally considered mandatory. In contrast, where an entry is only shown as “Recommended”, many practitioners consider this to be optional and avoid achieving it by providing a suitable rationale. Thus, a test object assigned to SIL 3 is normally tested to achieve 100% branch coverage (it achieves 100% statement coverage automatically, as shown by the subsumes ordering).

IEC 61508 SIL100% Statement coverage100% Branch coverage100% MC/DC
1RecommendedRecommendedRecommended
2Highly recommendedRecommendedRecommended
3Highly recommendedHighly recommendedRecommended
4Highly recommendedHighly recommendedHighly recommended
Note

The above SILs and requirements on coverage levels from IEC 61508 are different in ISO 26262, and different again in DO-178C.

Chapter 2 in one screen

Coverage and 100%
Full coverage means the technique suggests no further useful tests, not that testing is complete. Expected results come from a source external to the code structure.
Statement testing
Coverage = statements executed ÷ total executable statements. A minimum for all code, but may miss logic defects; unreachable code can make 100% impossible.
Decision testing
Coverage = decision outcomes exercised ÷ total decision outcomes. Considers the decision as a whole; may miss defects caused by combinations of condition outcomes. Branch and decision coverage are equivalent for nearly all programs.
MC/DC
Each atomic condition independently and correctly affects the decision outcome; usually N+1 tests for N conditions. Used in aerospace, automotive and other safety-critical sectors; hampered by coupled conditions and short-circuiting.
Multiple condition testing
All combinations of atomic conditions: 2N for N conditions. For high-risk and embedded software; the number of tests makes MC/DC more feasible for many conditions.
Basis path testing
Removed from syllabus v4.0 (TTA-2.6.1 removed).
API testing
A type of testing, not a technique, with no specific coverage level. Needs negative and combinatorial testing, recovery/retry and reliability testing, and usually specialized tools; finds interface, data handling, timing, lost/duplicated transaction and exception handling defects.
Subsumes hierarchy
Branch and decision subsume statement; MC/DC subsumes decision and branch; multiple condition subsumes MC/DC.
Selection, non-safety-related
Contract, customer, regulatory standard, test strategy, coding style, historical defect information, skills and experience, tools.
Selection, safety-related
A regulatory standard defines coverage by integrity level; IEC 61508 has four SILs, and SIL 3 normally needs 100% branch coverage (statement coverage follows automatically).
